The PANAS has no item stems, so item_text is the single adjective; no instruction text is shipped, because the paper describes the task without ever printing the instruction respondents were given.
- table: liu_2022_fragreading_cdq
  issue: |-
    The item text is the study's own Chinese wording, from the questionnaire in the PeerJ supplement, so it is what respondents actually read. What is inferred is which sentence goes with which item code: the questionnaire numbers its items 9.1-9.11 and the data columns are N9_1-N9_11, and that numbering is the only thing tying the two together. Checks against the live data confirm the reverse-item block (N9_6-N9_9) and the direction of the 1-5 anchors, but nothing distinguishes items within a block, so a swap of, say, N9_1 and N9_2 would not be detectable.
- table: liu_2022_fragreading_frq
  issue: |-
    Item text is shipped for all 22 items, including 8.6 and 8.10, which the study's own supplement marks as deleted after its confirmatory factor analysis. The IRW table carries all 22, so the wording is given for all 22; those two are also the weakest items in the data (item-rest correlations 0.204 and 0.272, against 0.375-0.613 for the other twenty), which is consistent with their counter-worded content.
- table: liu_2022_mice_skills
  issue: |-
    The item text here is the study's own English skill labels, taken verbatim from the header row of the deposited data file; the questionnaire was administered in Chinese and no Chinese wording is published in the paper or its supporting file. Note that each item code IS its label, so the item text adds no wording beyond the code. Only the end points of the 1-5 scale are labelled in the source (1 = very unimportant, 5 = very important); options 2-4 were never labelled and are left blank rather than filled in.
- table: liu_2023_adherence_tools
  issue: |-
    Item text is the administered Chinese, with the study authors' own English in the translated columns. Two things are transcribed exactly as the source has them rather than corrected: item 1 reads "MMS-8", which is the study's own typo for the MMAS-8 adherence scale, and the first response option ships the questionnaire's fuller wording rather than the abbreviated label stored in the data file. The authors' English renderings are much terser than their Chinese items throughout, and were kept as they wrote them.
- table: liu_2023_improve_adherence
  issue: |-
    For item 3 the data file's stored label is truncated, so the item text shipped is the fuller wording from the study's own administered Chinese questionnaire. The authors' published English for that item is much terser than the Chinese it translates — "Answering the patients' questions." against a Chinese item that also enumerates pathogenesis, harms, medication regimen and potential side effects — so the English and Chinese columns are not the same length of text here. That terseness is the authors' own, not an IRW abridgement.
- table: liu_2023_perceived_control
  issue: |-
    The three item codes PBC1-PBC3 are matched to the three Perceived Behavioral Control sentences in the paper's questionnaire annexure by listing order alone. The annexure attaches no code to any sentence, and no statistical route separates three positively worded items on one 1-5 scale, so a permutation within the construct cannot be ruled out. What is established is that these three sentences are the PBC block: that partition reproduces the paper's published Cronbach's alpha of 0.852. The item text is also the study's own English wording — the survey was administered in Chinese, which the deposit does not publish. One item is shipped with the source's own broken English unrepaired.
- table: liu_2023_purchase_intention
  issue: |-
    The survey was administered in Chinese to consumers of Hulunbuir agricultural products — the paper says its scales were translated and back-translated by the university's English department — but neither the article nor its supplements publish any Chinese wording, so the item text shown here is the authors' own English questionnaire rather than what respondents read. The three sentences also carry no item codes in that questionnaire. Their block is fixed: the partition reproduces all six of the paper's published Cronbach's alphas, 0.809 for this one. But which sentence is PI1, PI2 or PI3 follows the questionnaire's listing order and cannot be checked against the data, whose three items have means 3.72, 3.74 and 3.71 and SDs all 0.94-0.95. Only the two endpoints of the 1-5 scale are labelled in any source, so options 2, 3 and 4 carry no text.
- table: liu_2023_training_freq
  issue: |-
    Item text is the administered Chinese from the study's data file, with the authors' own English alongside. Two things to know about the response options and the English. The third of the five frequency levels ships the administered questionnaire's wording rather than the slightly different label stored in the data file. And the authors' English questionnaire prints these six items in a different order than both the data file and the Chinese questionnaire — its second and third items are swapped — so the English shipped here was matched to each Chinese item by content rather than by position.
- table: liu_2025_classroom_interaction
  issue: |-
    The questionnaire was administered in Chinese, but no Chinese wording appears anywhere in the article or its supplements, so the item text shown here is the authors' own English rendering (S1 Appendix) rather than what respondents read. Two of the eleven items are shipped in the fuller wording the S1 Appendix gives them, which differs slightly from the abbreviated column label used in the data workbook. Response options carry text at the two extremes only (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree); the paper labels no intermediate point.
- table: liu_2025_foreign_lang_enjoyment
  issue: |-
    The survey was administered in Chinese to 623 Chinese undergraduates — the paper says its English items were translated into Chinese and checked by a translation specialist — but neither the article nor its supplements publish any Chinese wording, so the item text shown here is the study's own English rather than what respondents read. Only the two endpoints of the 1-5 scale are labelled in any source, so options 2, 3 and 4 carry no text.

    Note that the article's prose disagrees with the study's own data about which items form which sub-scale. Section 2.2.4 assigns teacher appreciation to items 1-3 and personal enjoyment to items 4-6, but the data file and the S1 Appendix both put personal enjoyment at 1-3 and teacher appreciation at 4-6 — and the prose's own examples confirm the data rather than the prose, since "The teacher is friendly." is item 5 and "I've learnt interesting things." is item 2. The item codes here follow the data. Social enjoyment (items 7-9) is unaffected.
- table: liu_2025_learning_motivation
  issue: |-
    The questionnaire was administered in Chinese, and the Chinese item wording shown here is verbatim from the study's own data file, with the study's own English translation alongside. The English was matched to each Chinese item by content rather than by position, because the paper's S2 Appendix prints the sixteen items in a different order than the administered one. The response options are the exception to all of this: no Chinese anchor wording appears anywhere in the article, its appendix or the data file, so option_text carries the appendix's English endpoints (1 = Completely Disagree, 5 = Completely Agree) and options 2, 3 and 4 carry no text because no source labels them.
- table: liu_2025_nlgz
  issue: |-
    The questionnaire was administered in Chinese to middle-school students in Kaifeng, China, but neither the article nor its data deposit publishes any Chinese wording, so the item text shown here is the authors' own English rendering from their Dryad README rather than what respondents read. The five response points carry no text, because no source names an anchor for any of them; the README states only that higher numbers mean greater agreement.
- table: liu_2025_positive_cognition
  issue: |-
    The English item wording on this table was translated from the administered Chinese by IRW, not by the study's authors: no published English exists for the 12 items of this Chinese revision of the APNIS, whose original is paywalled. The Chinese in item_text is the study's own administered wording, verbatim from its data deposit, and the five response anchors are the study's own English.
- table: liu_2025_speaking_selfefficacy
  issue: |-
    The study administered these 14 items in Chinese translation, but the administered Chinese is not published anywhere in the deposit, so the wording shipped here is the authors' own English source version from the S1 Appendix rather than what respondents read. Only the 1 and 5 anchors of the five-point scale are labelled in any source.
- table: liu_2025_willingness_communicate
  issue: |-
    The questionnaire was administered in Chinese to 623 Chinese undergraduates — the paper says the English scale items were translated into Chinese and checked by a translation specialist — but neither the article nor its two supplements publish any Chinese wording, so the item text shown here is the authors' own English questionnaire rather than what respondents read. Only the two endpoints of the 1-5 scale are labelled in any source, so options 2, 3 and 4 carry no text.
- table: liu_2025_ydcy
  issue: |-
    The deposit's README describes this block as the Godin Leisure Time Exercise Questionnaire, but the data are the PARS-3: the file's own composite column equals YDCY2 x YDCY3 x YDCY4 exactly for all 879 respondents, while the README's Godin weighting reproduces 5 of 879. The item text shown here is therefore PARS-3 wording rather than the README's instrument.

    YDCY3 is the duration item, identifiable as the only one scored from 0. The 58 respondents who gave its lowest level ("under 10 minutes", stored as 0) were dropped as suspected data-entry errors when the response table was built, so YDCY3 carries 821 responses against 879 for the other items, and its lowest surviving value means "11 to 20 minutes". Those responses are valid PARS-3 duration scores and their removal is tracked as a data fix. Intensity and frequency (YDCY2, YDCY4) cannot be told apart from these data, because the composite is a product and so is symmetric in them; their assignment follows the canonical PARS-3 order. The survey was administered in Chinese and no Chinese wording is published anywhere in the deposit or the paper, so the English shown is a published English form of the same instrument rather than what respondents read.
- table: lorenz_2016_efficacy1
  issue: |-
    This study was run in German. The item text is the German General Self-Efficacy wording respondents read — three items verbatim from the paper's own S1 Appendix and the other seven from the scale authors' own page — with the instrument publisher's English alongside. The German and English versions of this scale are published in different item orders, so the English is a parallel version rather than a translation of the German sentence beside it. The study used a 6-point format instead of the scale's own 4-point one and publishes English labels only for its endpoints, so options 2 to 5 carry no text.

    Which self-efficacy item each of the codes efficacy1.1 to efficacy1.10 refers to is reconstructed rather than stated by the source. The reconstruction reproduces the paper's published confirmatory factor analysis exactly, but items whose published means are tied are not individually distinguished by it.
- table: lorenz_2016_hope
  issue: |-
    This study was run in German, but only half of its German wording was ever published. The paper's appendix prints the German for the three items that entered its CPC-12 analysis (hope1, hope4, hope5), and those ship as respondents read them with English alongside; for hope2, hope3 and hope6 no German appears in the paper or its supplements, so what is shown is the State Hope Scale's original English rather than the administered sentence. The study also used a 6-point format in place of the scale's original 8-point one and publishes English labels only for the two endpoints, so options 2 to 5 carry no text.

    Which State Hope Scale item each code refers to is reconstructed rather than stated by the source. hope1, hope3, hope4 and hope5 are each pinned individually by reproducing the paper's published factor loadings exactly, but hope2 and hope6 are both agency items outside that analysis and are not distinguished from one another.
- table: lorenz_2016_optimism2
  issue: |-
    This study was run in German. The item text is the German LOT-R wording respondents read, from the published German version the paper cites (Glaesmer et al. 2008), with the scale authors' own English alongside. The German and English LOT-R are parallel versions rather than sentence-for-sentence translations, so item 5 reads "I feel comfortable among my friends" in German where the English reads "I enjoy my friends a lot".

    Two things about the response values. The three pessimism items (optimism2.3, .7, .9) are stored **already reverse-coded**, so a 6 on those means the respondent chose "strongly disagree", and the option labels shipped for them run the opposite way from every other item. That was established from the data, not from any statement in the deposit: the six scored items as stored reproduce the paper's published alpha of .74, whereas recoding them as the LOT-R manual directs gives an alpha of -0.02. Separately, the study replaced the LOT-R's own 5-point format with a 6-point one and published English endpoint labels only, so options 2 to 5 carry no text.

    Which LOT-R item each code refers to is reconstructed. The reconstruction fixes the four filler items and the optimism/pessimism split and reproduces the paper's published factor analysis exactly, but optimism2.1 and optimism2.4 are not distinguished from each other, nor are the members of {optimism2.3, .7, .9} or of {optimism2.2, .6, .8}.
- table: lu_2017_gad7
  issue: |-
    The GAD-7 was administered in Chinese, but no Chinese wording is published in the paper or its two supplementary data files, so the item and option text shipped here is the instrument publisher's official English (phqscreeners.com) rather than the sentences respondents read.

    Note also that the response table covers the deposit's full 1296 respondents, more than the 1096 the paper reports analysing, and that it contains repeated id-item pairs. Those are not a doubled upload: they are a second wave of measurement for 129 respondents, and the responses differ across waves for many of them.
- table: lu_2017_phq9
  issue: |-
    The PHQ-9 was administered in Chinese, but no Chinese wording is published in the paper or its two supplementary data files, so the item and option text shipped here is the instrument publisher's official English (phqscreeners.com) rather than the sentences respondents read.

    Note also that the response table covers the deposit's full 1296 respondents, more than the 1096 the paper reports analysing, and that it contains repeated id-item pairs. Those are not a doubled upload: they are a second wave of measurement for 129 respondents.
- table: lunacortes_2019_satisfaction
  issue: |-
    Item wording for this table comes from the source article's Table 1, which PLOS publishes only as an image, so the three sentences were transcribed by eye rather than extracted as text. Their bullets are unnumbered, so the assignment of wording to satis_1, satis_2 and satis_3 follows bullet order. That is corroborated by the data — the observed single-factor loadings 0.78/0.72/0.66 reproduce the paper's published rank order — which separates satis_3 firmly but leaves the satis_1/satis_2 ordering resting on a small gap.

    The instrument was administered in Spanish; the shipped text is the English the authors translated from, since the Spanish wording is not published anywhere in the article or its supplement. Only the two endpoints of the 1-7 scale are labelled in the source, so options 2 to 6 carry no text.
- table: lunacortes_2019_social_value
  issue: |-
    Item wording for this table comes from the source article's Table 1, which PLOS publishes only as an image, so the three sentences were transcribed by eye. Their bullets are unnumbered, so the assignment of wording to social_val1, social_val2 and social_val3 follows bullet order.

    social_val3 is pinned independently: the paper dropped its third social-value item from the confirmatory analysis, and its published two-item alpha of 0.822 is reproduced only by the pair social_val1 + social_val2 (0.8219, against 0.34 and 0.46 for the other pairs); social_val3 is also the weakest indicator in the data. The social_val1 vs social_val2 ordering is not pinned, since the paper's loadings for those two share an identical robust t. The instrument was administered in Spanish; the shipped text is the English the authors translated from, as the Spanish is not published.
- table: luo_2021_conational_ties
  issue: |-
    This instrument's wording survives only in the deposit's SPSS column names, which SPSS caps at 64 characters and strips of spaces. All four are cut off mid-word, so **only the first 48 to 61 characters of each shipped question are the study's own text**; the remainder of each sentence, together with all punctuation and word spacing, was completed from the same four Multi-Dimensional Support Scale questions as printed in a different paper (Wei 2025, Front Psychol 16:1607241).

    Which of the four questions each item code refers to is nonetheless exact: each item's live response distribution matches its source column cell for cell, and only 1 of the 24 possible orderings fits. Scale points 2 and 3 carry no option text, because the study labels only 1 = never and 4 = always.
- table: ly_2021_animal_empathy
  issue: |-
    Each item is one emotion rating for one 10-second video clip; the item text is the emotion name and the clip is described in the section prompt. The study published a single interviewer blurb per video *code*, and each code covers two different exemplar clips shown to different halves of the sample (CB1 and CB2, for instance), so those pairs carry identical section_prompt text even though respondents saw different videos.
- table: ma2026_bsmas
  issue: |-
    The scale was administered in Chinese to primary school students, but neither the study's figshare deposit nor its preprint publishes the Chinese wording, so the item text shown here is the canonical English rather than what respondents read. Note that item 6's canonical reference to "your job/studies" is the original scale's wording and not something these primary-school respondents would have been asked.
- table: ma2026_sabas
  issue: |-
    The scale was administered in Chinese to primary school students, but neither the study's figshare deposit nor its preprint publishes the Chinese wording, so the item text shown here is the instrument developers' own English rather than what these respondents read.
- table: machado_2020_cat_separation
  issue: |-
    The questionnaire was administered in Portuguese, but the only wording published in the article or its supplement is the authors' own English version, so that is what is shown here rather than what respondents read. The translated columns are empty for the same reason: there is no second version to put in them.
- table: makai_2023_entrepreneurial_transdanubia
  issue: |-
    Item text for this table is the English wording published in the study's own S1 File. The survey was administered to Hungarian students and the Hungarian original is not published anywhere in the paper or its supplement, so no administered-language text is available. One item code carries a typo present in the source file ("cfareer").
- table: makowska_2023_pdts
  issue: |-
    The paper numbers this scale's items differently from the data file. Its Table 2 lists the "irritated" item as item 2 and the "no control over ICT changes" item as item 3, while the deposited SPSS files label the columns the other way round — and those labels carry the item numbers inside the label text itself (`PDTS2. How often have you felt that you had no control…`). IRW follows the data file, which is the direct tie to the codes in this table, and the response data weakly corroborates it: the undisputed "upset" item correlates 0.783 with PDTS3 against 0.733 with PDTS2 in the paper's Study 1, and 0.660 against 0.611 in Study 2, as expected if PDTS3 is the near-synonymous "irritated" item. **Readers comparing against the paper's item numbers should be aware that PDTS2 and PDTS3 may be interchanged**; the other four items are unambiguous.

    Separately, the item text and response options are shipped in the administered Polish. The English in the translated columns for the *response options* was written by IRW, because the study's own English renderings of those anchors are inconsistent across its files.
- table: makransky_2016_mcq_correct
  issue: |-
    This table's resp is a 0/1 score, not a chosen option, and for **MCQ7** the score and the published answer key disagree. The paper's S1 Table marks "the differential agent" as correct, but the deposited data score the alternative "a carbon source": every one of the 60 pre-test and 56 post-test responses scored 1 chose that option, and the counts match exactly, so the disagreement is systematic rather than a few coding slips.

    The published key is the scientifically correct one — in mannitol salt agar the salt is the selective agent and mannitol is the differential agent — so this is best read as a scoring error in the study's own data. `correct_response` therefore carries the published key, while `resp` faithfully reproduces the study's scoring. The practical consequence: for MCQ7 only, `resp = 1` means the respondent chose "a carbon source", not the answer named in `correct_response`.
- table: makransky_2016_self_efficacy
  issue: |-
    The response anchors shipped here are the ones in the study's own data file and S1 Table ("Completely disagree" to "Completely agree"), which differ in wording from the article body's description of the same scale as running "Strongly disagree" to "Strongly agree". The two level-1 sources agree with each other, so the article's phrasing is the outlier.
- table: malik_2018_individual_motivation
  issue: |-
    Item text is the study's own terse SPSS variable labels (for example "Interest in job", "Availability of adequate food") rather than the full sentences respondents read. The questionnaire's own item phrasing and its instructions are not published in the article or its supplement, so the short labels are all that exists.
- table: malik_2018_organizational_motivation
  issue: |-
    As with its sibling tables, the item text is the study's terse SPSS variable labels rather than the sentences respondents read. Two caveats specific to this table. One item ("Career advancement and growth") carries no response-option labels in the source file, so the 1-5 anchors shared by the other 35 items in the same block were applied to it — an inference, not a transcription. And two typos are shipped verbatim as the source has them: "Availability of proper of proper dressing rooms", and a double space in "Number of staff  available during work".
- table: malik_2018_social_motivation
  issue: |-
    The source questionnaire's socio-cultural section has 15 items but this table carries 14. The processing script treated the data file's `SC3` and `CS4` as the same variable when they are two different items with different wording and different responses, so `SC3` ("I am satisfied with my personal life issues") is absent from IRW altogether, and every code from the third onward is shifted: `social_3` carries `CS4`'s wording ("I am satisfied with the team work around me during work").

    The item text shown is faithful to the data as it currently stands — each code is labelled with the column genuinely behind it. The missing item is a defect in the response data, tracked separately, and fixing it will renumber these codes.

    Item text here is also the study's terse SPSS variable labels rather than the sentences respondents read.
- table: malinowska_2021_saq_nurses
  issue: |-
    Item text is the Polish SAQ-SF PL as administered, with English alongside; the English item stems and response anchors are the instrument's own published English rather than a translation of the Polish, while the instructions, the section prompt for items 24-28 and the 'ward manager'/'hospital director' labels were translated by IRW. Items 24-28 were each rated twice, for the ward manager (kier_24a..kier_28a) and for the hospital director (bezp_24..bezp_28); the raw file labels neither, so that assignment is inferred and is documented in the table's verification record.
- table: malinowska_2021_saq_physicians
  issue: |-
    resp = 6 is not a sixth agreement level: it is the questionnaire's "Nie dotyczy" (not applicable) option, which sits outside the 1-5 "Zdecydowanie nie zgadzam sie".."Zdecydowanie sie zgadzam" scale and should be treated as missing rather than as the top of the scale -- 1.7% of responses overall, but 122 of 738 on bezp_35, the pharmacist-collaboration item. Questions 24-28 were each rated twice, for the ward manager and for the hospital director; kier_24a-28a is read as the ward-manager rating and bezp_24-28 as the hospital-director rating, and the bracketed referent in item_text ([kier. oddzialu] / [dyr. szpitala]) is an editorial addition rather than part of the printed stem. The English for those ten items' section prompt was translated by IRW; every other English field is the University of Texas SAQ-SF's own wording.
- table: mancone_2024_ravlt_recall
  issue: |-
    The five items are the five successive immediate-recall trials of one 15-word list, not five different questions, so item_text is blank by design and resp is the raw count of words correctly recalled on that trial (0-15); the study publishes neither the 15-word stimulus list nor a participant-facing instruction script, so `instructions` holds the paper's own third-person description of the administration
- table: marquessanchez_2023_kidmed
  issue: |-
    For item ALIDES the response coding is the complement of the item as worded: the KIDMED item reads 'No desayuna' / 'Skips breakfast', but in this table resp=1 marks a respondent who does NOT skip breakfast (it adds +1 to the study's own KIDMED total and is absent from the study's negative-item composite, and 79.6% of respondents sit at 1). The shipped option_text is flipped for that item alone; the other 15 items are coded resp=1 = 'Sí'
- table: marcussonclavertz_2019_velten
  issue: |-
    The item text is the study's own variable labels from its data supplement, with a survey-software artifact prefix stripped; the item codes are the source column names, so text and code are tied at the source with no inference. Note that the instructions field is not the instruction respondents read: the study does not publish that, so what is shown is the paper's own third-person description of the task from its Methods section.
- table: mascherini_2021_meddiet
  issue: |-
    Each of the 11 food-frequency items was administered twice, once for habits before the COVID-19 lockdown (wave 1) and once for habits during it (wave 2); the two administrations differ only in tense, and the past-tense wave-1 wording is what ships. The study was run in Italian but publishes only the authors' own English version of the questionnaire, so item_text and option_text are that English rather than what respondents read. resp is the MedDietScore, not the raw frequency: for red meat, white meat, dairy products and alcohol a HIGH resp means LOW consumption, and the option_text on those four items is mapped accordingly.
- table: matarboumosleh_2017_gad2
  issue: |-
    The column headers in the study's data file are terse abbreviations rather than administered wording, so while they pin which item is which, the words shown here are the official GAD-7 form's own published item text rather than anything this study printed. The response-option wording is likewise the official form's, because the data file carries no value labels and the paper prints no anchors.
- table: matarboumosleh_2017_phq2
  issue: |-
    As with its sibling table, the study's data file carries only terse column headers rather than administered wording, so the item and response-option text shown here is the official PHQ form's own published wording rather than anything this study printed.
- table: matarboumosleh_2017_spai26
  issue: |-
    Note which instrument this is. "SPAI" here is the 26-item **Smartphone Addiction Inventory** (Lin et al. 2014), not the Social Phobia and Anxiety Inventory, which is a different 45-item instrument that shares the abbreviation. All 26 items are smartphone-use content. The item wording comes from the paper's Table 2, which is published only as an image.
- table: medvedev_2018_oxh
  issue: |-
    Item wording for this table is the canonical Oxford Happiness Questionnaire (Hills & Argyle 2002); the study's own supplement labels its columns only OXH1..OXH29 and prints no item text. The alignment of item code to item number is corroborated by the data rather than stated by the source: the twelve items the data show as reverse-keyed are exactly the OHQ's canonical reverse-scored set, the reverse-scored scale mean (4.18, SD 0.63, alpha 0.90) reproduces the paper's published values, and oxh_2 is the one weak item the paper singles out. Order within each keying direction is not independently pinned.
- table: medvedev_2018_pan
  issue: |-
    The Medvedev (2018) PeerJ deposit labels its PANAS columns only PAN1..PAN20 and the article reproduces just three of the twenty adjectives as examples, so the item text shown here is the canonical Watson, Clark & Tellegen (1988) PANAS wording assigned by item number rather than wording transcribed from this study's own materials. The assignment is confirmed to the level of valence: the study's own PANPOS and PANNEG composite columns reproduce exactly as raw sums of the canonical positive and negative item positions for all 172-173 scored respondents, so no adjective is on the wrong subscale, but nothing in the source distinguishes one adjective from another within a subscale. The instructions respondents were given are not published anywhere in the source and are left blank.
- table: megart_tonkovic_2021
  issue: |-
    The Croatian instructions shipped for this table are the task description from the study's informed-consent form, not the on-screen instructions participants read during the lexical decision task -- those are locked in an encrypted E-Prime script file -- and their English translation was produced by IRW; item_text repeats the stimulus letter string, which is also the item code, and is left untranslated because half the stimuli are meaningless pseudowords
- table: meloni_2015_child_disab_knowledge
  issue: |-
    The 16 statements were administered in Italian to Italian schoolchildren, but neither the PLOS ONE article nor its supplementary files publish the Italian wording, so the item text shown is the authors' own English version from the S2 File codebook rather than what the children heard; the codebook lists the statements in two unnumbered lists, so their order within each block of item codes is inferred rather than stated.
- table: meloni_2015_child_ia_frequency
  issue: |-
    The interviews were conducted in Italian with Italian primary-school children, but neither the article nor its supplements publish any Italian wording, so the item text shown here is the English description of each activity given in the study's own S2 File codebook; the activities were administered as pictures rather than as printed sentences, and the within-block order of the item codes was inferred from that codebook's list order
- table: meloni_2015_child_ia_satisfaction
  issue: |-
    The interviews were conducted in Italian with Italian primary-school children, but neither the article nor its supplements publish any Italian wording, so the item text shown here is the English description of each activity given in the study's own S2 File codebook; the activities were administered as pictures rather than as printed sentences, the within-block order of the item codes was inferred from that codebook's list order, and note that the instructions quoted here cover the whole task and so also name the Never/Once-a-year/Once-a-week card, which scores the sibling table meloni_2015_child_ia_frequency -- this table's 1-5 is the preference ordering, 1 = liked the least, 5 = liked the most
- table: meloni_2015_deq_ce_child
  issue: |-
    The interviews were conducted in Italian with Italian primary-school children, but neither the article nor its supplements publish any Italian wording, so the item text shown here is the English of the study's own S2 File codebook; that codebook prints only the masculine form of the eleven statements, so the items for the two female stimuli (Maria and Elena) also show the masculine wording rather than the feminine wording the children actually heard, and the statement numbering DEQ1..DEQ11 follows the codebook's list order, which the data corroborate but do not fully pin
- table: meloni_2015_deq_ce_parent
  issue: |-
    The parent questionnaire was administered in Italian, and neither the article nor its supplements publish any Italian wording, so the item text shown here is the English given in the study's own S2 File codebook; the codebook also prints only the masculine form of the eleven statements, although two of the four stimuli (Maria, blind; Elena, able-bodied) are female and were administered in feminine form, so the masculine wording is shown for all 44 items.
- table: meloni_2015_deq_oe_child
  issue: |-
    The 36 "items" here are not questions the children answered. Each child gave one spoken free-text explanation for each of four stimuli (a man in a wheelchair, a blind woman, an autistic child, an able-bodied woman), and two coders blind to the hypotheses then counted how many expressions in that answer fell into each of nine disability-model categories, so the response is a count of coded mentions rather than a chosen option: the item text is the S2 File codebook's own verbatim coding criterion for the category being counted, the question actually put to the child is given as the section prompt, and no response-option wording exists to show. The interviews were conducted in Italian with Italian primary-school children and neither the article nor its supplements publish any Italian wording, so everything shown here is the English of the study's own codebook. The grouping of the nine categories into the individual, social and biopsychosocial models, and the identity of the able-bodied stimulus, are pinned by the article's Fig 1; the order within the ethical/aesthetic/religious group and the separation of the wheelchair and blind stimuli follow the codebook's list order and the categories' own content, which the data corroborate but do not fully pin.
- table: meloni_2015_deq_oe_parent
  issue: |-
    As for the sibling table meloni_2015_deq_oe_child, the 36 "items" are not administered questions: parents wrote a free-text answer to each of four stimuli (a man in a wheelchair, a blind woman, an autistic child, an able-bodied woman) and two blind coders then assigned those answers to nine disability-model categories, so the response is a count of coded mentions, the item text names the coding category, the question actually asked is in the section prompt, and there is no response-option wording. This table shows the bare category heading ("Ethical Model") where the child table shows the codebook's fuller coding criterion for the same category; both are the source's own text. The questionnaire was administered in Italian and neither the article nor its supplements publish any Italian wording, so the text shown is the English given in the study's own S2 File codebook. The macro-model grouping and the able-bodied stimulus are pinned by the article's Fig 1 to within 0.008; the order within the individual and social groups, and the separation of the three disability stimuli, rest on the categories' content rather than a published per-condition number.
- table: meloni_2015_parent_divers_ed
  issue: |-
    The questionnaire was administered in Italian and neither the article nor its supplements
    publish any Italian wording, so the item text shown here is the English given in the study's
    own S2 File codebook. Each of the five sections corresponds to a photograph shown to the
    parent -- a person with a physical disability, a person with Down's syndrome, a boatload of
    migrants, two gay men kissing, a pelican covered in oil -- and section_prompt holds the
    study's own description of that image, not a caption respondents read; the twelve statements
    were repeated in randomised order under every image.
- table: meloni_2015_parent_interests
  issue: |-
    The questionnaire was administered in Italian to Italian parents, but neither the PLOS ONE
    article nor its two supporting files publish any Italian wording, so the item text shown here
    is the authors' own English from the S2 File codebook rather than what the parents read; the
    codebook lists the 25 statements as one unnumbered roman-numbered run tied to no variable
    code, so the order of the items within each conceptual block (music, religious, sport,
    cultural, social) is inferred from that list order. The response labels are also partly IRW's:
    the codebook says only 'Scale: Important/Not Important from 1 to 5' and never labels a scale
    point, so 'Not Important' is shown at 1 and 'Important' at 5 - a placement supported by the
    data (reading books averages 4.46 and watching sport on television 1.96) - and points 2 to 4
    are deliberately left blank.
- table: menaldi_2023_brief_cope
  issue: |-
    The English in option_text_translated was written by IRW: the study administered its own
    Indonesian frequency anchors (Tidak pernah / Kadang-kadang / Cukup sering / Sangat sering)
    rather than the Brief COPE's published anchors, so no authors' English exists for them.
    item_text_translated is Carver's original English for the correspondingly numbered item, a
    parallel version rather than a translation of the Indonesian wording.
- table: mendes_2019_snycq
  issue: |-
    The Short-NYC-Q was administered at MPI-CBS Leipzig to native German speakers, but no German
    wording is published in the deposit or the paper, so the item text shown here is the English
    wording from the deposit's own SNYCQ.json data dictionary; responses are a continuous 0-100
    visual-analogue scale, so only the two endpoints carry option text
- table: meng_2017_referent_assignment
  issue: |-
    Item codes EQ and EQ2 each cover two literal wordings under the study's counterbalanced design
    -- the name question in name-first (NC) trials and the color question in color-first (CN)
    trials (the trial's order is in cov_pattern) -- so both are given in item_text with the
    condition named in brackets; AQ, AQ2 and AQ3 share one identical question ("What about this?")
    and are distinguished only by their position in the fixed EQ/AQ/EQ2/AQ2/AQ3 sequence, not by
    wording.
- table: merlo2025_eet
  issue: |-
    The questionnaire was administered in Italian; item_text and instructions are the administered
    Italian verbatim from the deposit's own data dictionary, and the English in the *_translated
    columns was produced by IRW rather than by the authors. The Italian response anchors were
    never published, so option_text instead carries the authors' English
    (never/rarely/sometimes/often/almost always/always, coded 1-6) taken from the paper; the
    direction is confirmed by the questionnaire's own attention-check item EET_17, whose wording
    is "Seleziona la risposta Mai" and which 1034 of 1065 respondents answered with resp = 1. Note
    that EET_17 is that attention check and not a food, so it should be dropped from any diet
    score pooling the other 28 items.
- table: merlo2025_eng_cognitive
  issue: |-
    The questionnaire was administered in Italian; item_text and instructions are the administered
    Italian verbatim from the deposit's own data dictionary, and the English in the *_translated
    columns was produced by IRW rather than by the authors. The Italian response anchors were
    never published, so option_text instead carries the authors' English for the two ends of the
    scale only - Never at resp = 1 and Always at resp = 7, per Merlo et al. sec. 3.2.6 and Mameli
    & Passini (2017) - and the five interior scale points are left blank because no source labels
    them. The direction is confirmed numerically: rebuilding the paper's own ENG_C composite from
    the live data gives mean 4.229 and skew -0.318 against a published 4.229 and -0.317, where the
    reversed coding would give 3.771 and +0.318. Note also that the deposit's data dictionary has
    had its commas and colons flattened to spaces by its exporter, and the shipped Italian
    reproduces it as-is without restoring punctuation.
- table: merlo2025_eng_emotional
  issue: |-
    The questionnaire was administered in Italian; item_text and instructions are the administered
    Italian verbatim from the deposit's own data dictionary, and the English in the *_translated
    columns was produced by IRW rather than by the authors. The Italian response anchors were
    never published, so option_text instead carries the English coding stated in the paper (1 =
    completely disagree to 7 = totally agree) with the five interior points left blank because the
    source labels only the two ends. One item is stored reverse-scored: ENG_EMO_09 ("Penso che
    studiare sia noioso" / "I think studying is boring") correlates +0.21 to +0.39 with all eight
    positively worded items and Cronbach alpha is 0.890 as stored against 0.820 with it flipped,
    so for that item alone resp 7 means "completely disagree" and resp 1 means "totally agree"; do
    not reverse it again before scoring.
- table: mhscdc_fried_2020_ema
  issue: |-
    This EMA table carries TWO different 1-5 response ladders and nothing in the resp values
    distinguishes them: Q1-Q10 are momentary affect items scored 1 'Not at all' to 5 'Extremely',
    while Q11-Q18 are duration items scored 1 '0 min', 2 '1 - 15 min', 3 '15 - 60 min', 4 '1 - 2
    hours', 5 '> 2 hours'. Do not read one common scale across the table. Item wording is
    transcribed from the deposit's administered survey form (Measures_EMA.pdf), which differs in
    several places from the paraphrased Item column of Codebook_EMA.xlsx.
- table: mistry_2022_hardship
  issue: |-
    For mistry_2022_hardship the option_text values are the labels of the collapsed binary recode
    the deposit ships ('No difficulty'/'Some difficulty'), not the response options respondents
    were offered, which for the food, medicine and routine-care items were None/some/much/unable
    or very difficult; and the item_text for memory and difficulty_earning is cut off mid-phrase
    because the source Stata variable labels hit Stata's 80-character cap
- table: mobility
  issue: |-
    The item wording for this table is the English text documented in the ltm R package, not the
    Bengali in which the Bangladesh Fertility Survey 1989 was administered to rural Bangladeshi
    women; no Bengali original is published in the source, and the instructions field is the
    documentation's description of what respondents were asked rather than a verbatim administered
    instruction.
- table: moe2025_erq
  issue: |-
    The ERQ was administered to Italian teachers, but the figshare deposit is a single SPSS file
    with no item wording in any language and no accompanying article or supplement could be
    located, so the item text shown here is Gross & John's (2003) canonical English ERQ rather
    than the Italian sentences the teachers read. Item codes ERQ1_pre-ERQ10_pre are matched to the
    instrument's own printed item numbers; the assignment of reappraisal versus suppression
    wording is confirmed by the deposit's own Reappraisal composite, which is the mean of exactly
    ERQ1/3/5/7/8/10 (the unique such six-item subset of 210, next-best deviation 0.83), but
    nothing in the data distinguishes the near-parallel reappraisal items 1, 3, 7 and 10 from one
    another. Scale points 2, 3, 5 and 6 carry no option text because the ERQ form labels only 1, 4
    and 7.
- table: mohammed_2021_patient_safety_culture
  issue: |-
    The only item wording this study ever published is the variable labels inside its SPSS data
    file, and those labels are truncated: they stop at 70 characters (so some items lose their
    final words) and they are also cut at the start, so many begin with a word fragment such as
    'fied.' or '. '. They are shipped exactly as the file stores them rather than repaired,
    because this administration is not the canonical AHRQ HSOPSC: 18 items are negated rewrites of
    AHRQ's reverse-worded items, and the responses run in the labels' direction (all 18 correlate
    +0.13 to +0.55 with the other items rather than negatively), so substituting the standard
    wording would have inverted them.
- table: monier_2026_pot
  issue: |-
    Item text for this table is the study authors' English rendering; the questions were
    administered in French, and no French original is published in the paper or its S1 Table, so
    the administered wording could not be shipped.
- table: monier_2026_sti
  issue: |-
    Item text for this table is the English wording printed in the study's own Table 6; the
    inventory was administered in French, and no full French original is published in the paper or
    its S1 Table, so the administered wording could not be shipped. The paper never states the
    7-point response anchors, so option text is blank.
- table: morales_2021_erq
  issue: |-
    The ERQ was administered in Spanish (the Cabello et al., 2013 adaptation) to a mostly Chilean
    sample, but neither the PeerJ deposit nor the paper's supplement contains any Spanish item
    wording -- the deposit's ERQ columns are bare codes ERQ_1..ERQ_10 -- so the item text shown
    here is Gross and John's (2003) canonical English ERQ rather than the sentences participants
    read. Item codes erq1-erq10 follow the instrument's printed item numbers; the split into
    reappraisal (erq1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10) and suppression (erq2, 4, 6, 9) wording is confirmed by the
    paper's Table S.5, whose twelve published subscale statistics reproduce exactly under that key
    and under no other of the 210 possible six-item splits, but nothing in the data distinguishes
    the near-parallel reappraisal items 1, 3, 7 and 10 from one another. Scale points 2, 3, 5 and
    6 carry no option text because the ERQ form labels only 1, 4 and 7.
- table: motion
  issue: |-
    The items of `motion` are stimulus conditions in a random-dot motion task, not questions: each
    item code is block number and motion coherence (e.g. '1 6' = block 1, 6% coherence), and the
    item_text IRW ships is a description of that stimulus rather than wording the child read. The
    only verbatim on-screen text is in the instructions field. resp is scored accuracy (1 =
    correct direction judgement), not the left/right key the child pressed.
- table: much_tte_2025_matrixreasoning
  issue: |-
    The speed/accuracy block instruction was counterbalanced across participants (Group 1 saw the
    non-speeded framing first, Group 2 the speeded), so the instructions field reproduces both
    verbatim rather than the one wording any single respondent read; item_text is blank because
    the OMIB matrix stimuli are figures, not text.
- table: muslih_2024_rses
  issue: |-
    The item text shipped for this table is the English wording the paper prints in its Table 2;
    the scale was administered to participants in Indonesian, and no Indonesian wording is
    published in the paper or its S1 Dataset.
- table: najari_2024_bpqsf_awareness
  issue: |-
    This table is named for the BPQ-SF's Body Awareness subscale but actually contains the whole
    46-item BPQ-SF: q1-q26 are Body Awareness, q27-q40 Supradiaphragmatic Reactivity and q41-q46
    Subdiaphragmatic Reactivity, per Table 2 of the source paper.
- table: nam_2024_function
  issue: |-
    The survey was administered online in Korean and neither the article nor its S1 Data
    supplement publishes any Korean wording, so the item text shown here is the Washington Group's
    own canonical English WG-SS wording; the assignment of FL1-FL6 to the six domains follows the
    canonical WG-SS order that the paper's Methods reproduces, and the data confirm the mobility
    and self-care items (FL3, FL5) and the seeing/hearing pair (FL1, FL2) but cannot tell seeing
    from hearing.
- table: narcissistic_personality_inventory
  issue: |-
    This is the forced-choice NPI-40, so `item_text` is blank for all 40 items by design and both
    statements of each pair are carried as `option_text` at resp 1 and 2. The 80 statements are
    the 2014 deposit's own codebook wording. The `instructions` line, however, was transcribed
    from the live openpsychometrics NPI form as it stood in 2026, because the deposit's codebook
    only describes how the test was administered rather than quoting the instruction respondents
    read; the 80 item statements on that live form are byte-identical to the 2014 codebook, so it
    is the same instrument, but the instruction wording itself is current-page evidence for a 2014
    administration.
- table: neurodegenerative_huizinga_2019_dass
  issue: |-
    The study does not say which Dutch DASS-21 translation it administered, and two are
    distributed that differ in items 1-3; IRW ships the 2010 revised de Beurs version, chosen
    because DASS.1 behaves as a stress item (corrected r .618 stress vs .448 anxiety, where the
    2001 form's item 1 loads equally on both) and DASS.2 behaves as the dry-mouth item (weakest
    item in the scale, r .329, yet the most endorsed anxiety item at mean .502) rather than the
    2001 form's sweating item; the instructions are the paper form's and mention circling a
    number, though this battery was administered online
- table: neurodegenerative_huizinga_2019_vfq
  issue: |-
    Item text is the NEI VFQ-25's official ENGLISH wording; the study administered the
    questionnaire in Dutch and neither the paper's appendices nor the DataverseNL deposit publish
    the Dutch form, so this is a same-instrument substitute rather than what respondents read.
    Note also that resp is the RAND-converted 0-100 item score rescaled (higher = better vision-
    related functioning), not the response number printed on the questionnaire, so for items 1-14,
    15c, 16 and 16a the option order is the reverse of the printed one.
- table: ni_2025_open_innovation
  issue: |-
    The item text shipped for this table is the English wording the source paper prints in its
    Methods; the questionnaire was administered to participants in Chinese, and no Chinese wording
    is published in the paper or its S1 Data. The order of items within each of the two blocks
    (OI1-1..OI1-4 and OI2-1..OI2-4) is inferred from the paper's presentation order rather than
    from an explicit item-code label.
- table: ni_2025_strategic_orientation
  issue: |-
    The questionnaire was administered in Chinese to managers of Chinese SMEs, but neither the
    article nor its S1 Data supplement publishes any Chinese wording, so the item text shown here
    is the English the authors print in section 3.2 of the paper; the assignment of items to the
    codes SO3-1..SO3-3 follows the paper's own listing order, which the published factor loadings
    (0.914/0.920/0.919, reproduced from the live data as 0.9144/0.9199/0.9189) pin to the column
    order but not to the wording order, and the paper publishes no labels for the five Likert
    points, so option_text is blank
- table: niazi_2020_mfq
  issue: |-
    The item text here is the canonical MFQ30 wording (moralfoundations.org, MFQ30.doc, July
    2008), not the study's own variable labels: those labels are an abridgement, dropping the stem
    "Whether or not " throughout Part 1 and carrying the depositor's scoring notes on two items.
    The labels are what tie code to text and they reconcile 32/32 to the sentences shipped here.
    Note also that MATH and GOOD are the MFQ30's two catch items and belong to no foundation
    subscale, so a five-foundation score computed over all 32 items in this table would be wrong.
- table: niazi_2020_mfq_stereotype
  issue: |-
    The item wording here is the standard self-report MFQ30 form, but this table is the study's
    stereotype condition: respondents rated each statement as they predicted a typical member of
    the opposite gender would answer it. The authors' reworded stereotype instructions are not
    published in the paper or its supporting information, so the instruction and section-prompt
    fields are blank rather than carrying the self-referential canonical prompts.
- table: nomt_hooper_2024_study1
  issue: |-
    Study 1 randomly assigned participants to an English- or Spanish-language version of the same
    task (63 English, 56 Spanish); the item text shipped here is the English wording, and the IRW
    response table does not record which language a given participant received.
- table: QCDQES_Oliveira_2022
  issue: |-
    The Portuguese item, option and instruction wording here is the study's own, transcribed from
    its SPSS value labels. The English in the `_translated` columns was produced by IRW -- it is not
    the study's wording and has not been reviewed or back-translated by a Portuguese speaker. Treat
    it as a reading aid rather than a validated English instrument.
- table: qi_2025_panas
  issue: |-
    The instrument is the Qiu, Zheng & Wang (2008) Chinese revision of the PANAS, not Watson et al.'s
    20-item original: it has 18 items and six of them (grateful, joyful, elated and jittery among
    them) are not Watson adjectives. Neither the study's OSF deposit nor its supplement contains any
    questionnaire wording, so the Chinese item, anchor and instruction text was taken from the
    Institute of Psychology (CAS) Cognitive Experiment Standard Toolbox's own administration of that
    instrument and corroborated item-for-item against a second independent reproduction. The English
    in the `_translated` columns was produced by IRW, not by the study.
- table: queiros_2018_qcae
  issue: |-
    Two things to know. The response options ship in the administered Portuguese ('Discordo
    Fortemente' ... 'Concordo Fortemente') with the QCAE authors' own English alongside, and all 31
    items are stored RAW -- so the four reverse-worded items (`QCAE_1`, `QCAE_2`, `QCAE_17`,
    `QCAE_29`) still need reversing before scoring; the source deposit's pre-reversed copies of those
    four were dropped by the IRW build. Separately, the English *instructions* are an IRW translation
    of the Portuguese, because this adaptation's instruction text was never published in English. The
    English item and option wording, by contrast, is the QCAE authors' own.
- table: qiang_2025_workplace_friendship
  issue: |-
    Item `fr5` is questionnaire item 35, which the IRW processing script had dropped as a presumed
    Chinese duplicate of item 36. The response data shows they are different administered items --
    they agree on only 81 of 396 rows, r = 0.208 -- so it was restored on 2026-09-10 and the response
    table rebuilt from 1,584 to 1,980 rows. It is coded `fr5` rather than inserted in questionnaire
    order because `fr1`-`fr4` were already published item codes. Item 35 is the one item in this
    block the deposit prints only in Chinese, so unlike the other four its English here was written
    by IRW rather than by the study.
- table: PMT_Trzcinska_2023_PMT
  issue: |-
    The Polish item text ships both gender-matched forms of every item in one field, marked
    [girls' form] and [boys' form], because the item code does not record which form a child saw. The
    32 `TWO*` item codes are the same 32 questions re-administered two weeks later to a 27-child
    retest subsample, not new items. The English in the `_translated` columns was assembled by IRW
    from the paper's own English wording of each picture and question; the study never prints them as
    sentences.
- table: poza2026_hlseu
  issue: |-
    This table was administered in two languages -- 93 of the 101 respondents answered the Arabic form
    and 8 the French form -- so `item_text` carries both administered wordings in one field, marked
    [Arabic version] and [French version]. The English in the `_translated` columns was written by
    IRW, not by the study. The response labels shipped for 0 and 1 are the data file's own Spanish
    labels for the study's difficult/easy dichotomisation ('DIFICIL/MUY DIFICIL', 'MUY FACIL/FACIL'),
    because the administered Arabic and French anchors are published nowhere.
- table: rinaldi_2021_mas
  issue: |-
    This table's 61 items were administered in Italian, but no Italian wording is published in the study's paper or in its only supplementary file (an SPSS data file that carries no variable or value labels for the items), so IRW ships the original English MAS wording that the paper reproduces in its own Table 2. Separately, that table documents 60 items for 61 data columns: the alignment verified against the published per-item means, the reverse-keying pattern and the paper's factor structure is Mas_1-Mas_56 to Table 2 items 1-56 and Mas_58-Mas_61 to items 57-60, leaving Mas_57 with no published wording at all -- its item_text is blank rather than guessed
- table: rodriguezandres_2016_mnemocity_usability
  issue: |-
    The item wording here was read from the article's Table 2 and Table 3, which PLOS publishes only as images, so it is worth a spot-check; two caveats on content. First, item SA1 asks 'How much fun did you have?' but Table 2 gives it an agreement scale (Strongly disagree..Strongly agree) while Table 3 gives the identical question a Very boring..Very fun scale -- the source's Table 2 anchors are shipped as printed rather than corrected, so SA1's response options may be a copy-paste error in the paper. Second, the 160 respondents were Spanish children aged 5-10 who answered in Spanish, but no Spanish wording appears in the article or its single supplement, so the English shown is the authors' own from those tables.
- table: rodriguezquiroga_2024_epistemic_trust
  issue: |-
    The Spanish item wording is the study's own; the English alongside it is Campbell et al. (2021)'s official ETMCQ, while the English instructions and the four intermediate response-scale labels were written by IRW because the instrument's publisher printed only the 1/4/7 anchors.
- table: roelen_2020_dietary_diversity
  issue: |-
    This household food-group checklist was administered in Haitian Creole and the study's deposit publishes no Creole wording, so the item text shown is the English of the dataset's own Stata variable labels; two of those labels hit Stata's 80-character cap and are therefore shipped truncated in mid-phrase (q_306 ends 'Irish potatoes, brea' and q_311 ends 'coconut, lemon,'), and the deposit publishes no framing question for the block, so no instructions or section prompt are given
- table: roelen_2020_k6
  issue: |-
    The K6 here was administered in Haitian Creole but only English wording was ever published, so the item text shipped is the study's English rendering from its Stata deposit and the paper's Table 3, not what respondents heard; note also that the IRW resp coding runs 0 = 'None (0 day)' to 4 = 'All (30 days)' (higher = more distress), which is the reverse of the direction the paper's own K6 total score uses (its mean of 19.0 is a sum of 1 = all 30 days .. 5 = none).
- table: roelen_2020_rses
  issue: |-
    This table's 10 Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale items were administered orally in Haitian Creole to women in rural Haiti, but no Creole wording is published in the paper or in its single supplementary data file, so IRW ships the English wording that the study's own Stata file and its Table 3 carry. Note also that responses are stored RAW: the five negatively worded items (q_408, q_411, q_412, q_414, q_415) are not reverse-scored in this table, and the deposited Stata file's own numeric codes run in the opposite direction to the IRW resp values -- the anchors shipped here (1 = Strongly disagree ... 4 = Strongly agree) were confirmed against the data, with all 40 item-by-level counts matching and q_414 reproducing the paper's reported 94.7% agree/strongly-agree exactly
- table: roettl_2018_brand_recognition
  issue: |-
    resp in this table is the study's 0/1 scoring of a four-alternative forced-choice logo recognition item, not the choice itself, so option_text carries the scoring labels ('wrong'/'right') rather than the four logo names respondents actually saw; those alternatives are listed per category in the paper's S2 Appendix.
- table: rosetti2023_gad7
  issue: |-
    The GAD-7 here was administered to Mexican university students, but the figshare deposit publishes no item wording and the source paper is closed access, so the item and option text shipped is the instrument publisher's official English (phqscreeners.com) rather than the Spanish sentences respondents read; the mapping of GAD7_q1..q7 to the canonical GAD-7 items rests on the column numbering, and only q5 (restlessness) and q6 (irritability) are independently pinned by the data
- table: rosetti_2023_cas
  issue: |-
    The Rosetti et al. study was run with Mexican university students and was almost certainly administered in Spanish, but neither the figshare deposit (a single fully anglicised CSV) nor the closed-access Ecopsychology article publishes the Spanish wording, so the item and option text shipped here is Clayton & Karazsia's English original rather than the sentences respondents actually read.
- table: rosetti_2023_gad7
  issue: |-
    The GAD-7 was administered in Spanish to Mexican university students, but no Spanish wording is published in the study's figshare deposit and its paper is closed access, so the item and option text shipped here is the instrument publisher's official English (phqscreeners.com) rather than the sentences respondents read
- table: rosharudin_2023_dass21
  issue: |-
    The live table records five response levels (0-4), but the paper and the Malay DASS-21 form it administered both describe a four-point 0-3 scale with four labelled anchors, so no option text and no instructions could be shipped for this table; the fifth level is genuine rather than a missing-value code, since counting it as 4 reproduces the paper's published subscale standard deviations to within 0.02.
- table: rosharudin_2023_ders18
  issue: |-
    The three Awareness items (@1_A, @4_A_A, @6_A) are stored RAW in the IRW table, so a higher response means MORE emotional awareness -- the opposite direction from the other 15 items, and the reverse of how the source paper's Table 2 reports them. Reverse-code them before summing a DERS-18 total. Verified from the data: each of the three matches its published floor/ceiling percentages only with floor and ceiling swapped (e.g. item 6, published 11.47/18.72 vs observed 18.72/11.47). The five response-option labels are the canonical English DERS-18 anchors, not the Malay wording respondents saw, which the study never published.
- table: rr98_accuracy
  issue: |-
    Item text for this table describes the visual stimulus, not a question read to the participant: rr98's items are pixel arrays, so IRW composed each item_text from the source package's own definition of the stimulus-strength variable rather than transcribing administered wording, which does not exist. Note also that resp is trial accuracy (1 = the response matched the distribution the stimulus was drawn from), not the participant's dark/light choice.
- table: RvKDCS_Romiacg_Miroshnik_2020_CBI
  issue: |-
    The English in the *_translated columns was produced by IRW from the administered Russian; the Russian items are the study's own adaptation of Hocevar's Creative Behavior Inventory, so this English is a rendering of what respondents read rather than Hocevar's original wording.
- table: rzeszutek_2020_wwii_matgrandfather
  issue: |-
    Each of the 29 questions was administered with three responses - TAK (yes), NIE (no) and NIE WIEM (don't know) - but the IRW table drops 'don't know' as missing, so only the two option rows 0=NIE and 1=TAK exist and per-item n runs 84-263 of 500 respondents; the item wording is the questionnaire's shared grandmother/grandfather row text, and this table is specifically the mother's-side (great)grandfather column of the grid
- table: rzeszutek_2020_wwii_matgrandmother
  issue: |-
    Each of the 29 questions was administered with three responses - TAK (yes), NIE (no) and NIE WIEM (don't know) - but the IRW table drops 'don't know' as missing, so only the two option rows 0=NIE and 1=TAK exist and per-item n runs 106-322 of 500 respondents; the item wording is the questionnaire's shared grandmother/grandfather row text, and this table is specifically the mother's-side (great)grandmother column of the grid
- table: rzeszutek_2020_wwii_patgrandfather
  issue: |-
    Each of the 29 questions was administered with three responses - TAK (yes), NIE (no) and NIE WIEM (don't know) - but the IRW table drops 'don't know' as missing, so only the two option rows 0=NIE and 1=TAK exist and per-item n runs 76-216 of 500 respondents; the item wording is the questionnaire's shared grandmother/grandfather row text, and this table is specifically the father's-side (great)grandfather column of the grid
- table: rzeszutek_2020_wwii_patgrandmother
  issue: |-
    Each of the 29 questions was administered with three responses, TAK (yes), NIE (no) and NIE WIEM (don't know), but the IRW table drops 'don't know' as missing, so only the two option rows 0=NIE and 1=TAK exist and per-item n runs 90-238 of 500 respondents. The item wording is the questionnaire's shared grandmother/grandfather row text, and this table is the father's-side (great)grandmother column of the grid. Item owojb23 is grouped with items 9-22 as in the English form, although the Polish father's-side form prints it under the 'witness to' heading.
- table: SABFI2_Gallardo_Pujol_2018_LOT
  issue: |-
    This study administered the Spanish LOT-R, whose wording is not in the study's deposit or paper, so item_text is the scale authors' own English LOT-R standing in for it and the response labels are the paper's English description of a five-point strongly disagree to strongly agree scale; LOT2, LOT4 and LOT5 are the pessimism items and are stored unreversed, and which optimism (or pessimism) item each code denotes follows the published item order, which the data confirm by polarity class but cannot confirm within a class.
- table: roettl_2018_scepticism
  issue: |-
    The nine items are the SKEP advertising-scepticism scale's pro-advertising statements ('Advertising
    is generally truthful'), stored raw and agreement-keyed 1-7 with no reverse scoring applied, so
    despite the table's name a HIGH `resp` means LOW scepticism. Live per-item means run 2.15 to 3.50
    (n=234 on all nine). This is a property of the response data, not of the item text. Two smaller
    notes: the study's S2 Appendix numbers this block F29_1-F29_9 while the data columns, and so the
    IRW item codes, are F31_1-F31_9 -- the two were tied by exact string identity of the English
    wording, not by position; and only the two scale poles carry labels in the source, so `option_text`
    is blank for `resp` 2-6 rather than padded.
- table: ruiz_parra_2023_rfq8
  issue: |-
    The RFQ-8 was administered here in Spanish. The English item and anchor wording is the
    original English RFQ printed in the study's S1 Appendix -- a parallel published version
    rather than a translation of the Spanish items -- but the English instructions
    (`instructions_translated`) were translated by IRW from the Spanish and are not the
    study's own words. Item 7 ("Siempre se lo que siento") is reverse-keyed and is stored
    unreversed. The instrument's authors note that the RFQ is freely available for research
    but is not yet suited for clinical purposes.
- table: safiye_2023_rfq
  issue: |-
    The RFQ-8 was administered to this sample in Serbian, but neither the study's data
    deposit nor its paper contains the Serbian item wording, so the item text shipped here
    is the standard English RFQ-8 wording standing in for what respondents actually read.
    The response labels are the study's own English labels from its data file. Item RFQ7
    ("I always know what I feel") is reverse-keyed and is stored unreversed. The
    instrument's authors note that the RFQ is not yet suited for clinical purposes.
- table: salleh_2023_aim_iam_fim
  issue: |-
    The item wording is the data file's combined "Program MIICA/ KOSPEN" label. These 170
    respondents are the study's KOSPEN pilot, but the only questionnaire the study published
    is the MIICA form, which names a single programme -- so the programme name these
    respondents actually read is not confirmed. Seven item labels were truncated by one
    character in the data file and have been restored from the paper's Table 2.
- table: schafer_2016_music_effects
  issue: |-
    The diary was administered in German and no German wording is published, so the item
    text is the author's own English rendering from the paper's Method section. The study's
    data file labels the third item "emotion and mood" while the paper's question words it
    "arousal and mood regulation"; that item's mean, 6.17, matches the paper's 6.2 for the
    same function.
- table: schafer_2016_music_goals
  issue: |-
    The diary study was run at a German university and was very likely administered in
    German, but neither the paper nor its data supplements publish the German questions, so
    the item text here is the English rendering printed in the author's own article. Scale
    points 2-9 carry no labels in the source and are left blank rather than padded.
- table: schalet_2016_hrsa
  issue: |-
    The study published no item wording for its anxiety measure and its data file carries
    only generic variable labels, so the item and option wording here is the canonical
    Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale taken from a public-domain reproduction sheet. The
    instructions shown are that sheet's rater instruction and have not been confirmed as
    the ones this trial used. Subscale membership is pinned by the paper's Table 2 and 10
    of 14 items are pinned individually, but the order within two pairs (a03/a05 and
    a07/a08) is not verified.
- table: schmidt_2017_pds
  issue: |-
    Items pub_2_1 and pub_3_1 each hold two sex-specific questions under one code (girls:
    breast growth and menstruation; boys: beard growth and voice change), and for pub_3_1
    the lowest and highest levels combine the girls' yes/no answers with the boys' anchors.
    The item text is the study's own abbreviated German data-file labels, ending in
    ellipses, rather than the full administered questionnaire wording, and the English in
    the `_translated` columns was produced by IRW rather than by the study's authors.
- table: science_ltm
  issue: |-
    For Environment, Technology and Industry -- the three negatively worded statements --
    `resp` is reverse-scored relative to the `ltm` package's documentation and to this
    table's own `resp_raw` column: `resp` 4 means the respondent strongly DISAGREED with the
    statement as worded. The Eurobarometer 38.1 Great Britain codebook marginals confirm the
    direction shipped here (Industry: 39% strongly disagree in the survey against 41% at
    `resp` 4 in this table), so `option_text` follows the data rather than `resp_raw`.
- table: shi_2021_gentrification
  issue: |-
    The questionnaire was distributed mainly through a Chinese survey platform to
    respondents who were almost all Chinese nationals, but the study publishes only English
    factor names, so the item text shown is the authors' English and may not be the wording
    most respondents read. The paper does not state the administered language.
- table: shi_2025_dass21
  issue: |-
    Response codes are not consistent across waves in this table. Baseline (wave 0)
    responses run 1-4, while post-intervention and follow-up (waves 1-2) run 0-4 with five
    levels -- against the four-point 0-3 scale the source paper describes. Because no single
    labelling is correct across all three waves, the response options are left unlabelled.
    The item text is the canonical English DASS-21, as the administered simplified Chinese
    wording was not published.
- table: shineha_2024_gef_accept_factors
  issue: |-
    This survey was administered in Japanese and the Japanese wording is not in the study's
    supplements, so `item_text` is the authors' own English translation of the
    questionnaire, which they describe as tentative. Each item is a 0/1 indicator of whether
    the respondent chose that factor as one of three important for social acceptance;
    respondents who chose "There are no important things" chose only that option.
- table: shineha_2024_gef_attitudes
  issue: |-
    The survey was administered in Japanese and only the authors' English translation of the
    questionnaire is published, so the wording shown is that translation. For Fig1b
    ("accepted in society") the translated questionnaire prints Strongly agree...Strongly
    disagree anchors, which are the ones shipped here, while the study's data file labels
    the same codes Strongly acceptable...Strongly unacceptable. Both run in the same
    direction, with 7 the most positive. The item codes are not questionnaire order.
- table: shineha_2024_gef_info_topics
  issue: |-
    The questionnaire and the paper both instruct respondents to "choose three" topics, but
    in the data every respondent selected either exactly five topics (3,614) or only
    "Nothing in particular that I need to know" (784) -- and the paper's own Figure 3
    percentages, which sum to well over 100%, were computed from these same five-selection
    data. The public and expert samples also saw different prompts ("What do you want to
    know?" against "What do you want to inform?"). The English throughout is the authors'
    translation of a Japanese questionnaire, and `option_text` is blank because the 0/1
    selection indicators carry no printed labels.
- table: shinohara_2021_testimony
  issue: |-
    Item codes are puppet roles, not fixed puppets: which coloured puppet and which video
    version filled each role, and the presentation order, were counterbalanced, and the
    valence-testimony and first-hand-observation puppets were prosocial for the
    positive-condition half of the sample and antisocial for the negative-condition half
    (cov_condition). Allocation and anticipation are stored as ranks where 1 is the highest
    reward or first choice and 3 the lowest. The English prompts are the paper's
    descriptions of a procedure administered in Japanese, not a published script
- table: shu_2024_gad7
  issue: |-
    The GAD-7 was administered in Chinese, but the study's deposit carries only its own
    English rendering of the items and response options, which is what is shipped here; it
    is neither the Chinese respondents read nor the official English GAD-7 wording
- table: shu_2024_phq9
  issue: |-
    This PHQ-9 was administered in Chinese to adolescents in China, but the study's data
    file publishes only an English rendering, so item_text is the study's own English (not
    the canonical PHQ-9 wording and not what respondents read). PHQ1's label was truncated
    in the file and its final words 'doing things' were completed by IRW, and the
    instructions' embedded anchor legend words the middle options differently from the
    response labels
- table: silva_2018_mbds
  issue: |-
    resp is not a chosen response option: each MBDS item was rated for importance (1-10) and
    on a 5-point agreement/frequency scale, and resp is importance/10 multiplied by that
    rating (0.1-5.0), so option_text is blank for all 28 observed values. The Portuguese
    wording is the reduced-form reprint in Da Silva et al. (2017), which the study cites as
    the version used, not the study's own materials
- table: silva_2023_ecohis
  issue: |-
    The study describes its ECOHIS as a 5-point scale and prints no anchor labels, but the
    published ECOHIS has six options including "Don't know", and in these data code 5
    behaves like a non-ordinal answer (respondents choosing 5 have lower caries counts and
    lower scores on the other items than those choosing 4), so option_text is left blank and
    resp 5 should not be assumed to mean "Very often". Item wording is the authors' English
    rendering of the Brazilian Portuguese version they administered
- table: simsalRbim_Human_LargeValence_2017
  issue: |-
    Item text is blank by design because the stimuli are OASIS photographs (the item code
    names the image, e.g. Lake = Lake_9.jpg); each pairwise trial contributes two rows, resp
    1 for the image chosen and 0 for the image not chosen, and the instructions are
    transcribed from the study's publicly hosted online version of the experiment rather
    than a separately published copy of the 2017 laboratory script
- table: simsalRbim_Human_LowValence_2017
  issue: |-
    Pictures, not text, were the stimuli: item codes name the OASIS image shown (Sunset_1,
    Flowers_3, Food_4, Grass_1, House_1, Monkey_2, Timber_1), and resp = 1 means that
    picture was the one chosen from its pair. The deposit contains 63 participants where the
    source paper reports 48 for this picture set
- table: sinche_2017_skill_importance
  issue: |-
    The study's data file labels this scale strongly disagree..strongly agree, but the paper
    reports it was rated from "not at all important" (1) to "extremely important" (5); the
    paper's anchors are shipped and the wording of points 2-4 was not published
- table: singleton_2021_carbon_reduction
  issue: |-
    The seven even-numbered items (Q2, Q4, Q6, Q8, Q10, Q12, Q14) are the NEP's
    anti-ecological statements and are stored already reverse-scored as the study scored
    them, so for those items resp=1 is 'strongly agree' and resp=5 is 'strongly disagree'
    (the option_text rows are mapped accordingly); for odd-numbered items resp=5 is
    'strongly agree', so higher resp means a more pro-ecological response on every item
- table: sleboda_2021_risk_benefit
  issue: |-
    For the five New items the anchor direction differs by technology, following the study's
    SPSS value labels and the data: for gene technology (plant breeding, stem cells) and
    pesticides 1 = completely new and 11 = very familiar, while for E-number food additives
    and vaccination 1 = very familiar and 11 = completely new; the study's English
