    supplement states 1 = old, 11 = new for all five. Item and technology wording is the
    study's English rendering of a Swedish administration
- table: smpi_lorenzoluaces_2020_gad7
  issue: |-
    The GAD-7 item and response-option wording here is the published instrument's; the
    study's paper describes its 0-3 scale endpoints as "none of the days" and "all the days"
    rather than the GAD-7's "Not at all" and "Nearly every day", and no source shows the
    labels respondents actually saw
- table: smpi_lorenzoluaces_2020_phq9
  issue: |-
    The PHQ-9 item and response-option wording here is the published instrument's; the
    study's paper describes its 0-3 scale endpoints as "none of the days" and "all the days"
    rather than the PHQ-9's "Not at all" and "Nearly every day", and no source shows the
    labels respondents actually saw
- table: song_2023_rses
  issue: |-
    Respondents were Chinese medical students, but neither the paper nor its data deposit
    publishes the questionnaire wording (or states its language outright), so IRW ships the
    Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale's English original, with language recorded as Chinese.
    Responses are stored already reverse-scored, so higher is always higher self-esteem: for
    RSES3, RSES5, RSES9 and RSES10 a 4 means Strongly disagree. RSES8 ('I wish I could have
    more respect for myself') is an exception to the paper's own keying: the paper lists it
    as negatively rated, but its stored values behave as unreversed agreement (91% at 3-4,
    clustering with the positive items), so it ships with 4 = Strongly agree; the study
    published no anchors, so this direction is inferred from the data
- table: srivani_2022_education4
  issue: |-
    The questionnaire offered five options (Strongly agree 2 to Strongly disagree -2), but
    the response table omits the 20 'Disagree' (-1) responses recorded in the source file
    for items ELN, LET, ELS, TDE and ECT, so only the Neutral, Agree and Strongly agree
    options appear here
- table: stachl_2020_belonging
  issue: |-
    Each item was a cartoon illustration; item_text transcribes only the text in its speech
    and thought bubbles, and the six negatively-worded (Low SB) items are stored
    reverse-scored, so for them resp 4 means Do Not Relate
- table: stenhouse_2026_math_anxiety
  issue: |-
    The response table drops the endpoint responses of the two 1-10 anxiety ratings (items
    17.1 and 20.1): the source stored 1 and 10 as the labels '1 - Not anxious' and '10 -
    Very anxious', which the processing script discarded, so 54 and 40 responses
    respectively are missing and those items only take values 2-9
- table: strohacker_2024_arms_readiness
  issue: |-
    The study administered these items in English to its US cohort and in an unpublished
    German translation to its German cohort, and the data carry no cohort flag, so item_text
    is not the wording German-cohort respondents read
- table: sugiura_2015_disaster_characteristics
  issue: |-
    The questionnaire was administered in Japanese; the item text shown is the authors' own
    English translation from the study's data file, which differs in minor wording from the
    versions printed in the paper's Table 2 for 8 items
- table: sun_2016_risky_choice_graph
  issue: |-
    Respondents saw each gamble pair as a coordinate graph with a caption (the paper prints
    it only for pair 1: 'A denotes 80% chance of receiving ¥50 and 20% chance of receiving
    0; B denotes 40% chance of receiving ¥100 and 60% chance of receiving 0'), so item_text
    is blank and option_text gives each option's win probability and prize in the paper's
    Table 1 shorthand; graph-scale condition is in cov_graph_condition
- table: sun_2021_blockchain_loan_adoption
  issue: |-
    The survey of SMEs was run in China and does not state its administration language; only
    the authors' English questionnaire is published, so item_text is that English rather
    than the wording respondents read. Only the 1 and 7 anchors are labelled, and the order
    of items within each three-item construct rests on the paper's numbering, which no
    published item-level statistic confirms
- table: sun_2024_innovation
  issue: |-
    The survey of 281 Chinese SME CEOs does not state its administration language and
    publishes only the authors' English wording, which is what is shipped here, so it may
    not be the wording respondents read
- table: sun_2024_performance_expectancy
  issue: |-
    The survey of 281 Chinese SME CEOs does not state its administration language and
    publishes only the authors' English wording, which is what is shipped here, so it may
    not be the wording respondents read
- table: sun_2024_price_value
  issue: |-
    The survey of 281 Chinese SME CEOs does not state its administration language and
    publishes only the authors' English wording, which is what is shipped here, so it may
    not be the wording respondents read
- table: sun_2024_risk
  issue: |-
    The survey of 281 Chinese SME CEOs does not state its administration language and
    publishes only the authors' English wording, which is what is shipped here, so it may
    not be the wording respondents read
- table: sun_2024_task_tech_fit
  issue: |-
    The survey of 281 Chinese SME CEOs does not state its administration language and
    publishes only the authors' English wording, which is what is shipped here, so it may
    not be the wording respondents read
- table: sun_2024_usage
  issue: |-
    The survey of 281 Chinese SME CEOs does not state its administration language and
    publishes only the authors' English wording, which is what is shipped here, so it may
    not be the wording respondents read
- table: sun_2026_eap_content
  issue: |-
    The questionnaire was distributed through a Chinese survey platform (Wenjuanxing) to
    students and teachers at a Chinese art institute, but the study publishes only an
    English version, so the item text shown is the authors' English and may not be the
    wording respondents read; the paper does not state the administered language
- table: sun_2026_eap_difficulty
  issue: |-
    The questionnaire was distributed through a Chinese survey platform to students and
    teachers at a Chinese art institute, but the study publishes only an English version, so
    the item text shown is the authors' English and may not be the wording respondents read;
    the paper does not state the administered language. The question asks respondents to
    rate each difficulty by its severity, but the published response scale is an agreement
    scale (Strongly Disagree to Strongly Agree)
- table: sun_2026_eap_methods
  issue: |-
    The questionnaire was distributed through a Chinese survey platform to students and
    teachers at a Chinese art institute, but the study publishes only an English version, so
    the item text shown is the authors' English and may not be the wording respondents read;
    the paper does not state the administered language. The question asks respondents to
    rate each teaching method by its effectiveness, but the published response scale is an
    agreement scale (Strongly Disagree to Strongly Agree)
- table: sun_2026_eap_usage
  issue: |-
    The questionnaire was distributed through a Chinese survey platform to students and
    teachers at a Chinese art institute, but the study publishes only an English version, so
    the item text shown is the authors' English and may not be the wording respondents read;
    the paper does not state the administered language. The question asks respondents to
    rate the importance or frequency of each scenario, but the published response scale is
    an importance scale (Not Important at All to Very Important)
- table: sun_2026_tiktok_travel
  issue: |-
    The survey was administered in Chinese but only the authors' English questionnaire is
    published, which is shipped here; that English form prints the disagree-side anchors as
    2 = 'Somewhat disagree' and 3 = 'Disagree', an order that is almost certainly transposed
    but is reproduced as printed because no source confirms the administered labels
- table: szameitat_2015_multitask_examples
  issue: |-
    Item text is the study's English questionnaire; respondents in Turkey, the Netherlands
    and Germany (about 60% of this table) answered the authors' own Turkish, Dutch and
    German translations, which were not published
- table: szameitat_2015_occupation_multitask
  issue: |-
    The questionnaire was also administered in German, Dutch and Turkish translations (209
    of the 347 respondents here, per cov_country), whose wording was never published, so the
    English version shipped is what only the UK, US and International respondents read
- table: tan_2026_stem_technology_integration
  issue: |-
    Response options 1-5 carry no labels in the source, so the direction of the scale is
    undocumented; negatively worded items 9 and 10 correlate positively (r = 0.22 to 0.48)
    with the other 13 items, and the source does not say whether they were reverse-coded
- table: taylorabdulai_2025_incentives
  issue: |-
    Item text is the source paper's Table 4 labels for the question 'What will make you
    accept COVID-19 vaccine' (the questionnaire itself was not published); the pattern of
    answers (120 of 377 respondents endorse none of the seven factors, 179 exactly one)
    indicates a select-all-that-apply question, so resp = 0 ('No' in the deposit) most
    likely means the factor was not selected rather than explicitly rejected
- table: teicher_2015_mace_distress_helpless
  issue: |-
    Item text is the published MACE-X form, which differs from the version administered for
    four items (Attempt_sex_sib, Intercourse_sib, H_Adults_argue, O_Adults_argue -- the
    study's own paper describes the last two as hearing and observing adults arguing), so
    those four ship without item text; also, resp = 0 (Helpless box not checked) is recorded
    for every respondent who never experienced the event, which is 92% of the zeros
- table: teicher_2015_mace_distress_terrified
  issue: |-
    Item text comes from the published MACE-X form, which words four positions differently
    from the version this study administered, so item_text is blank for H_Adults_argue and
    O_Adults_argue (hearing vs. observing adults argue) and Attempt_sex_sib and
    Intercourse_sib (witnessing attempted vs. actual intercourse with a sibling); resp = 1
    means the respondent ticked 'Terrified' for that event and resp = 0 means they did not,
    which includes the large majority of rows (26,542 of 30,503) from respondents who
    reported never experiencing the event
- table: teicher_2015_mace_emot_neglect
  issue: |-
    Responses are stored as answered (1 = Yes, 0 = No) and are not reverse-scored: for the
    three positively worded items (felt loved, felt important or special, family a source of
    strength and support) a 1 indicates the absence of emotional neglect
- table: teicher_2015_mace_nonverbal
  issue: |-
    This table holds 5 of the 6 items the MACE scores as parental non-verbal emotional
    abuse: item 65 of the MACE-X, 'You felt that you had to shoulder adult
    responsibilities.' (33.9% Yes in the source paper), is in the study's data file but was
    not included in the response table
- table: teicher_2015_mace_phys_neglect
  issue: |-
    Responses are stored as answered (1 = Yes, 0 = No) and are not reverse-scored, so for
    the three positively worded items (P_protect, P_ER, Looked_out_each_other) a 1 indicates
    the absence of physical neglect; item_text for P_ER is the study's experimental MACE-X
    wording ('... if the need ever arose.'), while the authors' final MACE adds ', or would
    have if needed.', and which wording the online administration used is not published
- table: teicher_2015_mace_sexual
  issue: |-
    The source paper's Table 9 labels the item scored from o_touch_them as 'Other adults
    touched or fondled you in sexual way', but the study's published MACE and MACE-X forms
    word it 'Had you touch their body in a sexual way', which is the text shipped here; the
    response pattern supports the forms (o_fondled 10.4% Yes vs o_touch_them 5.8%, mirroring
    the parental items Fondled 2.9% vs Touch_them 1.5%)
- table: teicher_2015_mace_witness_parent
  issue: |-
    Item text comes from the published MACE-X form, whose items 31/32 (adults arguing with
    your mother / father) differ from the two arguing items this study administered -- the
    paper describes them as hearing and observing adults arguing, and the data agree (448 of
    458 who observed also heard) -- so H_Adults_argue and O_Adults_argue ship without item
    text; Adults_hit_med is the father item (adults hurt your father so that he needed
    medical attention) despite lacking the _f suffix
- table: teicher_2015_mace_witness_sib
  issue: |-
    Item text comes from the published MACE-X form, which at two positions words the items
    differently from the version this study administered (the study's paper describes them
    as separate attempted and actual intercourse items), so Attempt_sex_sib and
    Intercourse_sib ship without item text
- table: temesgen_2025_elephant_park_attitude
  issue: |-
    Respondents were interviewed in Tigrinya from a questionnaire the authors wrote in
    English, and no Tigrinya wording was published, so the item text is the authors'
    English; for item Q7 the response data do not reproduce the percentages the source paper
    reports for that statement (38.7% agree / 7.9% neutral / 53.4% disagree in the data vs
    34.17 / 11.65 / 54.18 in the paper's Table 6), while the other six items match to 0.01
    points
- table: teq_novak_2021_selfesteem
  issue: |-
    Item text for this Czech-administered Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale table is the English
    RSES wording, not the Czech wording respondents read, and the item codes carry no
    labels: they are matched to the commonly circulated RSES order (negatively worded items
    2, 5, 6, 8, 9), which the data support for each item's polarity and for item 8 but which
    does not distinguish item 3 from 4, item 1 from 10, or the negatively worded items 2, 5,
    6, 9 from one another. Responses are stored so that a higher value means lower
    self-esteem on every item (0 = Strongly Agree for positively worded items, 0 = Strongly
    Disagree for negatively worded ones), the opposite of the source paper's statement that
    higher scores indicate higher self-esteem
- table: thanh_2025_attitude
  issue: |-
    Respondents answered a Vietnamese translation that was not published, so the item text
    is the authors' English; the responses stored for ATT4 and ATT5 (items the authors
    dropped from their analysis) are statistically indistinguishable from uniform random
    numbers -- near-flat counts across 1-5 and correlations of at most 0.11 with any other
    item in the study -- so they should not be analysed as responses to that wording without
    checking with the authors
- table: thanh_2025_environ_concern
  issue: |-
    The study was administered in Vietnamese but only the authors' English wording is
    published, so that English is shown here; item EC6 ('I worry about the greenhouse
    effect') was dropped by the authors and its responses are essentially uncorrelated with
    every other item in the deposited data (r = 0.01-0.06 with EC1-EC5, including 'I worry
    about global warming'), so treat it with caution
- table: thanh_2025_green_behavior
  issue: |-
    The item text is the authors' published English; the survey was administered in
    Vietnamese after translation by the authors' bilingual experts, and the Vietnamese
    wording was not published. Items EGB6-EGB8 were dropped by the authors for low factor
    loadings, and in the deposited data their responses are spread almost evenly across 1-5
    and are uncorrelated with every other item (|r| at most 0.12), so they may not reflect
    genuine responses
- table: thanh_2025_green_knowledge
  issue: |-
    Respondents answered a Vietnamese translation that was not published, so the item text
    is the authors' English; separately, responses to GK5 and GK6 (the two items the authors
    dropped) are spread almost evenly over 1-5 and are essentially uncorrelated with GK1-GK4
    (|r| <= 0.08, versus 0.74-0.82 among GK1-GK4), and should be treated with caution
- table: thanh_2025_perceived_control
  issue: |-
    Item wording is the study's own English rendering of a questionnaire administered in
    Vietnamese, whose wording was not published
- table: theobald_2017_group_dynamics
  issue: |-
    The dominator item's wording is shipped as printed in the paper's Table 1 ('today’s
    [topic] activity'); the Methods text quotes it as 'today’s group activity', and the
    specific topic shown to students varied by survey wave (cov_topic)
- table: tian2026_digital_competence
  issue: |-
    The English item wording in item_text_translated is a machine translation made by IRW
    from the administered Chinese, not the authors' own English; the response anchors are
    the paper's English endpoint labels because the Chinese anchors were not published, and
    three typos in the source's Chinese (items 14, 20, 23) are kept as administered
- table: tomioka_2022_srh_future_needs
  issue: |-
    The English in the _translated columns is the study's own rendering and condenses the
    Japanese options (e.g. B9-4 'Consultation with expert' translates a longer option about
    establishing expert consultation and supervision systems); resp 1 means the option was
    circled
- table: tomioka_2022_srh_importance
  issue: |-
    The study's English rendering is shorter than the administered Japanese, which asks
    about explaining the effects of the cancer and its treatment on sexual and reproductive
    function (including that there are none); both questions offered a fourth option, 'Not
    important' (4), which no nurse chose, so it has no row here
- table: tomioka_2022_srh_support_types
  issue: |-
    The English in the _translated columns is the study's own rendering: its Q7 carries only
    the heading 'Support for sexual and reproductive issues' where the administered Japanese
    asks nurses to circle every kind of support they provide, and several options are
    condensed (e.g. B7-1 'Referral to other professionals' for referral to specialist
    physicians, counsellors or treatment institutions); resp 1 means the option was circled,
    and B7-11 is the 'None' option
- table: torices_2025_bapq
  issue: |-
    The BAPQ was administered to this sample in Spanish, but neither the data deposit nor a
    published paper contains the Spanish item wording, so item_text is the standard English
    BAPQ wording standing in for what respondents read; the response labels are the study's
    own Spanish labels from its codebook, with English alongside. Response 6 ('Muy a
    menudo', very often) occurs only on BAPQ_01 (17 of 108 respondents) and never on the
    other 35 items, where answers pile up at 5, so the top category appears not to have been
    available or recorded for items 2-36. The 15 reverse-keyed items (1, 3, 7, 9, 12, 15,
    16, 19, 21, 23, 25, 28, 30, 34, 36) are stored unreversed
- table: tran_2023_gad7
  issue: |-
    The GAD-7 was administered in Vietnamese to medical students in Vietnam, but the study's
    deposit and paper publish no item wording, so the item and option text shipped is the
    instrument publisher's official English rather than what respondents read; the mapping
    of GAD1..GAD7 to the canonical items rests on the column numbering and is only partly
    confirmed by the data
- table: tran_2023_phq9
  issue: |-
    The PHQ-9 was administered in Vietnamese, but no Vietnamese wording is published in the
    paper or its data deposit, so the item and option text shipped here is the instrument
    publisher's official English rather than the sentences respondents read
- table: tsai_2017_treeit_tam_bi
  issue: |-
    The TAM questionnaire was administered to Mandarin-Chinese-reading older adults in
    Taiwan, but only the study's English version is published, so the item text is that
    English rendering
- table: tsai_2017_treeit_tam_peou
  issue: |-
    The TAM questionnaire was administered to Mandarin-Chinese-reading older adults in
    Taiwan, but only the study's English version is published, so the item text is that
    English rendering
- table: tsai_2017_treeit_tam_pu
  issue: |-
    The TAM questionnaire was administered to Mandarin-Chinese-reading older adults in
    Taiwan, but only the study's English version is published, so the item text is that
    English rendering
- table: tuason_2021_covid_coping_enjoy
  issue: |-
    In the source data file the 0/1 selection columns were filled in only for the low and
    high well-being groups the paper analysed, so 321 of the 322 respondents in the middle
    well-being group are coded 0 on every item even though each selected five options; treat
    their zeros as missing, not as non-selection
- table: uffler_2017_lecture_seating
  issue: |-
    Item text is shown in English. Uffler et al. administered the MSLQ in French
    translation and neither the paper nor the deposit publishes the French wording, so
    the English printed in the study's own codebook ships instead of what respondents
    read.
- table: vanteffelen_2020_foa
  issue: |-
    The Forms of Aggression questionnaire was administered in Dutch and item_text ships
    that Dutch verbatim from the study's own SPSS variable labels; the English in the
    _translated columns was produced by IRW, not by the authors. The questionnaire's
    instructions are not published in either the paper or the deposit, so instructions
    is blank -- the items are bare behaviour phrases ('Ruzie beginnen te maken') whose
    frequency framing survives only in the response anchors.
- table: vaporova_2020_imitation
  issue: |-
    Item text for this table describes behaviour that was coded, not questions that were
    asked: the three items are the demonstrated target actions of a mitten-on-a-puppet
    imitation task scored 0/1 by observers, and the single instructions line is the
    paper's English rendering of an utterance made to German-speaking infants and
    4-year-olds.
- table: verbagg
  issue: |-
    Item text is shown in English: Vansteelandt's questionnaire was administered in
    Dutch to Dutch-speaking Belgian students and no Dutch wording is published in the
    lme4 deposit or in De Boeck and Wilson's online materials, so the English rendering
    reproduced in the psychotools and difR package documentation ships instead, with the
    'I would curse' form of the do-mode items written as the parallel of the published
    'I would want to curse'; note also that resp=1 merges the administered 'perhaps' and
    'yes' options because the table stores lme4's dichotomised r2
- table: wang2022_dass_anxiety
  issue: |-
    Item text for this table is shown in English: Wang et al. (2022) administered the
    Chinese DASS-21 (Wang K et al., 2016) and no Chinese wording is published in the
    study's deposit -- the figshare .xlsx labels its DASS columns DASS1..DASS21 with no
    variable or value labels -- so Lovibond & Lovibond's original English for the seven
    anxiety items ships instead. The response options are the study's own English for
    its endpoints only ('0 = completely inconsistent', '3 = completely in line'); 1 and
    2 are blank because the paper labels no middle anchors, and the canonical DASS
    anchors were deliberately not substituted because this administration relabelled the
    scale. Which canonical anxiety item each code dass_anx_1..7 refers to is inferred
    from the deposit's column numbering: the subscale itself is confirmed against the
    data (alpha 0.8436 for these seven, 0.8729 and 0.8602 for the depression and stress
    triples, against the paper's published 0.84 / 0.87 / 0.86) and each item reproduces
    one deposit column exactly, but a permutation of the seven sentences among those
    columns would not be detectable.
- table: wang2022_dass_depression
  issue: |-
    Item text for this table is shown in English: Wang et al. (2022) administered the
    Chinese DASS-21 (Wang K et al., 2016) and no Chinese wording is published in the
    study's deposit -- the figshare .xlsx labels its DASS columns DASS1..DASS21 with no
    variable or value labels -- so Lovibond & Lovibond's original English for the seven
    depression items ships instead. The response options are the study's own English for
    its endpoints only ('0 = completely inconsistent', '3 = completely in line'); 1 and
    2 are blank because the paper labels no middle anchors, and the canonical DASS
    anchors were deliberately not substituted because this administration relabelled the
    scale. Which canonical depression item each code dass_dep_1..7 refers to is inferred
    from the deposit's column numbering: the subscale itself is confirmed against the
    data (alpha 0.8729 for these seven against the paper's published 0.87, and all
    twelve per-gender cells of the paper's Table 1 reproduce to two decimals) and each
    item's full response distribution matches exactly one deposit column and no other,
    but a permutation of the seven sentences among those columns would not be
    detectable.
- table: wang2022_dass_stress
  issue: |-
    Item text for this table is shown in English: Wang et al. (2022) administered the
    Chinese DASS-21 (Wang K et al., 2016) and no Chinese wording is published in the
    study's deposit -- the figshare .xlsx labels its DASS columns DASS1..DASS21 with no
    variable or value labels -- so Lovibond & Lovibond's original English for the seven
    stress items ships instead. The response options are the study's own English for its
    endpoints only ('0 = completely inconsistent', '3 = completely in line'); 1 and 2
    are blank because the paper labels no middle anchors, and the canonical DASS anchors
    were deliberately not substituted because this administration relabelled the scale.
    Which canonical stress item each code dass_str_1..7 refers to is inferred from the
    deposit's column numbering: the subscale itself is confirmed against the data (alpha
    0.8602 for these seven against the paper's published 0.86, and the paper's Table 1
    stress means by gender and grade reproduce to two decimals) and each item reproduces
    one deposit column exactly, but a permutation of the seven sentences among those
    columns would not be detectable
- table: wang_2016_study1_authliving
  issue: |-
    Item text is shown in English: Wang (2016) administered a Chinese translation of the
    Authenticity Scale and no Chinese wording is published in the PLOS deposit (the SPSS
    file carries no variable or value labels), so Wood et al.'s (2008) original English
    for Authentic Living items 1, 8, 9 and 11 ships instead, with the study's own 1
    (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree) anchors in place of Wood's 1-7 anchors.
    Which of those four canonical items each code authliving1-4 refers to is inferred
    from the standard subscale numbering and could not be checked against the data --
    the block as a whole is verified (the three authenticity tables sum to the paper's
    published total of 42.49, SD 6.18), but a permutation within the four items would
    not be detectable.
- table: wang_2016_study1_power
  issue: |-
    Item text here is shown in English: Wang (2016) administered the authors' own
    Chinese translation of the Sense of Power Scale and no Chinese wording is published
    anywhere in the PLOS deposit (the SPSS file carries no variable or value labels), so
    Anderson, John & Keltner's (2012) original English ships instead. Two things to read
    carefully. The four reverse-worded items (power2, power4, power6, power7) are stored
    ALREADY REVERSE-SCORED -- Cronbach's alpha of the table as stored is .713 against
    the paper's published .71, and un-reversing those four collapses it to .099 -- so
    their option_text is deliberately flipped: resp 1 is 'strongly agree' with the
    printed statement and resp 5 'strongly disagree', the opposite of the other four
    items. And which canonical item each code power1..power8 refers to is inferred from
    the standard Sense of Power numbering: the scale total (27.71, SD 3.78), its
    correlation with self-esteem (.61) and its alpha all reproduce the paper exactly,
    but a permutation within the eight items would not be detectable from the data.
- table: wang_2016_study1_se
  issue: |-
    Item text for this table is shown in English: Wang (2016) administered a Chinese
    translation of the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale and no Chinese item wording is
    published in the PLOS deposit (none of the three SPSS files carries a variable
    label), so Rosenberg's original English ships instead, in the item order of the
    edition the paper cites. The response options ARE the administered Chinese, taken
    from the same article's Study 2 and Study 3 files, with an English translation
    written by IRW alongside; note that they are deliberately reversed for se2, se5,
    se6, se8 and se9, because the live responses are stored already reverse-coded (every
    pair of items correlates positively and the column sum reproduces the paper's
    published total of 38.34, SD 5.08), so a 5 on those items means the respondent
    rejected the negative statement.
- table: wang_2016_study3_auth
  issue: |-
    Item wording is shown in English: Wang (2016) Study 3 administered a Chinese version
    of the Authenticity Scale and no Chinese item wording is published anywhere in the
    PLOS deposit (the S3 SPSS file carries no variable labels), so Wood et al.'s (2008)
    original English ships in its place. The response options are different -- those ARE
    the administered Chinese, taken verbatim from the same file's value labels, with an
    IRW English rendering beside them. Which of the twelve canonical Authenticity Scale
    items each code a1-a12 refers to is inferred from the scale's own numbering: the
    three subscale blocks are confirmed against the data (every item correlates more
    strongly with its canonical block than with either other block, and the scale total
    reproduces the paper's published 38.38/6.88), but a permutation of the four items
    within a block would not be detectable
- table: wang_2016_study3_power
  issue: |-
    Item wording here is shown in English: Wang (2016) Study 3 administered a Chinese
    translation of the Sense of Power Scale and no Chinese item wording is published
    anywhere in the PLOS deposit (the S3 SPSS file carries no variable labels), so
    Anderson, John & Keltner's (2012) original English ships in its place. The response
    options are different -- those ARE the administered Chinese, taken verbatim from the
    same file's value labels, with an IRW English rendering beside them. Read two things
    carefully. The four reverse-worded items (p2, p4, p6, p7) are stored ALREADY
    REVERSE-SCORED -- the raw column sum reproduces the paper's published power total of
    29.37 (SD 5.37) exactly and alpha is .878 against the published .88, while un-
    reversing those four drops alpha to .441 -- so their option text is deliberately
    flipped: a 5 means the respondent rejected the printed negative statement. And which
    canonical Sense of Power item each code p1-p8 refers to is inferred from the scale's
    standard numbering; the forward/reverse split is confirmed against the data (rank 1
    of all 35 possible 4/4 splits on the wording method factor), but a permutation of
    items within either the forward or the reverse group would not be detectable.
- table: wang_2016_study3_se
  issue: |-
    Item wording for this table is shown in English: Wang (2016) Study 3 administered a
    Chinese translation of the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale and no Chinese item wording
    is published anywhere in the PLOS deposit (the S3 SPSS file carries no variable
    labels), so Rosenberg's original English ships instead, in the item order of the
    edition the paper cites. The response options ARE the administered Chinese, taken
    verbatim from that file's value labels, with an English rendering written by IRW
    alongside. Note that the anchors are deliberately reversed for se2, se5, se6, se8
    and se9: the responses are stored already reverse-coded (all 45 inter-item
    correlations are positive and the column sum reproduces the paper's published 39.12,
    SD 6.95, with alpha .898 against a published .90), so a 5 on those items means the
    respondent rejected the negative statement. Which of the ten canonical RSES
    sentences each code se1-se10 names is inferred from that edition's numbering; the
    split into the five negatively and five positively worded items is confirmed against
    the data (rank 1 of all 126 possible 5/5 splits), but a permutation within either
    group would not be detectable.
- table: wang_2025_green_space_wellbeing
  issue: |-
    The English item text for this table was translated from the administered Chinese by
    IRW, not by the study authors; the Chinese wording respondents actually read ships
    alongside it in item_text. The study published no response-option labels for its 1-5
    scale, so option_text is blank
- table: wang_2026_attitude
  issue: |-
    Item wording for this table is shown in English. Wang & Zou administered a Chinese
    translation and back-translation of the attitude scale and no Chinese wording is
    published anywhere in the deposit, so the English from the study's own S1 Appendix
    questionnaire ships in its place. Which of the three items each code ATT1-ATT3
    refers to follows the appendix's own AT1/AT2/AT3 numbering; the data confirm the
    paper's codes sit on these columns (recomputed loadings 0.824/0.818/0.834 against
    the published 0.825/0.815/0.836, with alpha, CR and AVE exact), but the three items
    are near-synonymous enjoyment statements with means of 3.79, 3.72 and 3.73, so a
    permutation among them would not be detectable from the responses.
- table: wang_2026_behavioral_intention
  issue: |-
    Item and response wording for this table is shown in English. Wang and Zou (2026)
    administered a Chinese translation of these behavioural-intention items and no
    Chinese wording is published anywhere in the study's deposit -- the S1 Appendix
    questionnaire and the S2 Appendix data file both contain zero Chinese characters --
    so the authors' own English from the S1 Appendix ships in its place. Which item each
    code BI1-BI5 refers to is not in doubt: the appendix prints the code as a prefix to
    every item, and each live item's response-level counts reproduce the identically-
    named deposit column exactly.
- table: wang_2026_perceived_usefulness
  issue: |-
    Item and response wording for this table is shown in English. Wang and Zou (2026)
    administered a Chinese translation of these perceived-usefulness items and no
    Chinese wording is published anywhere in the study's deposit -- the S1 Appendix
    questionnaire and the S2 Appendix data file both contain no Chinese characters -- so
    the authors' own English from the S1 Appendix ships in its place. Which item each
    code PU1-PU3 refers to is not in doubt: the appendix prints the code as a prefix to
    every item, each live item's response-level counts reproduce the identically-named
    deposit column exactly, and the paper's published per-item VIFs (1.626 / 1.554 /
    1.500) recompute from those columns to three decimal places.
- table: warwas_2022_sharing_economy
  issue: |-
    The survey was conducted by telephone in Polish with a representative sample of
    adult Polish residents, but the only questionnaire published with the study is
    written in English, so the item text shipped here is that English rendering rather
    than the Polish respondents heard
- table: weeldenburg_2022_targetmtpq
  issue: |-
    Item wording for this table is shown in English. Weeldenburg et al. (2022)
    administered the Mastery Teaching Perception Questionnaire in Dutch to 3,150 Dutch
    secondary-school students, and no Dutch wording is published anywhere in the deposit
    -- the SPSS file labels its 26 item columns with bare internal codes (TA_1, AU_1,
    RE_1, ...) and the only questionnaire supplement is the authors' own English
    version, which is what ships. Response options carry only the two endpoints
    ('strongly disagree', 'strongly agree'); 2, 3 and 4 are blank because the source
    labels no middle anchors. Which of the 26 numbered questionnaire items each code
    refers to is inferred within each TARGET construct from the questionnaire's block-
    interleaved numbering: construct membership is confirmed against the data (each
    block reproduces the paper's Table 1 exactly -- Task 3.56/.70/alpha .78, Authority
    3.00/.85/.79, Recognition 3.66/.79/.85, Grouping 3.37/.81/.80, Evaluation
    3.44/.79/.82) and two Authority positions are confirmed by content (Authority_2 is
    the only Authority item correlating most with the Evaluation block, Authority_5 the
    only one correlating most with Grouping), but a permutation of items inside a
    construct block would not be detectable.
- table: wen_2022_pyd
  issue: |-
    Item wording is the authors' own published English; respondents read a Chinese
    questionnaire whose wording the study never deposited, and the 1-5 response anchors
    are not published anywhere, so option_text is blank.
- table: wesselmann_2018_distress
  issue: |-
    The paper prints only the two endpoint anchors of the 1-6 scale ('All of the time',
    'Never') and the deposited SPSS file carries no value labels at all, so option_text
    is blank for the four middle points rather than filled in from the canonical MHI
    wording this study renames; the instructions field carries the instrument's standard
    item stem ('How much of the time during the past month have you...'), which the
    paper corroborates but never prints
- table: wesselmann_2018_pcl
  issue: |-
    The item text is the deposited file's own variable labels, which differ from the
    current PCL-5 form at three items (pcl9 'no one else can be trusted', pcl14 'having
    loving feelings', pcl17's quotation marks) and are shipped as administered rather
    than normalised; the instructions and the five response labels come from the
    published PCL-5 form, because the study's own codebook prints another scale's prompt
    and response options against its PCL-5 block
- table: wirs
  issue: |-
    The item wording is transcribed from the documentation of the R package that
    distributes this dataset rather than from a questionnaire form, and the source never
    states the direction of the 0/1 coding or publishes response labels, so option_text
    is blank throughout
- table: wolf_2017_study1_posaff
  issue: |-
    Despite the table name and dictionary description, these 12 items are a 12-adjective
    selection from the full PANAS and include six negative-affect adjectives
    (distressed, upset, guilty, scared, hostile, irritable) as well as six positive
    ones; the stored responses are raw, so the negative items must be reverse-scored
    before a positive-affect score is computed.
- table: wolf_2017_study2_posaff_post
  issue: |-
    Despite the table name and description, these 12 items are a 12-adjective selection
    from the full PANAS and include six negative-affect adjectives (distressed, upset,
    guilty, scared, hostile, irritable) as well as six positive ones; the stored
    responses are raw, so the negative items must be reverse-scored before a positive-
    affect score is computed.
- table: wolf_2017_study2_posaff_pre
  issue: |-
    Despite the table name and description, these 8 items are an 8-adjective selection
    from the PANAS and include four negative-affect adjectives (upset, scared, hostile,
    irritable) as well as four positive ones (proud, enthusiastic, interested, alert);
    the stored responses are raw, so the negative items must be reverse-scored before a
    positive-affect score is computed.
- table: wolters2026_panas_na
  issue: |-
    Respondents completed the German PANAS (Krohne et al., 1996); the wording IRW ships
    is the English original (Watson, Clark & Tellegen, 1988) mapped item-for-item onto
    it, because the deposit contains no item wording at all and the German version is
    published only under non-commercial, permission-required terms that IRW does not
    redistribute under
- table: wolters2026_panas_pa
  issue: |-
    Respondents completed the German PANAS (Krohne et al., 1996); the wording IRW ships
    is the English original (Watson, Clark & Tellegen, 1988) mapped item-for-item onto
    it, because the deposit contains no item wording at all and the German version is
    published only under non-commercial, permission-required terms that IRW does not
    redistribute under
- table: wolters2026_wi
  issue: |-
    Item wording for this table is shown in English: the study was run in German and no
    German wording is published in its figshare deposit (a plain spreadsheet whose only
    WI content is the column names WI_1..WI_14), so the Whiteley Index's English, as
    reproduced by Eslami, Ahmadipour & Bagheri (2017), ships instead. Two things to read
    carefully. Which of the fourteen canonical Whiteley items each code wi_1..wi_14
    refers to is inferred from the instrument's own numbering, not stated by the source:
    the item-rest profile matches published per-item loadings at Spearman 0.54
    (permutation p = 0.026), which rules out a scrambled mapping but would not detect a
    swap between two items of similar loading. And the responses are Whiteley SCORES,
    not raw answers, so for wi_9 -- the scale's one reverse-keyed item -- a 1 means the
    respondent answered 'no', the opposite of every other item; its item-rest
    correlation is +0.32 where raw storage would be negative.
- table: wu2026_liking
  issue: |-
    The ten items of this table are ten ceramic vase photographs, not ten different
    questions: every item carries the same single statement, 'This vase is pleasing to
    see.', and the vases themselves (Fig 1 of the source paper) are images with no
    published descriptions, so nothing in the item text distinguishes one item from
    another. The English shown is the paper's own wording; the survey was run face-to-
    face with 200 native Chinese speakers and no Chinese version of the statement
    appears anywhere in the deposit.
- table: wu_2024_resilience
  issue: |-
    wu_2024_resilience was administered in Chinese (the Chen et al. 2020 Chinese Brief
    Resilience Scale), but the Chinese wording is published nowhere in the study's
    deposit or supplements, so the item and option text shipped here is Smith et al.'s
    (2008) original English BRS rather than what respondents read; the instruction line
    is likewise the BRS's printed paper-form instruction, while this study was
    administered online
- table: wu2026_novel
  issue: |-
    Each of the ten items rates a different photographed ceramic vase, so all ten share
    the same single-item wording "This is a novel vase." and the stimulus is identified
    only by the item code: Novel_k is vase k of Fig 1 of the source paper. The shipped
    wording is the paper's English; the survey was run face-to-face with native Chinese
    speakers and no Chinese wording is published in the deposit or supplements. Only the
    1 and 7 scale points are labelled, as in the source.
- table: wu2026_typical
  issue: |-
    The ten items of this table are ten ceramic vase photographs, not ten different
    questions: every item carries the same single statement, 'This is a typical vase.',
    and the vases themselves (Fig 1 of the source paper) are images with no published
    descriptions, so nothing in the item text distinguishes one item from another. The
    English shown is the paper's own wording; the survey was run face-to-face with 200
    native Chinese speakers and no Chinese version of the statement appears anywhere in
    the deposit.
- table: wurm_2016_mdi
  issue: |-
    The Wurm et al. physicians were surveyed in German, but the German MDI wording is in
    neither the deposited SPSS file nor the paper's supplements, so the item text
    shipped here is the canonical English MDI (Nielsen, Oernboel, Bech & Christensen
    2019, Table 2) rather than what respondents read. Items mdi8_neu and mdi10_neu are
    each scored as the higher of two sub-items -- restless vs slowed down, and reduced
    vs increased appetite -- so their item_text carries both alternatives and a response
    of 4 does not say which of the two produced it.
- table: xiao_2026_entrepreneurial_intention
  issue: |-
    The shipped item text is the authors' own English; respondents answered a Chinese
    version whose wording the study does not publish. The four entrepreneurial-intention
    items are In1-In4 in the data but EI1-EI4 in the study's codebook, and their one-to-
    one correspondence follows the codebook's listing order rather than any stated key.
- table: xiong_2025_dass21
  issue: |-
    The DASS-21 instructions and 0-3 anchors shipped for this table are the official
    paper form's wording ("Please read each statement and circle a number 0, 1, 2 or
    3"); Xiong et al. administered the scale online through Google Forms, so respondents
    selected rather than circled a number. The item wording is the same official form's,
    verbatim.
- table: xu_2022_ples_aa
  issue: |-
    The wording shipped for item_1.1 is the deposited questionnaire's own header, 'Field
    of Higher Education, Implement PLE Platform's information disclosure policy.', which
    differs in substance from item 1.1 of the final published PLES-AA ('Provide a
    rationale for the implementation of PLE in Higher Education', S1 Appendix); the
    other 15 items agree between the two. Separately, the survey was administered in
    Chinese via WenJuanXing and no Chinese wording appears anywhere in the deposit or
    supplements, so all item text here is the study's own English.
- table: xu_2025_hcq_p
  issue: |-
    For the 23 items Xu et al. list as reverse-scored (HCQ-P 2, 5, 6, 12, 13, 14, 17,
    19, 21, 22, 24, 25, 26, 27, 30, 32, 34, 38, 39, 40, 43, 45, 48) the stored resp is
    already reverse-scored, so their shipped anchors run 1 = Strongly agree to 6 =
    Strongly disagree while the remaining 26 items run the other way; separately, the
    item wording is the administered Chinese but the two anchor labels are the paper's
    English, because no Chinese anchor wording is published and scale points 2-5 are
    unlabelled.
- table: yandun2026_logical_thinking
  issue: |-
    The item wording shipped for this table is the authors' own English translation,
    deposited as DATA_MATRIX_TRANSLATED.xlsx; the assessment itself was administered in
    Spanish in Ecuador and no Spanish wording was deposited. The 1-5 anchors are
    published only at the endpoints (1 = Never, 5 = Always), so options 2-4 carry no
    text.
- table: yandun2026_memory
  issue: |-
    The item wording shipped for this table is the authors' own English translation,
    deposited as DATA_MATRIX_TRANSLATED.xlsx; the assessment itself was administered in
    Spanish in Ecuador and no Spanish wording was deposited. The 1-5 anchors are
    published only at the endpoints (1 = Never, 5 = Always), so options 2-4 carry no
    text.
- table: yang2026_efl_learner_perspective
  issue: |-
    The four rating items (item_29-item_32) are stored with 1 = strongest agreement and
    4 = weakest, the reverse of the 1=lowest/4=highest scoring the source paper reports;
    the paper's means 2.98/2.96/3.08/3.21 equal 5 minus the stored means. No response-
    option wording is shipped because neither the deposit nor the paper publishes
    anchors, and the 0/1 items are select-all-that-apply checkboxes where 1 = option
    selected.
- table: yang_2018_cesd
  issue: |-
    The Yang et al. respondents answered a Chinese CES-D, but no Chinese wording appears
    in the deposited SPSS file or the paper's supplements, so the item text shipped here
    is the canonical English Radloff (1977) CES-D and the response anchors are the
    authors' own English labels from that file; the items are stored raw (resp 1 = least
    frequent) for all twenty, including the four positively worded ones (E4, E8, E12,
    E16), which the authors reverse before summing.
- table: yang_2023_consumption_intent
  issue: |-
    This table is misnamed: its items F1-F4 are the study's CUSTOMER PERCEIVED VALUE
    scale, not consumption intention -- the paper's Tables 1 and 3 assign F1-F4 to
    perceived value and E1-E3 to consumption intention, and recomputing Cronbach's alpha
    per block from the study's own S1 File reproduces all six published alphas to three
    decimals (this block .849, matching 'Customer perceived value'; the consumption-
    intention alpha is .934, which this block misses by .085). The consumption-intention
    items are in the sibling table yang_2023_perceived_value. The item wording shown is
    also English: the survey was administered in Chinese and no Chinese wording is
    published in the article's single supplementary file, so the authors' own English
    from Table 1 is what ships, transcribed from a table published only as an image.
- table: yang_2023_emotional_eating_cesd
  issue: |-
    The respondents were Chinese undergraduates answering a Chinese CES-D, but the
    study's single supplementary file contains no Chinese text at all, so the item
    wording shipped here is the authors' own English column headers from that file
    (rough, unpunctuated, and rendering both CES-D items 6 and 18 as 'I feel sad'). One
    item, CESD_2, has no header wording of its own -- the survey export overwrote it
    with the block instruction -- so it carries the canonical English CES-D item 1
    wording, identified by elimination and corroborated against the file's own
    precomputed total score. Note also that CESD_1 and CESD_2 are canonical CES-D items
    2 and 1 in that order, not 1 and 2. No response-option wording is shipped: the
    source publishes none and the paper's description of the response scale contradicts
    itself.
- table: yang_2023_emotional_eating_ders
  issue: |-
    The survey was administered in Chinese and no Chinese wording is published in the
    article's single supplementary file, so the item text shipped here is the English
    column headers of the authors' own deposited workbook, transcribed verbatim
    including their rough phrasing and typos. Two rows are not the study's words: item
    DERS_1, whose source column header was the block's instruction text rather than an
    item, carries the canonical Gratz & Roemer (2004) DERS item 1 placed by elimination;
    and the five response anchors, which are the canonical DERS labels (the paper
    misstates the format as 1-4 while the data carry five levels). Responses are stored
    RAW, so the 11 reverse-keyed items (DERS_1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 10, 17, 20, 22, 24, 34) must
    be reversed before summing a DERS total.
- table: yang_2023_emotional_eating_eesr
  issue: |-
    The wording shown for this table is English taken from the column headers of the
    study's own deposited data file; the scale was administered in Chinese (Zhu Hong's
    2012 Chinese revision of the Emotional Eating Scale) and no Chinese wording is
    published in the article's single supplementary file. Two consequences a user should
    know: item EESR_1 carries no text at all, because the survey export overwrote that
    column's label with the question stem shown in `instructions`, and two pairs of
    distinct items share an identical English label (EESR_5 and EESR_20 both read
    'hostile'; EESR_13 and EESR_22 both read 'depressed') because the deposit's English
    does not distinguish the underlying Chinese words. The 1-5 response options carry no
    text: the paper describes only the endpoints (1 = a total lack of the emotion, 5 = a
    high degree) and never publishes anchor labels.
- table: yang_2023_emotional_eating_uppsp
  issue: |-
    The scale was administered in Chinese and the article's single supplementary file
    contains no Chinese text, so the wording shown here is the English column headers of
    the study's own deposited workbook, transcribed verbatim including their rough
    phrasing and their mid-sentence truncations (UPPSP_12 and UPPSP_14 simply stop part-
    way). Two things are not the study's words: UPPSP_1, whose header the survey export
    overwrote with the block instruction and truncated to the single letter 'I', carries
    the canonical SUPPS-P item 'I generally like to see things through to the end.'
    placed by elimination on the scoring key and corroborated in the data; and the two
    response anchors, which are shipped 1 = strongly disagree, 4 = strongly agree -- the
    REVERSE of the paper's Measures sentence, because the negative-urgency items
    correlate +0.54 with the study's own depression total, which is only possible if the
    high codes are the agreeing pole. The two middle levels carry no text because the
    study publishes none. Responses are stored raw, so the premeditation and
    perseverance items (UPPSP_1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 11, 12, 19) must be reversed before summing
    an impulsivity total.
- table: yang_2023_green_brand_image
  issue: |-
    The wording shown is English: the survey was administered in Chinese and no Chinese
    wording is published in the article's single supplementary file, so the authors' own
    English from the paper's Table 1 is what ships. One item code needs care: the
    paper's tables print the third social-image item as C3, while the study's raw data
    file (and therefore this table) calls that column C4 -- the item shipped for C4 is
    the one the paper labels C3, confirmed by reproducing the paper's published
    reliability for that three-item factor (.712) from C1, C2 and C4 exactly. Only the
    two endpoints of the 1-5 scale are published (1 = disagree, 5 = agree), so options
    2-4 carry no text.
- table: yang_2023_perceived_value
  issue: |-
    This table is misnamed: its items E1-E3 are the study's CONSUMPTION INTENTION scale,
    not perceived value -- the paper's Tables 1 and 3 both assign E1-E3 to consumption
    intention and F1-F4 to customer perceived value, and recomputing Cronbach's alpha
    per block from the study's own S1 File reproduces all six published alphas to three
    decimals (this block .934, matching 'Consumption intention'; the customer-perceived-
    value alpha is .849, which this block misses by .085). The perceived-value items are
    in the sibling table yang_2023_consumption_intent. The wording shown is also
    English: the survey was administered in Chinese and no Chinese wording appears in
    the article's single supplementary file, so the authors' own English from Table 1 is
    what ships, transcribed from a table published only as an image; item E3 ends mid-
    phrase ('...information and knowledge of') in the source and was not repaired.
- table: yang_2026_igd_benefits
  issue: |-
    Despite the table name, only two of the four items rate perceived BENEFITS of
    internet gaming (benefit_a = at present, benefit_c = in the future); benefit_b and
    benefit_d rate perceived COSTS at present and in the future, which the shipped item
    text states. Only the scale endpoints were published (1 = none, 10 = extremely
    strong), so response options 2-9 carry no text.
- table: yang_2026_pars3
  issue: |-
    Item wording for yang_2026_pars3 is the source paper's own English rendering of a
    Chinese-administered PARS-3, and the paper introduces each stem with 'e.g.', so the
    stems are illustrative rather than a verbatim transcript; the administered Chinese
    wording is not published anywhere in the deposit.
- table: yin_2022_gad7
  issue: |-
    The seven item codes in this table are the source workbook's own column headers
    ('GAD-7 question: afraid' and so on), which name each symptom but are not the
    sentences respondents answered; the item text, instructions and the four response
    labels shipped here are the official GAD-7 English form's verbatim wording. The
    study's own Methods section independently reproduces all seven stems word for word
    in the same order as the columns, so only capitalisation and the form's '(Use a tick
    to indicate your answer)' line differ -- that line is dropped because this study
    used a Google Form. The paper prints only the endpoints of the 0-3 scale, so the
    middle anchors 'Several days' and 'More than half the days' also come from the
    official form. Separately, 'GAD-7 question: trouble relaxing' has 151 responses
    where the other six have 153, from two blank cells in the source file.
- table: yu_2025_bedtime_procrastination
  issue: |-
    Item text for yu_2025_bedtime_procrastination is the canonical English Bedtime
    Procrastination Scale (Kroese et al. 2014); the study administered a Chinese
    revision whose wording is published nowhere in the deposit or the article. Two
    caveats on the response options: the source paper's own anchor list prints
    'sometimes' twice (1 = never; 2 = sometimes; 3 = sometimes; 4 = often; 5 = always)
    and is transcribed as printed, and for BP2, BP3, BP7 and BP9 the stored resp is the
    already-reverse-scored value rather than the administered answer, so those four
    items carry the anchors in descending order (resp 1 = always ... 5 = never).
- table: yu_2025_physical_activity
  issue: |-
    Item text for yu_2025_physical_activity is a third-party paper's published English
    rendering of the Chinese-administered PARS-3 (Zhang & Zhang 2022, IJERPH 19:11451,
    Table 1), not the wording the study's adolescents read, and the assignment of
    PE1/PE2/PE3 to intensity/duration/frequency is inferred from the paper's stated
    dimension order rather than verified against the data -- the source publishes no
    per-item statistics, and every PA-block statistic it does publish (alpha
    0.828/0.688/0.730, KMO) is unchanged by any relabelling of the three items.
- table: yuebo_2024_netbenefit
  issue: |-
    Item text for yuebo_2024_netbenefit is the study's own English version of a
    questionnaire that was administered in Chinese; the administered Chinese wording is
    published in neither the paper nor its supplements. No response-option labels are
    shipped because the source states only that the items used a 5-point Likert scale
    and prints no anchors.
- table: lys_2020_rape_3_kpnts
  issue: |-
    The English in `item_text_translated` is a MACHINE TRANSLATION produced by IRW from the
    administered Polish -- it is not the instrument's own English and has not been reviewed
    by a Polish speaker. `item_text` is the administered Polish, which is authoritative;
    where the two diverge the translation follows the Polish, so `kpnts7` and `kpnts19` read
    'better' / 'worse' groups rather than the canonical scale's 'superior' / 'inferior'. Two
    further things to know about this table. The item codes are not contiguous -- kpnts2, 3,
    5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 13, 14, 16, 17, 19, 20, 22, 23, 24, sixteen items drawn from a longer
    block -- and the eight reverse-worded items (kpnts3, 8, 10, 14, 16, 20, 23, 24) are
    **already recoded in the deposit**, so higher `resp` means more social dominance
    orientation for every item and the deposit's SDO score is the plain sum of all sixteen
    (reproduced exactly for 370 of 370 complete rows). Do not reverse them again. Finally,
    the code misleads: despite `kpnts`, this table IS the Social Dominance Scale, while
    `lys_2020_rape_3_sds` is NOT -- it is the 29-item social DESIRABILITY scale.
- table: zamzuri_2021_rpap_attitude
  issue: |-
    Respondents completed a bilingual English/Malay form; only the English wording is
    published, so the Malay text they may have read is not included.
- table: zamzuri_2021_rpap_practice
  issue: |-
    Respondents completed a bilingual English/Malay form; only the English wording is
    published, so the Malay text they may have read is not included.
- table: zamzuri_2021_rpap_risk_perception
  issue: |-
    Respondents completed a bilingual English/Malay form; only the English wording is
    published, so the Malay text they may have read is not included. In the response
    data, items D2, D3, D7, D8, D9, D10, D11 and D12 are stored reverse-scored (1 =
    strongly agree), so their anchors here are reversed to match; D1, D4, D5 and D6 keep
    1 = strongly disagree.
- table: zautra_2015_tmms24
  issue: |-
    Item wording is transcribed verbatim from the study's own codebook, including its
    spelling slips (e.g. 'attention' and 'definer' in items 8 and 10 for Spanish
    'atención' and 'definir'); the English translations were produced by IRW, because
    the English printed by the study is the original English TMMS rather than a
    translation of the Spanish items administered.
- table: zeng_2026_gai_exploitation
  issue: |-
    Administered in Chinese; the item text shown is the authors' own English rendering
    published in the paper, as the Chinese wording was not released.
- table: zeng_2026_gai_inst_support
  issue: |-
    Administered in Chinese; the item text shown is the authors' own English rendering
    published in the paper, as the Chinese wording was not released.
- table: zeng_2026_gai_learning_effect
  issue: |-
    Administered in Chinese; the item text shown is the authors' own English rendering
