    was not accessible. The printed form flips option direction between items, but the deposited
    file stores one uniform direction (3 = most positive), so for items 1, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 15, 17,
    18 and 20 the option text is shipped in the reverse of the printed order to match the data.
- table: gilbert_meta_68
  issue: |-
    Item text is the study's own English task label (e.g. 'Comprehension', 'Word dictation'), not
    the Hindi question a child read: the written Hindi test came in parallel samples and the table
    records no sample, so items within a family share one label (eight read 'Comprehension', four
    'Word dictation'). The Haryana data label items only by question number, so the labels are
    bridged from the study's dictionary for its Bihar/Uttarakhand arm by matching question numbers
    -- an inference resting on Haryana having used the same forms. Only sample 1 of the Haryana test
    is deposited, so its Hindi wording is deliberately not shipped. resp is 0/1 with 1 = correct
    inferred from the deposit's scoring code; option_text is blank.
- table: gilbert_meta_69
  issue: |-
    Item text is the study's own English task label (e.g. 'Multiplication', 'Addition(2-3 digit)'),
    not the specific sum a child was given: the written mathematics test came in parallel samples
    and the table records no sample, so several items share one label (five read 'Multiplication',
    four 'Addition(2-3 digit)'). The Haryana data label items only by question number, so the labels
    are bridged from the study's dictionary for its Bihar/Uttarakhand arm by matching question
    numbers -- an inference resting on Haryana having used the same forms. Only sample 1 of the
    Haryana test is deposited, so its wording is deliberately not shipped. resp is 0/1 with 1 =
    correct inferred from the deposit's scoring code; option_text is blank.
- table: hui_2024_gbfs
  issue: |-
    The item text here is the administered Chinese from the study's S1 File. The English in
    item_text_translated is not a translation of it but the original English General Benefit Finding
    Scale (Cassidy, McLaughlin & Giles 2014) aligned item for item, so it diverges where the Chinese
    adaptation did -- item b18 reads roughly 'made me more confident in others' in Chinese against
    the original's 'Led me to feel more positive about others'. The English instructions and
    response anchors have no published source and were written by IRW.
- table: iandolo_2021_asq
  issue: |-
    Items ASQ_20, ASQ_21 and ASQ_33 are stored raw for the Spanish subsample (cov_country = 1) but
    already reverse-scored for the Italian and Japanese subsamples (cov_country = 2 and 3) -- the
    published subscale means reproduce only under that split -- so no single anchor mapping is
    correct for those three items and their option text is blank. The item wording is the study's
    Spanish version, which only the 139 Spanish respondents read; the 85 Italian and 130 Japanese
    respondents read back-translated versions the deposit does not publish. The English in
    item_text_translated is Feeney, Noller & Hanrahan's original ASQ wording, not a translation of
    the Spanish.
- table: karpudewan_2022_stp_cca
  issue: |-
    The paper describes a five-point response scale, 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree),
    but no response of 5 occurs anywhere in the authors' data (11,513 responses here and 9,900 in
    the companion EFA sample are all 1-4), so the form as administered appears to have been four-
    point and the response labels are left blank rather than attached to the wrong levels. The
    instructions field is the paper's own sentence describing the task, not the questionnaire's
    instruction text, which is not published.
- table: nas_rogoza_2024_study5_nas
  issue: |-
    Study 5 was a Polish daily diary, so the item text is the administered Polish with English
    alongside; the four English adjectives and the 0-100 slider anchors are the authors' own from
    their OSF NAS.xlsx, but the daily instruction was never published in English and its English
    here was produced by IRW. The deposited .sav has no labels, so the adjective assigned to
    NAS1-NAS4 follows the order of the study's daily codebook (which differs from the 16-item form's
    order). The data confirm NAS2 (Lekceważący / Depreciating) and NAS3 (Wyzyskujący / Exploitative)
    but cannot tell NAS1 from NAS4 (Znieważający / Abusive vs Bezczelny / Nasty), whose means differ
    by 0.5 points on the 0-100 slider.
- table: nas_rogoza_2024_study5_ngs
  issue: |-
    Study 5 was a Polish daily diary, so the item text is the administered Polish with English
    alongside; the English adjectives and the 0/100 anchors are the authors' own from the paper, but
    the daily instruction was never published in English and its English here was produced by IRW.
    The deposited .sav has no labels, so the assignment of NGS1-NGS4 to Brilliant, Glorious,
    Powerful and Prestigious follows the order in the study's daily codebook and the paper. The data
    confirm the split between the two higher-endorsed adjectives (NGS1, NGS2) and the two lower ones
    (NGS3, NGS4), but cannot distinguish Brilliant from Glorious or Powerful from Prestigious.
- table: nas_rogoza_2024_study5_nvs
  issue: |-
    Study 5 was a Polish daily diary, so the item text is the administered Polish with English
    alongside; the English adjectives and anchors are the authors' own (from the article and the
    deposit's NAS.xlsx), but the daily instruction was never published in English and its English
    here was produced by IRW. The deposited .sav has no labels, so the assignment of NVS1-NVS4 to
    Ignored, Resentful, Misunderstood and Underappreciated follows the order three of the study's
    documents share; the data confirm NVS3 and NVS4 as the more strongly endorsed pair but cannot
    separate Ignored from Resentful or Misunderstood from Underappreciated. NVS1's Polish
    'Zleckewazony' is reproduced as both state-protocol codebooks spell it; it is a misspelling of
    'Zlekcewazony'.
- table: number_pattern_game
  issue: |-
    Each item is one stimulus set, not one question: participants judged 30 different candidate
    numbers against each set, but the IRW table drops the source file's `target` column, so which
    number a given 0/1 response referred to is not recoverable. item_text therefore ships the on-
    screen question template with [TARGET] in the slot where the number appeared.
- table: papp_silva-martins2023
  issue: |-
    The item text here is the administered European Portuguese form. The English in
    item_text_translated is not a translation of it but O'Connor et al.'s (2014) original English
    PPAPP wording for the same numbered items, and three items diverge from the Portuguese: item 9
    (Portuguese 'futebol ou basquetebol', English 'soccer or baseball'), item 13 (the Portuguese
    names lessons, practices or games) and item 16 (the Portuguese switches to past tense, 'how many
    times did you fail to enrol'). The English instructions and the five response-option labels were
    translated from the Portuguese by IRW; O'Connor's own anchors differ ('often' where the
    Portuguese has 'almost always'). Despite the table name, the instrument is the PPAPP, not the
    PAPP item bank.
- table: phq_BrummerHoffman_2021
  issue: |-
    This table pools two administration arms whose wording differed by design: the text shown is the
    Study 1 grid form (the shared frame in section_prompt, the symptom in item_text), while Study 2
    respondents saw each item as one complete Portuguese sentence, e.g. 'Nas ultimas duas semanas,
    em quantos dias voce teve pouco interesse ou prazer em fazer as coisas?'. The English translated
    columns are mixed provenance -- seven symptom phrases come from the deposit's own English
    questionnaire, but the frame stems, all anchors and the insomnia and suicide rows were
    translated for IRW, because the deposit's English form prints canonical PHQ-9 anchors and an
    oversleeping clause that were not administered.
- table: previc_bohn2023
  issue: |-
    This table holds the PREVIC's initial 379-word calibration pool, not the 89-word published
    PREVIC; each item code is the German word on the card, and the per-word English glosses are the
    study authors' own. The English instructions and the YES/NO option labels were translated from
    the German by IRW -- the on-screen controls were an unlabelled check mark and cross. The German
    instructions come from the public 2025 demo of the task app, so minor wording drift from the
    2021 administration cannot be excluded.
- table: protestant_workethic
  issue: |-
    Only items 1-19 of this table are Protestant Work Ethic Scale items. Items 20-29 are the Ten
    Item Personality Inventory (1-7 scale) and items 30-45 are a 16-word vocabulary check-list (0 =
    unchecked, 1 = checked, including the non-words 'cuivocal', 'florted' and 'verdid' as a validity
    check), both administered after the PWE in the same session.
- table: turner_2022_sr_belief_change
  issue: |-
    The study's S2 File numbers its items by factor-loading rank rather than by the question codes
    in the data, so the text-to-code mapping was reconstructed by reproducing the paper's published
    loadings and cross-loadings. Q34_SRchange and Q35_Srchange publish near-identical loadings
    (.693/.036 and .690/.037) and are separated only by their endorsement means, so a swap of those
    two texts cannot be fully excluded.
- table: ucla_BrummerHoffman_2021
  issue: |-
    The second item is coded ucla_left_out, but the Portuguese actually administered reads
    'Abandonado' (abandoned) rather than a translation of the canonical 'How often do you feel left
    out?'; item_text_translated follows the administered Portuguese ('Abandoned'), while the study's
    own English questionnaire prints the canonical wording. The other two item translations and the
    anchors come from that English questionnaire, but the English of the shared stem was translated
    by IRW.
- table: valdivia_2023_oms
  issue: |-
    Item text is the administered Mexican Spanish from the study's S1 File. The English in
    item_text_translated is the instrument's official OMS-HC-15 wording rather than a translation of
    the Spanish, and for item 2 the two diverge -- the Spanish reads 'comodo(a) trabajando con el'
    (comfortable working with him) and appears to omit a verb, while the English reads 'I would be
    as willing to work with him/her'. The English of the instructions was written by IRW, not by the
    study.
- table: valverdeberrocoso_2021_tictip
  issue: |-
    The English item wording is the study's own (paper Table 2), but its item 9 renders the
    administered 'mensajeria instantanea (v.gr. Rayuela)' as '(e.g. Scratch)'; IRW ships 'Rayuela'
    to match what respondents read. The English of the instructions was written by IRW, not by the
    study.
- table: vanteffelen_2020_aq_hostility
  issue: |-
    The paper describes a 10-item hostility scale anchored 'extremely uncharacteristic of me' to
    'extremely characteristic of me', but the deposited data hold the 8 canonical Buss-Perry
    hostility items and the file's own value labels are a Dutch agreement scale whose midpoint is
    'Weet niet' (don't know); the text shipped follows the deposit. The English in
    item_text_translated is Buss & Perry's (1992) published wording, not a translation of the Dutch,
    and the English of the response options was written by IRW.
- table: vocabulary_iq
  issue: |-
    Only items 1-45 are vocabulary questions. Items 46-75 are the optional post-test personality
    survey (S1-S30), whose 1-5 agreement responses were lost when the processing script scored the
    whole table against the vocabulary answer key, so every one of those 30 items reads resp = 0 for
    every respondent and carries no response option text. Among the vocabulary items, resp = 0 means
    'not the correct pair', which also absorbs the 0.87% of cells where the respondent skipped the
    question; the 13.3% of cells where they chose 'don't know' are missing rather than 0.
- table: FAD_fadplus_goto2021
  issue: |-
    The 54 item codes are 27 items, not 54: the same 27 FAD-Plus items appear in two different
    Japanese translations, both given to the same respondents -- FAD_G_* is the FAD-J (Goto et al.
    2015) and FAD_W_* is the FAD+ (Watanabe et al. 2014), although the table name mentions only
    Goto. item_text is the administered Japanese; the `_translated` column holds the English
    FAD-Plus original from the study's supplementary table, not a translation of the Japanese.
- table: FEDSP_Trzcinska_2023_MonKnow
  issue: |-
    item_text is IRW's bracketed description of what the preschoolers were shown ('[children were
    shown: ...]'), not wording anyone read or heard: the spoken question put to the child is not
    published in the deposit and the paper is paywalled. The zloty amounts come from the study's
    data file; the framing and the coin/note distinction are IRW's. The task was administered in
    Polish, but the description is in English.
- table: IJLS_Eersel_2024_IJLSreaction
  issue: |-
    The item text is the administered Dutch from the paper's Appendix, with the authors' own
    English in the `_translated` column, but the response anchors are not what respondents read:
    no Dutch anchors are published, so option_text shows the English labels from the study's SPSS
    value labels (1 = Never to 5 = Always).
- table: NAMPRB_Siwiak_2024_SSUB
  issue: |-
    The table carries 25 item codes for a 20-item scale. The five religious items (1, 5, 14, 15,
    19) appear as SSUB_TRB_n at wave 0 and as SSUB_NAB_n at wave 1, because the retest columns
    were renamed in bulk; each pair is the same question and carries the same text here. The items
    are the administered Polish with the authors' English alongside, but the anchors (Strongly
    disagree to Strongly agree) are the English published in the study's preprint, not the Polish
    respondents saw. The ten reverse-scored items (3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18) are stored
    unreversed.
- table: Resistance
  issue: |-
    resp is not a rating: it is the absolute difference (0-5) between the respondent's ratings of
    the two frames of each framing problem, so each item_text carries both administered wordings
    under 'Gain frame:'/'Loss frame:' or 'Positive frame:'/'Negative frame:' labels that IRW added,
    and option_text is blank. The wording is the English version, which only the 261 North American
    respondents read; the other 245 answered a validated Bulgarian translation that is not shipped.
- table: carney_2023_substance_use
  issue: |-
    The eight items are indicators the study derived, not questions respondents answered: 1 means
    any use of that substance in the past three months on the WHO ASSIST, except alcohol, where 1
    means an AUDIT score above 8. The paper reproduces no ASSIST or AUDIT wording, so item_text
    describes each indicator in the paper's words and option_text gives the thresholds, not
    administered anchors.
- table: chile_2023_social-welfare-survey_rr
  issue: |-
    The item text here is the administered Spanish, which is what respondents read. The English
    in the `_translated` columns was produced by IRW rather than by the study's authors. Item
    texts are the survey's own abbreviated codebook labels (e.g. `fam.`, `serv.`, `RRSS`), which
    the translation expands.
- table: chile_2023_social-welfare-survey_ss
  issue: |-
    The item text here is the administered Spanish, which is what respondents read. The English
    in the `_translated` columns was produced by IRW rather than by the study's authors. Item
    texts are the survey's own abbreviated codebook labels, which the translation expands.
- table: chile_2023_social-welfare-survey_u
  issue: |-
    The item text here is the administered Spanish, which is what respondents read. The English
    in the `_translated` columns was produced by IRW rather than by the study's authors. Item
    texts are the survey's own abbreviated codebook labels, which the translation expands.
- table: enem_2023_1mil_ch
  issue: |-
    The wording is INEP's accessibility (screen-reader) edition of the exam, not the printed
    booklet candidates read: notation, units and symbols are written out in words, INEP's verbal
    descriptions of figures and tables are part of the text, and source credits can sit before a
    passage. Compared word by word with the standard booklet, only 24 of the 45 items came out
    identical. No English ships.
- table: enem_2023_1mil_cn
  issue: |-
    The wording is INEP's accessibility (screen-reader) edition of the exam, not the printed
    booklet candidates read: notation, units and symbols are written out in words and source
    credits can sit before a passage; only 5 of the 45 items came out identical to the standard
    booklet. Two items (78578, 54804) were transcribed from the standard booklet instead, and
    their figure, table and equation descriptions -- plus a replacement for item 60332's figure,
    which INEP declined to describe -- were generated by IRW and are marked inline '(gerada por
    IA)'. Item 78578's options are graphs, so its option_text is blank. No English ships.
- table: enem_2023_1mil_lc
  issue: |-
    The wording is INEP's accessibility (screen-reader) edition of the exam, not the printed
    booklet candidates read: notation is written out in words, INEP's figure descriptions are part
    of the text, and source credits can sit before a passage; 23 of the 50 items came out
    identical to the standard booklet. The 50 codes cover 45 positions because the five
    foreign-language questions exist in an English and a Spanish version. Four items (140595,
    140736, 140959, 15035) carry INEP's '[supressao de texto]' where copyrighted stimulus was
    withheld. No English ships.
- table: enem_2023_1mil_mt
  issue: |-
    The wording is INEP's accessibility (screen-reader) edition of the exam, not the printed
    booklet candidates read: notation, units and symbols are written out in words, and only 2 of
    the 44 items came out identical to the standard booklet. Two items (125902, 81742) were
    transcribed from the standard booklet instead, and their figure descriptions were generated by
    IRW and are marked inline '(gerada por IA)'. Item 125902's options are diagrams, so its
    option_text is blank. No English ships.
- table: enkavi_2019_gonogo
  issue: |-
    The go/no-go stimuli are wordless coloured squares, so item_text is blank by design. resp is
    trial accuracy, not the key pressed, so option_text reads Correct/Incorrect -- a scoring label
    rather than an option. The two colour words in the instructions were counterbalanced per
    participant and appear as the placeholders [go color] and [no-go color].
- table: enkavi_2019_simon
  issue: |-
    The Simon stimulus is a coloured box with no text, so item_text is blank by design and the
    item code (colour x side x congruency) describes the stimulus. resp is trial accuracy, so
    option_text reads Correct/Incorrect rather than a response option. The two arrow keys were
    counterbalanced across participants and appear in the instructions as the placeholders [KEY
    FOR RED]/[KEY FOR BLUE].
- table: enkavi_2019_stopsignal
  issue: |-
    The four stimuli are wordless shape images, so item_text is blank by design and the item code
    carries the shape. resp is trial accuracy, so option_text reads Correct/Incorrect rather than
    a response option, and there is no correct_response because the shape-to-key mapping was
    shuffled per session. '[prompt_text]' in the instructions stands for that per-session legend,
    which was shown as images.
- table: estcrm_selfeff
  issue: |-
    The item wording is the one-line English description of each column in the EstCRM R package
    documentation, not a transcript of the administered form. The scale (Kan 2009) comes from a
    Turkish study and was probably administered in Turkish, but no source states the language, so
    the English is likely a rendering rather than what respondents read.
- table: florida_twins_par
  issue: |-
    Two of the 31 codes are not questions: parstrict and parwarmth are the study's own sum scores
    over the other items, so they carry a bracketed IRW note in place of a stem and no option
    text. par6 is stored raw with 'As late as I want' folded to 0, which is not the recode the
    codebook prints for it.
- table: gilbert_meta_13
  issue: |-
    This table pools two different test forms (baseline and midline) under one set of item codes,
    and 12 of the 37 codes carry a different question at each wave, so their item_text is blank;
    do not assume a code means the same question at both waves. Arithmetic items read e.g. '12 + 6
    = 18' because the enumerator-facing form printed the answer; the child saw the problem alone.
    The object-identification and number items were pictures, so item_text is blank and the
    expected answer is in correct_response.
- table: gilbert_meta_14
  issue: |-
    This table pools two different test forms (baseline and midline) under one set of item codes,
    and 39 of the 69 codes carry a different question at each wave (e.g. addition_q2 is '6 + 1 =
    7' at baseline and '0 + 3 =' at midline; wordprob1 and wordprob2 swap), so their item_text is
    blank. Arithmetic items read e.g. '12 + 6 = 18' because the enumerator-facing form printed the
    answer; the child saw the problem alone.
- table: gilbert_meta_30
  issue: |-
    item_text is the study's own label for each task, not a fixed question: the enumerator picked
    the digits and numbers to ask from a printed pool, and the baseline and endline sheets print
    different numerals. resp is 1 only for a perfect count or a pass, not the count the study
    recorded. caser_math_read1 appears to be dichotomised one step too low (1.3% pass rate where
    the study's coding implies 58-64%), so treat its resp as unreliable.
- table: gilbert_meta_45
  issue: |-
    Item text for the 22 Maslach Burnout Inventory items is withheld on licence grounds; only the
    MBI response anchors ship. The 8 Personal Accomplishment items are already reverse-coded in the
    table, the opposite of the direction respondents answered in, so 'Never' maps to resp 6 and
    'Every day' to resp 0 on those items; the option rows reflect the reversal.
- table: gilbert_meta_71
  issue: |-
    The study used four parallel forms and the table does not record which one a child took, so
    for 12 of the 20 codes no single problem belongs to the code and item_text is blank; the 8
    positions that print the same problem on all eight booklets ship it. The test is in Hindi. resp
    1 = correct is inferred from the study's scoring code, not labelled, so option_text is blank.
- table: gilbert_meta_73
  issue: |-
    item_text is the task each item asks ('Multiplication', 'Solve the sums'), not the problem a
    child saw: the study used four parallel forms with different numbers and the table does not
    record which form a child took, so several codes share the same text. resp 1 = correct is
    inferred from the study's scoring code, not labelled, so option_text is blank.
- table: jablonska_2020_instagram_addiction
  issue: |-
    The item codes are an English rendering of the Polish taken from the data file's headers and
    can contradict the wording: code 5 reads 'Viewing Instagram is a good way to get bored' where
    the administered Polish and the study's English questionnaire both say it relieves boredom.
    Read the codes as identifiers only. The Polish anchors are aligned to resp 1-7 by the order
    the appendix prints them in.
- table: jordan_2020_burnout
  issue: |-
    For Q12_8, Q12_9 and Q12_10 the study used two anchor sets across administrations (Never/almost
    never..Always on most dates, Never..Very Often on 7/31-8/3/2018). option_text is the majority
    wording, but 54/41/87 of the resp = 2 rows on those items come from the other anchor set,
    whose other levels were dropped in processing.
- table: kiraly_2024_perinatal_mh_freq
  issue: |-
    Four items were asked on both the obstetrician and the pediatrician/NP survey forms with
    slightly different wording, and each code carries only one: the variant the deposit's column
    name reproduces. Respondents to the other form read the other wording.
- table: kraft_todd_2017_warmth
  issue: |-
    The questionnaire printed this scale as 0 (not at all) to 4 (very much), but the data store it
    as 1-5, so resp 1 is 'not at all' and resp 5 'very much'; the 'Does not apply' option is stored
    as missing. The adjectives are assigned to WARM1-WARM4 by the questionnaire's listing order,
    and 'Sincere' (WARM3) and 'Good natured' (WARM4) could not be told apart in the data.
- table: dvivdtws_ppmial_marcatto_2023_dtw
  issue: |-
    This table pools two administrations of the Dark Tetrad at Work scale, an Italian-language
    sample (cov_language = 1, n = 300) and an English-language sample (cov_language = 2, n = 253),
    but item_text is the Italian wording for every row. The English-speaking respondents read the
    original English DTW wording, which is in item_text_translated. The Italian response anchors
    and instructions were never published, so option_text and instructions are blank; the paper
    states the scale ran 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree.
- table: molino_2018_d5_scale
  issue: |-
    The table name signals one scale but the table pools two measures from section 5 of the
    questionnaire: d_5_1-d_5_5 are entrepreneurial intention (adapted from Linan & Chen, 2009)
    and d_5_6-d_5_8 are perceived support from family and friends. Item text is the administered
    Italian from the S2 Questionnaire, with the authors' own English in the `_translated`
    columns. Only the endpoints of the 7-point scale are labelled, so `option_text` is blank for
    2-6.
- table: mpsycho_avlancheprep
  issue: |-
    Item text is the terse stem the MPsychoR documentation gives for each column (info,
    discuss, gear, decision), not the full survey question skiers read; the Haegeli et al.
    (2012) paper was not available. Which `option_text` belongs to which `resp` value is
    inferred from the order the documentation lists the options in, since no numeric key is
    published: the data confirm the most-prepared and least-prepared ends for all four items,
    but the order of the middle categories is unverified.
- table: opladen2025_wi
  issue: |-
    The English in `item_text_translated` is not a translation of the items: it is the
    deposit's own short content gloss for each item (e.g. "worries about serious illness"). The
    German in `item_text` is the wording respondents read. The instrument is the 14-item
    Whiteley Index (Pilowsky, 1967) in German, not a body-image scale.
- table: ordak_2026_vaccine_misreasoning
  issue: |-
    This is a content analysis, not a questionnaire: each `id` is a Polish-language
    anti-vaccination Facebook post and each item is one of ten statistical-misreasoning
    categories a coder applied to it, so `item_text` is the paper's Table 1 definition of the
    category rather than wording anyone responded to. The response options were written by IRW
    ("Identified in the post" / "Not identified in the post") because the paper publishes no
    option labels; resp 1 = identified, which reproduces the paper's Table 2 counts for all ten
    categories.
- table: pedroso_2021_ifsq_laissezfaire
  issue: |-
    Item text is the administered Brazilian-Portuguese IFSQ-Br wording, but the response anchors
    are English: the study publishes only the IFSQ's English anchor sets, never the Portuguese
    respondents saw. Which of the two sets each item carried is inferred from item content --
    LF1-LF3 and LF6-LF9 are behaviour items (never ... always), LF4, LF5, LF10 and LF11 belief
    items (disagree ... agree). LF6recoded-LF9recoded are stored reverse-scored, so on those four
    resp 1 means "always" and 5 means "never", the opposite of every other item. The English
    item wording is the study's own back-translation (BT2).
- table: pedroso_2021_ifsq_responsiveness
  issue: |-
    Item text is the administered Brazilian-Portuguese IFSQ-Br wording, but the response anchors
    are English: the study publishes only the IFSQ's English anchor sets, never the Portuguese
    respondents saw. Which of the two sets each item carried is inferred from item content --
    RP6, RP7 and RP12 are belief items (disagree ... agree), the other nine behaviour items (never
    ... always) -- a split corroborated by those three being the only items with missing
    responses, since the study added a "don't know" option to belief items only. The English
    item wording is the study's own back-translation (BT2) of a pre-final draft and differs from
    the final Portuguese for RP1, RP2, RP8 and RP11.
- table: pedroso_2021_ifsq_restriction
  issue: |-
    Item text is the administered Brazilian-Portuguese IFSQ-Br wording, but the response anchors
    are English: the study publishes only the IFSQ's English anchor sets, never the Portuguese
    respondents saw. Which of the two sets each item carried is inferred from item content --
    RS1, RS2, RS5 and RS6 are behaviour items (never ... always), RS3, RS4 and RS7-RS11 belief
    items (disagree ... agree). RS5recoded and RS6recoded are stored reverse-scored, so on those
    two resp 1 means "always" and 5 means "never", the opposite of every other item. The English
    item wording is the study's own back-translation (BT2) of an earlier draft and lacks the
    parenthetical Brazilian food examples the final Portuguese adds to RS5-RS10.
- table: penningroth_2019_pm_concerns
  issue: |-
    The 15 items are content categories, not questions, and resp is a derived value rather than
    a response to the item shown: each participant listed up to five real-life prospective-memory
    tasks and marked, per task, which categories it related to as a concern, and resp 1 means at
    least one of the five tasks was concern-related in that category, 0 that none were.
    `option_text` describes that collapse rather than a printed option.
- table: penningroth_2019_pm_goals
  issue: |-
    The 15 items are content categories, not questions, and resp is a derived value rather than
    a response to the item shown: each participant listed up to five real-life prospective-memory
    tasks and judged each against all 15 goal categories, and resp 1 means at least one of the
    five tasks was related to that goal category, 0 that none were.
- table: peters_2025_att_exp_strength
  issue: |-
    This table pools the Your COVID-19 Risk tool's deployments in about 20 languages across 21
    countries, but only the English master wording from the study's question-definition sheet
    ships, so respondents outside the English deployments read a translation of it; each
    respondent's language is in `cov_language`. All 16 items share one identical stem and differ
    only in their anchor pair, so each item's content is in `option_text` at resp 1 and resp max,
    not in `item_text`. The 7-point items were displayed as -3..+3 and are stored 1..7 (stored 4
    is the midpoint); "weird" is a 1..5 item.
- table: peters_2025_att_instr_eval
  issue: |-
    This table pools the Your COVID-19 Risk tool's deployments in about 22 languages across 21
    countries, but only the English master wording from the study's question-definition sheet
    ships, so respondents outside the English deployments read a translation of it; each
    respondent's language is in `cov_language`. The bipolar items were displayed as -3..+3 and
    are stored 1..7, with wording only at the two poles.
- table: peters_2025_gen_risk_strength
  issue: |-
    This table pools the Your COVID-19 Risk tool's deployments in many languages across 21
    countries, but only the English master wording from the study's question-definition sheet
    ships, so respondents outside the English deployments read a translation of it; each
    respondent's language is in `cov_language`. Only the endpoints of the 1-5 scale are
    labelled.
- table: peters_2025_gnrc_beliefs
  issue: |-
    This table pools the Your COVID-19 Risk tool's deployments in about 20 languages across 21
    countries, but only the English master wording from the study's question-definition sheet
    ships, so respondents outside the English deployments read a translation of it; each
    respondent's language is in `cov_language`. Only the endpoints of the 1-5 scale are
    labelled.
- table: peters_2025_nrm_inj_approval
  issue: |-
    This table pools the Your COVID-19 Risk tool's deployments in about 20 languages across 21
    countries, but only the English master wording from the study's question-definition sheet
    ships, so respondents outside the English deployments read a translation of it; each
    respondent's language is in `cov_language`. The bipolar items were displayed as -3..+3 and
    are stored 1..7 (stored 4 is the midpoint), with wording only at the poles, and
    "{{distRec}}" is the study's placeholder for the country's recommended physical distance.
- table: peters_2025_pbc_cond_power
  issue: |-
    This table pools the Your COVID-19 Risk tool's deployments in about 20 languages across 21
    countries, but only the English master wording from the study's question-definition sheet
    ships, so respondents outside the English deployments read a translation of it; each
    respondent's language is in `cov_language`. The bipolar items were displayed as -3..+3 and
    are stored 1..7, with wording only at the poles ("much harder" at 1, "much easier" at 7),
    and "{{distRec}}" is the study's placeholder for the country's recommended physical
    distance.
- table: peters_2025_pbc_cond_presence
  issue: |-
    This table pools the Your COVID-19 Risk tool's deployments in about 22 languages across 21
    countries, but only the English master wording from the study's question-definition sheet
    ships, so respondents outside the English deployments read a translation of it; each
    respondent's language is in `cov_language`. "{{distRec}}" is the study's placeholder for the
    country's recommended physical distance, and only the endpoints of the 1-5 scale ("very
    unlikely" / "very likely") are labelled.
- table: preussmattsson_2022_ownership
  issue: |-
    The 24 item codes are not 24 statements: they are the six body-ownership statements S1-S6
    crossed with the four visuo-vestibular x visuo-tactile synchrony conditions, and the code's
    suffix (AVVAVT, AVVSVT, SVVAVT, SVVSVT) names the condition. Each statement's wording
    therefore appears on four codes, and responses to the same statement under different
    conditions are separate items. The statements were read from the paper's Table 2 (an
    image). resp runs -3 to +3 and only the endpoints ("fully disagree", "fully agree") are
    published, so `option_text` is blank for the five middle points.
- table: quinn_2023_roommate_cesd
  issue: |-
    Items 4, 8, 12 and 16, the positively worded CES-D items, are stored raw rather than reverse
    scored, so the 0-3 frequency anchors apply as printed to all 20 items. The study
    reverse-scores those four: doing so reproduces the paper's published T1 total, while the raw
    sum does not.
- table: rahm_2017_panas
  issue: |-
    The 20 item words are the administered German adjectives from the study's SPSS labels, with
    the authors' English gloss alongside, but the response anchors are English ("very slightly or
    not at all" ... "extremely"): neither the deposit nor the paper records the German anchor
    wording participants saw. No instructions ship, and the reference period administered is not
    stated.
- table: rahman_2022_phq9
  issue: |-
    The study's two sources disagree on PHQ-9 item 8: the S1 Table prints only "Moving or
    speaking so slowly that other people could have noticed?", while the deposited Stata label
    continues "Or the opposi..." before Stata's 80-character limit cuts it off. The shorter S1
    Table wording ships, so the item text may lack the second clause respondents read.
- table: ravenscroft_2017_transition
  issue: |-
    The parent survey was administered in English, Bulgarian, Catalan, Greek and Romanian, but
    only the English master questionnaire is published, so the text is what 157 of the 306
    respondents read and an English equivalent of what the other 149 read. The response options
    are printed positive-first in the questionnaire, but the stored coding runs the other way:
    resp 5 is the first-printed (most positive or most frequent) option and resp 1 the last.
    Question text is matched to the data file's terse column labels by questionnaire order.
- table: regalado_2023_tourism_value
  issue: |-
    Item P4_14 ships with no Spanish item text: the study's Spanish SPSS file repeats P4_15's
    label on P4_14, so the administered wording is unrecoverable, and only the authors' English
    ("In general, Valuable and worth it") is given. The paper describes 12 items rated from "not
    important" to "very important", but the data hold 15 items (P4_13-P4_15 are overall
    evaluations) and the file's own anchors, which ship, run "Nada valioso" to "Muy valioso".
- table: shu_2025_translation_add
  issue: |-
    Two of the three questions are matched to their item codes on content; the third,
    addcompetitioninreha, is assigned by elimination and its code does not obviously describe the
    question it carries (pressure of current studies on career plans), so treat that wording as
    provisional. The questionnaire was administered in Mandarin but only the study's English
    ships. No response options are published, and that item uses four levels where the other two
    use five.
- table: simsalRbim_Human_LargeValence_2018
  issue: |-
    The items are OASIS photographs shown two at a time, not questions: the bracketed
    `item_text` identifying each image is a description written by IRW, not anything shown to
    subjects. resp is 1 when this image was chosen on that trial and 0 when the other image of
    the pair was.
- table: simsalRbim_Mice_LowValence
  issue: |-
    The items are liquids offered to mice two at a time, not questions: the bracketed
    `item_text` is a description written by IRW from the study's methods. resp is the number of
    corner visits with licks for that liquid in that pairing, a count rather than a rating. The
    code Sac stands for sucrose, not saccharin.
- table: tears
  issue: |-
    The wording shown is the paper's description of each rating dimension, not the text
    observers saw on screen, which is not published. Four items are 0-100 scales (negative
    valence, positive valence, arousal, genuineness); the other seven are emotion percentages
    that had to sum to 100 across the seven, so they are not independent ratings. `id` is the
    video clip being rated, not a person; the observer is in `rater`.
- table: twod_rotation_mather2023
  issue: |-
    The 304 items are figure stimuli, so `item_text` is blank; each picture is
    R2Dfigures/fig<NNNNN>.png in the study's OSF "Item Stimuli" archive, numbered as in the item
    code. Participants chose among eight picture options (A-C and E-G, D "None of these.", H "I
    don't know."), but resp is scored correctness, so `option_text` carries Incorrect/Correct
    scoring labels rather than the options presented.
- table: uffler_2017_seat_reasons
  issue: |-
    The seven items are categories the authors assigned to free-text answers to one open
    question ("Why did you sit in that place today?"), not a printed checklist; resp 1 means the
    reason was mentioned. The category labels are the study's French from its S1 figure, but the
    question itself ships only in the paper's English rendering because the French original is
    not published.
- table: wang_2015_donation_decision
  issue: |-
    Item wording is the paper's English, but 208 of the 371 respondents were Chinese students
    who read an unpublished Chinese version (their donation question offered 100 Yuan rather
    than 100 dollars). Distress and sympathy ship with no `option_text` because the paper
    describes a 7-point scale from "not at all" to "very much" while the data store eight codes,
    0-7, so the anchors cannot be placed.
- table: weatherspoon_2015_family_physicians_effectiveness
  issue: |-
    The survey's effectiveness column offered only Yes (1), No (2) and Don't know (9, dropped in
    processing), but the live table contains 25 responses coded 3, 4 or 5; those rows have no
    option text. Item wording was transcribed from an image of the questionnaire's Q12 grid.
- table: wiedemann_2021_risk_perception
  issue: |-
    The item stems are the administered German from the study's SPSS labels, but the scale
    anchors and instructions are the study's English translation because the German originals
    are not in the deposit. The items rate a hazard-communication text that differed by
    experimental condition (see `cov_risk_type`, `cov_factor1`, `cov_factor2`), so no single
    passage is shipped.
- table: wine_luckett2021
  issue: |-
    Item text is the raw data file's column header, not the question raters were asked:
    "Pleasantness" and "Familiarity" are one-word labels, and only intensity is a full question.
    The three items use different scales -- intensity a 0-100 line scale, pleasantness and
    familiarity 9-point scales -- and no anchors ship. `id` is the wine sample, not a person;
    the judge is in `rater`.
- table: pickova2025_moral_justifications
  issue: |-
    The instructions stem is shipped exactly as the study's Google Forms export records it:
    "Please indicate how much you 6 with the following statements...". The "6" is an artifact in
    the source file where "agree" belongs; respondents almost certainly read "agree", and IRW has
    not repaired it. The 1-7 scale has no published anchor labels, so option_text is blank and
    the direction of the scale is not established.
- table: dss_mouta_2021
  issue: |-
    The item text is the administered Brazilian Portuguese form from the study's OSF deposit. The
    English in the `_translated` columns has two sources. The items are the original Hamilton, Shih
    & Mohammed (2016) English DSS, a parallel version rather than a translation of the Portuguese,
    so the phrasing differs in places (item 2 'instinto' vs 'gut feelings'). The English
    instructions and the three middle response labels were machine-translated by IRW.
- table: mede_2025_clim_emotions
  issue: |-
    The item text is the English core questionnaire of the TISP study. Most respondents (68
    countries, 37 languages) answered a local translation, which is published per sample in the
    OSF deposit (05_survey-materials/questionnaire/countries/) but not reproduced here.
- table: mede_2025_clim_polsupport
  issue: |-
    The item text is the English core questionnaire of the TISP study. Most respondents (68
    countries, 37 languages) answered a local translation, published per sample in the OSF deposit
    but not reproduced here. Respondents were also offered 'Not applicable' (4) for every policy;
    those answers were set to missing in this table, so resp covers only 1-3.
- table: mede_2025_clim_weather_future
  issue: |-
    The item text is the English core questionnaire of the TISP study. Most respondents (68
    countries, 37 languages) answered a local translation, which is published per sample in the
    OSF deposit but not reproduced here. The instructions include the block's lead-in sentence
    ('please think about your country'), which the questionnaire prints once above the paired
    past-impact question.
- table: mede_2025_clim_weather_past
  issue: |-
    The item text is the English core questionnaire of the TISP study. Most respondents (68
    countries, 37 languages) answered a local translation, which is published per sample in the
    OSF deposit but not reproduced here.
- table: uti_newlands_2023_gad
  issue: |-
    The item wording is the GAD-7's standard English form, not text from the study's own materials:
    neither the paper nor the OSF codebook prints the items. resp is stored 1-4, one above the
    form's printed 0-3 scoring, so the GAD-7 total is sum(resp) - 7. Codes are matched to wording
    by the form's printed item numbering. The data pin gad_5 (restless) and support gad_4 (trouble
    relaxing), but nothing confirms the order of gad_1, gad_2, gad_3, gad_6 and gad_7.
- table: uti_newlands_2023_phq
  issue: |-
    The item wording is the PHQ-9's standard English form, not text from the study's own materials:
    neither the paper nor the OSF codebook prints the items. Codes are matched to wording by the
    form's printed item numbering. The data pin phq_3, phq_4, phq_8 and phq_9 and only narrowly
    support phq_2, but nothing confirms the order of phq_1, phq_5, phq_6 and phq_7.
- table: bfi_goldberg_1992_agreeableness
  issue: |-
    Despite the table name and its dictionary description ("Big Five Inventory"), these items are
    not the BFI-44. They are the Agreeableness scale of the 50-item IPIP Big-Five Factor Markers
    (Goldberg, 1992), as administered by the Open-Source Psychometrics Project.
- table: bfi_goldberg_1992_conscientiousness
  issue: |-
    Despite the table name and its dictionary description ("Big Five Inventory"), these items are
    not the BFI-44. They are the Conscientiousness scale of the 50-item IPIP Big-Five Factor
    Markers (Goldberg, 1992), as administered by the Open-Source Psychometrics Project.
- table: bfi_goldberg_1992_extraversion
  issue: |-
    Despite the table name and its dictionary description ("Big Five Inventory"), these items are
    not the BFI-44. They are the Extraversion scale of the 50-item IPIP Big-Five Factor Markers
    (Goldberg, 1992), as administered by the Open-Source Psychometrics Project.
- table: bfi_goldberg_1992_neuroticism
  issue: |-
    Despite the table name and its dictionary description ("Big Five Inventory"), these items are
    not the BFI-44. They are the IPIP Big-Five Factor Markers (Goldberg, 1992) Emotional Stability
    scale, labelled here as Neuroticism, as administered by the Open-Source Psychometrics Project.
    Under that label, items N2 and N4 are the reverse-keyed ones, and they are stored unreversed.
- table: bfi_goldberg_1992_openness_to_experience
  issue: |-
    Despite the table name and its dictionary description ("Big Five Inventory"), these items are
    not the BFI-44. They are the IPIP Big-Five Factor Markers (Goldberg, 1992) Intellect or
    Imagination scale, labelled here as Openness to Experience, as administered by the
    Open-Source Psychometrics Project.
- table: uti_newlands_2023_wpai
  issue: |-
    The item wording is the WPAI:SHP V2.0 English template from its rights holder, Reilly
    Associates, not the study's own form. The study adapted the questionnaire to urinary tract
    infection, but that wording is not published, so the template's placeholder PROBLEM is left
    in place rather than guessed. wpai_2 to wpai_4 are hours entered as numbers, not rating
    scales, so they have no response options. Codes are matched to wording by the form's
    question numbering; the skip pattern and the paper's published impairment scores confirm it.
    The form tells respondents who worked 0 hours to skip wpai_5, but 12 baseline and 7 retest
    respondents answered it anyway; those responses are kept as recorded.
- table: cordova2019_clinical_edu_environment
  issue: |-
    The item text is the administered Spanish, taken verbatim from the question headers of the
    study's own response file in the Harvard Dataverse deposit -- what the 391 respondents
    answered, and what reproduces all 200 item x resp cells. It differs on seven items from the
    Spanish printed in the paper's Table 1, which is a later rendering by the authors. The
    English in the `_translated` columns is a machine translation produced by IRW, not the
    study's wording, and has not been reviewed by a Spanish speaker; treat it as a reading aid.
    `option_text` is blank because the administered anchor labels were never published: the form
    stored 1-5 and the paper states only that the scale runs from "totally in disagreement" to
    "totally agree". The instrument is the PHEEM, not the DREEM the data dictionary's
    description names.
- table: codella_2020_school_efficacy
  issue: |-
    The item text is the administered Italian, taken from the deposited spreadsheet's own
    final row. The 1-5 response anchors ("Totally unable" ... "Totally capable") and the
    shared stem the items complete ("How well can you") are shipped in ENGLISH, because
    that is the only language the source publishes them in: the article states the anchors
    in English in its Measures section and the supplementary tables print the stem in
    English, while neither the deposit nor the article gives the Italian for either. So a
    single table mixes the administered wording of its items with an English rendering of
    its scale, and the anchors are not the words the children read.
- table: qi_2024_phq9
  issue: |-
    The item text and response options here come from the deposit's own "English-language
    codebook", which is the authors' English rendering of a questionnaire that was
    administered to Chinese nurses in Chinese. No Chinese wording is published in the
    deposit or the article, so this is not the text respondents read. The mapping from
    item code to text is the codebook's own and is exact; only the language is a
    substitute.
- table: qi_2024_mspss
  issue: |-
    As for `qi_2024_phq9`: the item text and options are the deposit's own
    "English-language codebook", not the Chinese wording respondents read. The 1-7 scale is
    labelled in the source at its endpoints only ("strongly disagree" / "strongly agree"),
    so codes 2-6 carry no option text rather than invented labels.
- table: qi_2024_somatic
  issue: |-
    Two things. First, the source instrument has TWENTY items and this IRW table carries
    FIFTEEN: five columns in the deposit's SSS block are mislabelled with other scales'
    names (`PHQ3.1`, `PHQ4.1`, `PHQ1.1`, `GAD1`, `PHQ7.1`) and were excluded when the
    response table was built. They are the missing SSS items -- the deposit's own
    `SSS Total score` equals the sum of the fifteen shipped items plus those five for every
    one of the 293 respondents, and equals the fifteen-item sum for none -- but which of
    items 16-20 each one is has not been established, so none of them appears here. Item
    text is shipped for the fifteen that are in the table. Second, as for `qi_2024_phq9`,
    that text is the deposit's own "English-language codebook" rather than the Chinese
    wording respondents read.
- table: ali_2021_isi
  issue: |-
    The item text is the canonical Insomnia Severity Index wording (Morin et al., 2011), not the
    wording in the study's own S1 File. The extraction silently normalised the source's column
    headers toward the canonical form, so six of the seven shipped items differ from the deposit:
    the source reads "Difficult falling asleep", "Difficult staying asleep" and "Problems waking
    up too early" where the shipped text reads "Difficulty falling asleep", "Difficulty staying
    asleep" and "Problem waking up too early". Those headers are abbreviated spreadsheet labels
    rather than administered sentences, so neither form is certainly what respondents read, and
    the instructions are the standard ISI preamble because the study publishes none. Items 1-3
    carry fewer responses (103/94/105 against 167-168) because those severity anchors are
    sometimes skipped as inapplicable.
- table: ojelabi_2019_sf36
  issue: |-
    The item text is the canonical RAND 36-Item Health Survey 1.0 wording, transcribed from RAND's
    own instrument page, not from the study: the article publishes no item wording and the PLOS S1
    workbook's headers are bare codes sf1..sf36 with no variable labels. Which canonical item each
    code carries is therefore an IRW reconstruction rather than anything the source states. It is
    verified two ways -- per-item response ranges reproduce the SF-36's block structure exactly
    (0 out-of-range responses, while all 35 cyclic shifts of the mapping produce 2-23 violations),
    and the workbook's own SF-6D health-state code is an exact function of the SF-6D input items
    under this numbering -- but a reader should know it was solved rather than read off a key. Two
    shipped option lists are one level wider than the sample used: sf21 never takes "Very severe"
    pain and sf2 never takes "Much worse".
- table: pierro_2018_selfforgive_s3
  issue: |-
    The item text here is the English wording printed in the study's own PLOS ONE article (its
    rendering of a 4-item adaptation of Wohl et al.'s State Self-Forgiveness Scale), but the scale
    was administered in Italian to 85 Italian respondents and neither the article nor its SPSS
    deposit publishes the Italian form, so these are not the sentences respondents read. Unlike
    the sibling tables pierro_2018_selfforgive_s1 and _s2, the two reverse-worded items
    (sforgiver1 "rejecting of myself", sforgiver3 "dislike toward myself") are stored RAW here,
    not reverse-recoded, so their anchors read as printed; this was confirmed by reproducing the
    paper's published composite. Only the endpoints of the 4-point scale are labelled, so
    option_text is blank for resp 2 and 3. The stem "I feel..." is printed once in the paper and
    is repeated on each item row here so every item carries its own referent.
- table: mturkddm_lexical
  issue: |-
    A lexical decision task: 4,588 letter strings, 2,295 real words and 2,293 nonwords, each flashed briefly on screen. The item code is the string itself. Participants pressed the right arrow for a real word and the left arrow for a nonword, and resp records whether that judgement was correct, so each string is listed twice -- once for the response that was correct for it and once for the response that was not. Items are grouped by the word-frequency pool they were drawn from.
- table: mturkddm_by
  issue: |-
    A dot-numerosity task: an array of yellow and blue dots was shown and the participant chose which colour was more numerous. The item code gives the two counts, yellow first -- so '10 15' means ten yellow dots and fifteen blue. resp is whether the choice was correct. The total dot area was also varied in the original experiment but is not part of the item code, so trials differing only in area are pooled here.
- table: polca_carcinoma
  issue: |-
    Seven pathologists each rated the same 118 slides for whether carcinoma was present in the uterine cervix. The items here are the pathologists, labelled A to G, and the persons being measured are the slides -- the reverse of a questionnaire. There is no question wording: each entry is one rater's verdict on one slide. Responses are 0 for no and 1 for yes; the original source coded these 1 and 2, which is kept alongside.
- table: much_tte_2025_effort
  issue: |-
    Five statements about how much effort the participant put into the test block they had just finished, answered from 1 (strongly disagree) to 4 (strongly agree). Only the two ends of the scale were labelled. The same five items were asked after each block; which block a given answer refers to is recorded in the response data rather than in the item.
- table: much_tte_2025_currentmotivation
  issue: |-
    Three statements about how much effort the participant intended to put into the test block they were about to start, answered on a sliding scale from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree' with 101 internal points. The number was not shown to the participant while answering. Two further items from the same source scale were dropped from this version because they could not be sensibly rephrased in the future tense.
- table: much_tte_2025_concentrationtask
  issue: |-
    Nine concentration items. Each showed a grid of visually confusable letters and one target letter, and the participant counted how many times the target appeared. The description here names the target letter and the true number of occurrences, which is also given as the correct answer; the grid itself was a picture and is not reproduced. Responses are 0 or 1 for whether the count given was right. The items came in three blocks of three.
- table: nas_rogoza_2024_study2_ngs
  issue: |-
    Thirteen adjectives from the Narcissistic Grandiosity Scale, answered from 1 (not at all) to 7 (extremely) for how well each word describes you in general. They were administered as part of a longer list of 42 narcissism adjectives, of which these are the grandiosity block. The words are shown in English; the study was run in Polish and the Polish wording is in the deposit but not reproduced here. Which adjective is item 1 versus item 2 follows the order the deposit's codebook prints them in.
- table: pass20_klosowska_2025_dass_online
  issue: |-
    The 21-item Depression Anxiety Stress Scales, asking how much each statement applied to you over the past week, from 0 (did not apply to me at all) to 3 (applied to me very much or most of the time). The items are grouped into the scale's three subscales of seven items each. The text is the English original -- the study was run in Polish and that wording is not published in the deposit, so what is shown here is a rendering rather than what respondents read.
- table: nomt_hooper_2024_study2
  issue: |-
    A visual memory test using novel, unfamiliar object categories. Participants first studied six target objects, then on each trial chose which of three objects shown was one of the targets. The item is the trial number and resp is whether the choice was correct; chance is one in three. There is no question wording because the stimuli are pictures, which are in the original deposit but not reproduced here. The study compared groups given English and Spanish instructions, but the trials themselves are nonverbal and identical across groups.
- table: imos_1992
  issue: |-
    The six problems of the 1992 International Mathematical Olympiad, each marked out of 7. Contestants sat problems 1-3 on the first day and 4-6 on the second, with four and a half hours for each paper. The problem statements are taken from the official English paper. NOTE ON NOTATION: the text is extracted from a PDF, so mathematical layout is flattened -- superscripts and fractions are lost, so n squared reads as 'n2' and one-over-n as '1 n'. Use the official PDF if you need the exact statement.
- table: imos_1995
  issue: |-
    The six problems of the 1995 International Mathematical Olympiad, each marked out of 7. Contestants sat problems 1-3 on the first day and 4-6 on the second, with four and a half hours for each paper. The problem statements are taken from the official English paper. NOTE ON NOTATION: the text is extracted from a PDF, so mathematical layout is flattened -- superscripts and fractions are lost, so n squared reads as 'n2' and one-over-n as '1 n'. Use the official PDF if you need the exact statement.
- table: imos_1998
  issue: |-
    The six problems of the 1998 International Mathematical Olympiad, each marked out of 7. Contestants sat problems 1-3 on the first day and 4-6 on the second, with four and a half hours for each paper. The problem statements are taken from the official English paper. NOTE ON NOTATION: the text is extracted from a PDF, so mathematical layout is flattened -- superscripts and fractions are lost, so n squared reads as 'n2' and one-over-n as '1 n'. Use the official PDF if you need the exact statement.

Use the official PDF if you need the exact statement.

NOTE ON NOTATION: the text is extracted from a PDF, so mathematical layout is flattened -- superscripts and fractions are lost, so n squared reads as 'n2' and one-over-n as '1 n'.
