```{r}
  issue: |-
    The six problems of the 2011 International Mathematical Olympiad, each marked out of 7. Contestants sat problems 1-3 on the first day and 4-6 on the second, with four and a half hours for each paper. The problem statements are taken from the official English paper. NOTE ON NOTATION: the text is extracted from a PDF, so mathematical layout is flattened -- superscripts and fractions are lost, so n squared reads as 'n2' and one-over-n as '1 n'. Use the official PDF if you need the exact statement.
- table: imos_2016
  issue: |-
    The six problems of the 2016 International Mathematical Olympiad, each marked out of 7, three on each of two days. The statements were read from images of the official English paper because its PDF text layer is corrupted, which means the mathematical notation here is more faithful than in the other Olympiad years in this batch -- superscripts and subscripts are preserved.
- table: ipip_openpsychometrics_sc
  issue: |-
    Ten items from the International Personality Item Pool's Social Confidence scale, answered from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Each item completes the stem 'I ...'. They were given as part of an online personality test alongside three other IPIP scales. A sixth response option meaning 'not answered' was recorded as 0 in the raw data and removed before this table was built.
- table: ipip_openpsychometrics_ad
  issue: |-
    Ten items from the International Personality Item Pool's Adventurousness scale, answered from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Each item completes the stem 'I ...'. They were given as part of an online personality test alongside three other IPIP scales. A sixth response option meaning 'not answered' was recorded as 0 in the raw data and removed before this table was built.
- table: iowa_gambling_task
  issue: |-
    A card-choice task. On each trial the participant picked a card from one of four decks; two decks lose money in the long run and two gain. The item is one trial, and the response records WHICH DECK was chosen (1 = A, 2 = B, 3 = C, 4 = D) rather than whether the choice was right -- there is no right answer to a single draw. Three versions of the task are pooled here, of 95, 100 and 150 trials, and the description of each item says which. TWO THINGS TO KNOW: the item numbers are not the trial numbers, because the processing script numbered items sequentially across the three pooled studies -- the trial number is given in the item description instead. And each study is missing its final trial, lost when the source files were read.
- table: imos_1985
  issue: |-
    The six problems of the 1985 International Mathematical Olympiad, each marked out of 7, with problems 1-3 sat on the first day and 4-6 on the second. NOTE ON NOTATION: the text is extracted from a PDF, so mathematical layout is flattened -- superscripts and fractions are lost, so n squared reads as 'n2'. Use the official paper if you need the exact statement.
- table: imos_1986
  issue: |-
    The six problems of the 1986 International Mathematical Olympiad, each marked out of 7, with problems 1-3 sat on the first day and 4-6 on the second. NOTE ON NOTATION: the text is extracted from a PDF, so mathematical layout is flattened -- superscripts and fractions are lost, so n squared reads as 'n2'. Use the official paper if you need the exact statement.
- table: iat_poverty
  issue: |-
    Twelve possible explanations for poverty, each rated for how important it is. They share the stem 'There are many poor people in the world because of...' and were answered from 1 (not at all important) to 5 (extremely important). They come from the Project Implicit demo-website dataset, where they sit alongside the race IAT itself. The third response label is printed 'Moderately Imporant' in the source and is left as found.
- table: gcbs_brotherton_2013_vcl
  issue: |-
    A sixteen-word vocabulary check-list: respondents ticked every word whose definition they were sure they knew. Three of the words -- cuivocal, florted and verdid -- are not real words, and were included so that over-claiming could be detected; they are marked as such here. resp is 1 for checked and 0 for unchecked. The list was given alongside a conspiracy-belief scale as a validity check.
- table: envirisk_lalot_2025
  issue: |-
    Twelve items on environmental risk. Six ask how much you agree that biodiversity loss or climate change poses a threat, on a 1-7 scale from strongly disagree to strongly agree. Four ask how acceptable you find a particular environmental policy, on a 1-7 scale from very low to very high acceptability. The last two are not attitude questions at all but political self-placements on 0-10 scales -- left to right, and liberal to conservative. Each group keeps its own anchors.
- table: franco_2024_unfolding
  issue: |-
    Six statements about how much value the respondent places on receiving attention from others, ranked from the one that describes them best (1) to the one that describes them worst (6) -- so the response is a rank, not a rating, and every respondent uses each number once. The statements were generated by ChatGPT for a tutorial on unfolding models and administered in Brazilian Portuguese, shown here with the authors' English alongside. They are ordered from the most to the least attention-seeking.
- table: gilbert_meta_28
  issue: |-
    Seventeen tasks from a numeracy and mobile-phone test given orally to mothers, covering number reading and identification, addition and subtraction, word problems, telling the time, and using a phone. The wording shown is the study's own short description of each task rather than what an enumerator read out. THE TEST CASCADES -- two-digit addition was only attempted by mothers who passed one-digit addition -- so the harder items have far fewer respondents and their pass rates are conditional on an already more able group. KNOWN PROBLEM WITH ONE ITEM: maser_math_read1 (reading digits 1-9) passes at under 2 per cent where identifying the same digits passes at 55 per cent, which is not possible; it appears to be dichotomised one step too low, the same fault already reported for the child version of this test. Its item text is correct; treat its resp as unreliable.
- table: gilbert_meta_95
  issue: |-
    Twelve clinical reasoning questions given to medical students, four each on three urinary tract infection scenarios: uncomplicated UTI, complicated UTI, and pyelonephritis. They are Key Features Questions, which present a case and ask for the decisions critical to resolving it, and they are marked with partial credit -- which is why the scores are fractional rather than right or wrong. THE QUESTIONS THEMSELVES ARE NOT SHOWN: the case vignettes are not published in the data deposit and the article is paywalled, so only the scenario and the question number are given.
- table: famous_melodies
  issue: |-
    Five things listeners rated about each of 109 well-known melodies: how positive or negative it sounds, how calming or exciting, how familiar it is, roughly what age they learned it, and whether they could name it. NOTE THAT THE ROWS ARE RATINGS OF A MELODY -- the melody is the id and the listener is the rater, the reverse of a questionnaire. The scales differ by dimension (naming is yes/no, age runs 1-8, the rest 0-4) and the labels for the scale points are not published, so the direction of each rating cannot be read off this table.
- table: anxiety_gastro_symptoms
  issue: |-
    Fifteen statements about anxiety and hypervigilance regarding gut symptoms, rated 1 = Strongly Disagree to 5 = Strongly Agree. Items aehas1-aehas9 form the anxiety subscale and aehas10-aehas15 the hypervigilance subscale. The source file codes the same anchors 0-4; the IRW values are one higher.
- table: audit_BrummerHoffman_2021
  issue: |-
    AUDIT-C administered in Brazilian Portuguese; the English alongside is the study's own translation. Two points to know before using the scores. The third item (six or more drinks on one occasion) is scored in the standard AUDIT-C direction, 0 = Nunca to 4 = Todos ou quase todos os dias -- the deposit's English questionnaire prints those options in the reverse order, which does not match the data. And on the second item, 'Nao bebo' (I do not drink) and '1 ou 2' were separate options on the form that both score 0, so a 0 there does not distinguish abstainers from light drinkers; the two are shown as one label because the value cannot tell them apart. The AUDIT is a World Health Organization instrument (WHO/MSD/MSB/01.6a, Babor et al. 2001) and WHO reserves all rights in it; WHO permits free reproduction for non-commercial purposes, which is the basis on which it appears here. The Brazilian Portuguese wording is the study's own translation, published in its OSF deposit, not a WHO translation.
- table: brand_raffaelli_2024_recognition_20
  issue: |-
    Old/new recognition memory for brand names and logos. An item code is a position in the Qualtrics loop, not a particular brand: the same code indexes a different serial position in the two subsamples (for item_family=name subtract one), and which brand or logo sits at that position depends on the respondent's cov_condition. resp is 1 for 'Old' and 2 for 'New'. Positions 1-50 of each subsample were the studied set for respondents in odd-numbered lists and the lures for even-numbered lists; positions 51-100 the reverse.
- table: cavalini_mokken
  issue: |-
    Seventeen ways of coping with a bad smell from a nearby factory, each rated 0 = never to 3 = always. The study was conducted in Dutch; the English shipped here is the mokken R package's rendering, which is the form in which this data set is distributed. The seventeen items form four scales (Sijtsma & Molenaar 2002, pp. 82-86).
- table: disgust_berger2014
  issue: |-
    The Disgust Scale-Revised as administered in Hebrew. Two sections: items 1-14 are agreement statements and 15-27 are ratings of how disgusting an experience would be, both 0-4 but with different anchor wording. Items 12 and 16 are the scale's catch items and are not in the data. Items Q1, Q6 and Q10 are reverse-keyed and are stored UN-reversed here, so a high value on those three means low disgust sensitivity; the standard scoring subtracts them from 4. The English alongside is the published DS-R, not a translation of this Hebrew form.
- table: ees_sarling_2024
  issue: |-
    Swedish Empathic Experience Scale, thirty items in two subscales -- Vicarious Experience (VE1-VE15) and Intuitive Understanding (IU1-IU15) -- administered interleaved, VE at odd positions and IU at even, rated 1 = Stammer inte alls to 5 = Stammer fullstandigt. The English alongside is the instrument's original wording from Innamorati et al. (2019), reproduced by the study's own supplement.
- table: IJLS_Eersel_2024_IUS
  issue: |-
    Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale, 12-item short form, rated 1 = Strongly disagree to 5 = Strongly agree. Administered in Dutch; the English here is the translation the deposit supplies.
- table: IJLS_Eersel_2024_Optimism
  issue: |-
    Life Orientation Test-Revised, six scored items, rated 1-5. Items 2, 3 and 5 are the pessimism-worded ones and are stored ALREADY REVERSE-SCORED, so for those three a high value means disagreement with the printed statement; their option labels are shipped inverted to match, as the source has them. Administered in Dutch; the English here is the translation the deposit supplies. The LOT-R's authors note that it is a research instrument and not intended for clinical applications.
- table: PEMAIW_Qiu_2020_PANAS
  issue: |-
    PANAS short form, twenty adjectives rated 1 = Very slightly or not at all to 5 = Extremely for how the respondent felt over the past week. Items 1, 3, 5, 9, 10, 12, 14, 16, 17 and 19 form the Positive Affect score and the other ten the Negative Affect score.
- table: QADT_Kleka_2023
  issue: |-
    Twelve forced-choice items about attainment of developmental tasks in school-aged children, administered in Polish with the authors' own English alongside. resp is 1 when the task is attained and 0 when it is not; six items were reverse-worded and the source has already recoded them, so the A/B statement attached to resp 1 differs by item. The items have no stems -- the two statements are the whole item -- and share one lead-in, 'Zycie szkolne jest:' ('School life is:').
- table: abortion
  issue: |-
    Four items on when the law should allow abortion, from the 1986 British Social Attitudes Survey, as distributed in the ltm R package. resp is 1 for 'the law should allow it'. Two caveats from the source: it does not label the 0/1 coding (the Yes/No labels here are inferred from the stem and from which item is least endorsed), and its text for item_1 is an incomplete sentence, shipped unaltered.
- table: alcoholhealthwarninglabel_brennan_2022_intentions_postexposure
  issue: |-
    Two post-exposure intention items from an alcohol health warning label trial, answered 1 = definitely will not to 4 = definitely will. A third statement in the same block ('avoid drinking alcohol completely') is not in this table because the source file holds only a binarised version of it. The wording is quoted from the paper: the deposit itself is behind an openICPSR login.
- table: aiquipa_2026_dgs
  issue: |-
    The English item text for this Spanish-administered scale is mixed provenance: five items
    reproduce the deposit appendix's own English original, while the English for COD3 and COD7 was
    written by IRW because the Peruvian adaptation changed those two items' meaning; response-
    option anchors are blank because the deposit never publishes them
- table: dou2025_ans
  issue: |-
    The English item text for this table was produced by IRW, not by the study authors; the
    administered wording is the Chinese in item_text. No response-option wording is shipped:
    respondents answered on a six-point scale whose anchors are published neither in the deposit
    nor in the paper, and the paper's stated 'seven-point ... 1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly
    agree' describes the original Aesthetic Needs Scale rather than the six-point form used here
    (the deposited data contain only the values 1-6).
- table: hannachi_2025_eco_anxiety_cas
  issue: |-
    Responses on this table are 0-4 on an agreement-type scale that the study documents only in
    English -- its supplementary materials state "Response categories: 0 = not at all to 4 =
    completely" -- and NOT on the Climate Change Anxiety Scale's own published 1-5 frequency
    anchors (1 = Never to 5 = Almost always); the administered French anchor wording was never
    published, so option_text is left blank rather than guessed
- table: ilearnathome_regalado_2025
  issue: |-
    Item text for this table is the depositors' own English rendering; the questionnaire was
    administered in Spanish to teachers in Chiclayo, Peru, and the deposit does not publish the
    Spanish wording.
- table: pellerin2020_3dws
  issue: |-
    Item text for pellerin2020_3dws is the 3D-WS-12's published English wording; the study
    administered the scale in French and no French version of the items appears in its OSF deposit
    or its article, so what is shown here is a parallel English version rather than the sentences
    respondents read. Within each facet the item-to-code order is inferred: the reflective block is
    verified against the instrument's published loadings and freed residual, and the three
    positively-worded items land exactly where the authors' own scoring key says they do, but
    Cog_1-Cog_4 could be any of the 24 orders of c9/c10/c11/c13 as far as the data can tell.
    Separately, the authors' own wisdom score excludes Cog_1, whose responses correlate negatively
    with the reflective items once keyed in the same direction as its facet-mates (r = -0.21,
    -0.21, -0.21 against Refl_2/Refl_3/Refl_4 at wave 0, n=674, the wave the authors' own score is
    computed on; -0.21 to -0.23 pooling all 1010 person-wave records); the IRW table keeps it.
- table: pellerin2020_asti
  issue: |-
    Item text for pellerin2020_asti is the ASTI's published English wording; the study administered
    the scale in French and no French version of the items or of the 1-7 anchors appears in its OSF
    deposit or its article, so what is shown here is a parallel English version rather than the
    sentences respondents actually read. The item-to-code mapping is a presentation-order inference
    that the response data confirms only in part: it ranks first of all 5040 possible assignments,
    and it fixes ST_4, ST_6 and ST_7, but it cannot distinguish ST_1 from ST_3 ('I feel that my
    individual life is a part of a greater whole' vs 'I feel part of something greater than
    myself', which correlate 0.76) or ST_2 from ST_5 ('...belonging with both earlier and future
    generations' vs '...oneness with nature'), so either of those two pairs could be swapped.
- table: pierro_2018_assessment_s4
  issue: |-
    The three reverse-worded items (assR1, assR5, assR11) are stored already reverse-recoded, so
    their shipped anchors are flipped: for these items resp=1 is 'Strongly Agree' and resp=6 is
    'Strongly Disagree' with the printed statement. Item wording is the original English Regulatory
    Mode Questionnaire; the study administered an Italian translation whose wording is not
    published in the deposit.
- table: pierro_2018_locomotion_s4
  issue: |-
    The two reverse-worded items (locR6, locR9) are stored already reverse-recoded, so their
    shipped anchors are flipped: for these items resp=1 is 'Strongly Agree' and resp=6 is 'Strongly
    Disagree' with the printed statement. Note this differs from the sibling
    pierro_2018_locomotion_s3, where the same two items are stored raw. Item wording is the
    original English Regulatory Mode Questionnaire; the study administered an Italian translation
    whose wording is not published in the deposit. Only the two endpoints of the 6-point scale are
    labelled, following the paper's own description; resp 2-5 carry no option text.
- table: pierro_2018_tf_present_s4
  issue: |-
    Item text here is the Temporal Focus Scale's original ENGLISH wording (Shipp, Edwards & Lambert
    2009); the study was run on Italian students and neither the PLOS ONE article nor its SPSS
    deposit publishes the Italian form, so this is a same-instrument substitute rather than what
    respondents read. Separately, the assignment of the four sentences to the codes
    TFpresent1-TFpresent4 is inferred from the instrument's own item order and cannot be checked
    against the data: the subscale identity is solid (the composite reproduces the paper's
    published Present statistics, M 5.115/SD 1.001/alpha .854 against 5.12/1.00/.85, and its entire
    Table 4 correlation row to within .004), but the four items are same-range, same-polarity near-
    synonyms, so a permutation among them would be undetectable. Treat the subscale as reliable and
    an individual sentence's attachment to an individual code as provisional.
- table: qin_2025_cultural_identity
  issue: |-
    The 547 respondents were domestic Chinese tourists answering a Chinese-language questionnaire,
    but no Chinese wording is published in the article or either of its supplements, so the item
    text shown here is the authors' own English from S1 Table; the 1-6 response scale's anchors are
    never stated by the source, so the response options are left blank rather than guessed
- table: ribeiro_2019_academic_motivation
  issue: |-
    The English item and anchor wording for this table was translated by IRW from the study's
    Portuguese; the source publishes no English version of the scale. The seven response labels
    come from the deposit's SPSS value labels, which name every point. The paper's Annex prints
    only five labels across the seven points, with 'Moderada correspondencia' spanning 3-5 and
    'Pouca correspondencia' at 2 where the data file has 'Muito Pouca Correspondencia'.
- table: rogers_2021_financial_knowledge
  issue: |-
    The response values are right/wrong scores rather than the option each student chose, so the
    response options shown here are the data file's own 'Resposta incorreta'/'Resposta correta'
    labels; the questionnaire's three-to-five multiple-choice alternatives (including a 'Nao sei'
    option) are published in the deposit's FinalForm.pdf but cannot be attached to a 0/1
    correctness code, and the English translations beside the Portuguese wording were produced by
    IRW, not by the study's authors
- table: song_2025_cs
  issue: |-
    Respondents were Chinese hotel frontline employees and the questionnaire was back-translated
    into Chinese, but neither the paper nor its data deposit publishes the Chinese wording, so IRW
    ships the English the paper itself prints in its Table 3, with language recorded as Chinese.
    The study reports only that a five-point Likert scale was used and never prints the anchor
    labels, so response options carry no text
- table: song_2025_er
  issue: |-
    Item text for song_2025_er is the English the paper printed, not the Chinese respondents
    answered (the study was administered in China with back translation and no Chinese wording is
    published); and in the paper's Table 3 two of the five items appear as bare descriptors rather
    than full items -- ER2 reads 'Level of satisfaction with job' and ER3 'Experience: Advancement
    Opportunities', transcribed as printed.
- table: song_2025_pj
  issue: |-
    The source article's Table 3 prints the same sentence, "Are your department's procedures
    consistent with ethical standards?", against both PJ3 and PJ4, so only three of this scale's
    four items have published wording; IRW attributes that sentence to PJ3 and ships PJ4's
    item_text blank rather than repeating it. No response anchors are shipped: the study reports
    only that a five-point Likert scale was used and never prints the labels.
- table: song_2025_pwb
  issue: |-
    The item wording shipped for this table is the English printed in the source article; the
    questionnaire was administered in Chinese (back-translated) and the Chinese original is
    published nowhere in the paper or its supplement. No response-option labels are shipped because
    the study reports only that a five-point Likert scale was used.
- table: song_2025_sc
  issue: |-
    Item text for song_2025_sc is the English the source article printed, not the Chinese
    respondents answered (the study was administered in China with back translation and no Chinese
    wording is published anywhere in the paper or its supplement), and no response-option labels
    are shipped because the study reports only that a five-point Likert scale was used. Note a
    direction mismatch in the response data: SC1-SC5 are stored reverse-keyed relative to the
    positive wording shipped for them -- they correlate -0.34 to -0.53 with SC6 ('There is a true
    commitment to service...'), and -0.43 to -0.53 with the same respondents' positively worded
    procedural-justice items -- so for SC1-SC5 a higher resp means less agreement with the sentence
    in item_text, while SC6 runs the natural way
- table: song_2025_wwb
  issue: |-
    The item wording shipped for this table is the English printed in the source article; the
    questionnaire was administered in Chinese (back-translated) and the Chinese original is
    published nowhere in the paper or its supplement. No response-option labels are shipped because
    the study reports only that a five-point Likert scale was used.
- table: wang_2016_study1_authalien
  issue: |-
    Item text is shown in English: Wang (2016) administered a Chinese translation of the
    Authenticity Scale and no Chinese wording is published in the PLOS deposit (the SPSS file
    carries no variable or value labels), so Wood et al.'s (2008) original English for Self-
    Alienation items 2, 7, 10 and 12 ships instead. IMPORTANT: these four items are stored ALREADY
    REVERSE-SCORED in the IRW table, so the response anchors shipped here run the opposite way to
    the study's stated administration -- resp = 1 is the respondent's 'strongly agree' with the
    alienation statement and resp = 5 is 'strongly disagree'. That direction is established from
    the data (all four items correlate +0.33 to +0.61 with the study's self-esteem total, and the
    three authenticity tables sum to the paper's published total of 42.49, SD 6.18, alpha .81), not
    assumed. Which of the four canonical items each code authalien1-4 refers to is inferred from
    the standard subscale numbering and could not be checked against the data -- the block and its
    direction are verified, but a permutation within the four items would not be detectable.
- table: wang_2016_study1_authexternal
  issue: |-
    Wang (2016) administered a Chinese translation of the Authenticity Scale and no Chinese wording
    is published in the PLOS deposit (the SPSS file carries no variable or value labels), so Wood
    et al.'s (2008) original English for Accepting External Influence items 3, 4, 5 and 6 ships
    instead. IMPORTANT: these four items are stored ALREADY REVERSE-SCORED in the IRW table, so the
    response anchors shipped here run the opposite way to the study's stated administration -- resp
    = 1 is the respondent's 'strongly agree' with the external-influence statement and resp = 5 is
    'strongly disagree'. That direction is established from the data (all four items correlate
    +0.26 to +0.38 with the study's self-esteem total, where the raw subscale must correlate
    negatively, and the three authenticity tables sum to the paper's published total of 42.49, SD
    6.18, alpha .81, against alpha .45 for the flipped reading), not assumed. Which of the four
    canonical items each code authexternal1-4 refers to is inferred from the standard subscale
    numbering and could not be checked against the data -- the block and its direction are
    verified, but a permutation within the four items would not be detectable.
- table: wang_2026_veteran_expectations
  issue: |-
    Item and response wording for this table is shown in English. Wang and Zhang (2026) surveyed
    veterans in Guizhou Province, China, and never state the administered language, but the
    questionnaire cannot have been given in English; no Chinese wording appears anywhere in the
    article or its single deposited file, so the authors' own English questionnaire (the paper's
    Table 1) ships in its place. That table is published as an image, so the item text is a
    transcription read from the image rather than copied as text. Which item each code B1-B3 refers
    to is not in doubt: Table 1 prints the data's own code as a label on every item, and each live
    item's counts of responses 1-7 reproduce the identically-named deposit column exactly (B1
    0,6,53,120,169,165,111; B2 10,31,105,166,148,99,65; B3 9,35,95,170,168,107,40). One caveat
    about the response data rather than the wording: the paper analyses 525 respondents while the
    deposited file and this table hold 624, and the published Cronbach's alpha of 0.76 for these
    three items recomputes to 0.66 on the 624.
- table: yandun2026_attention
  issue: |-
    The item wording shipped for this table is the authors' own English translation, deposited as
    DATA_MATRIX_TRANSLATED.xlsx; the assessment itself was administered in Spanish in Ecuador and
    no Spanish wording was deposited. The 1-5 anchors are published only at the endpoints (1 =
    Never, 5 = Always), so options 2-4 carry no text.
- table: FACIT_YOUNT_2021_clinic10
  issue: |-
    The deposit publishes no question stem for this medical-conditions checklist, so the item
    text shown here is the data file's own variable labels (for example "Ever had condition -
    Anxiety") rather than the sentence respondents read; the instructions and block prompt are
    blank for the same reason. The wording was never deposited -- the SPSS labels, the codebook
    PDF and the data dictionary were all checked. Item codes and response coding are exact:
    source-to-live per-item by per-level counts match in all 36 cells.
- table: afaya_2020_complications_knowledge
  issue: |-
    Item wording and the Yes / No / Don’t know anchors are transcribed verbatim from the study's
    own deposited codebook (S1 Data), and the item codes are that file's own column headers, so
    the code-to-text mapping is tied at the source. Two caveats. The paper's Methods describes a
    23-item Michigan Diabetes Knowledge Test, but the deposited questionnaire is a 66-item
    battery in seven labelled blocks, of which these seven are the 'Knowledge of Complications'
    block -- so the instrument is the study's own questionnaire rather than the published
    DKT-23. And although every question has one correct answer, neither the paper nor the
    codebook says which, so correct_response is left blank rather than asserted by IRW. The
    questionnaire was administered in English or Dagbani depending on the participant; the
    English version ships here and the Dagbani form is not published in the deposit.
- table: afaya_2020_diet_knowledge
  issue: |-
    Item wording and the Yes / No / Don’t know anchors are transcribed verbatim from the study's
    own deposited codebook (S1 Data), and the item codes are that file's own column headers, so
    the code-to-text mapping is tied at the source; every one of the 39 item-by-level cell
    counts in the raw spreadsheet matches the live table exactly. Two caveats. The paper's
    Methods describes a 23-item Michigan Diabetes Knowledge Test, but the deposited
    questionnaire is a 66-item battery in seven labelled blocks, of which these thirteen are the
    'Knowledge on Diet' block, and their wording is the study's own rather than the published
    DKT-23 -- so the instrument named here is the study's questionnaire, not DKT-23. And
    although every question has one correct answer, neither the paper nor the codebook says
    which, so correct_response is left blank rather than asserted by IRW. The questionnaire was
    administered in English or Dagbani depending on the participant; the English version ships
    here and the Dagbani form is not published in the deposit.
- table: afaya_2020_exercise_knowledge
  issue: |-
    Item wording and the Yes / No / Don’t know anchors are transcribed verbatim from the study's
    own deposited codebook (S1 Data), and the item codes are that file's own data-sheet column
    headers, so the code-to-text mapping is tied at the source; the source columns' own response
    counts reproduce the live per-item means (1.27, 1.14, 2.17, 1.98) and n=330 exactly for all
    four items. Two caveats. The paper's Methods describes a 23-item Michigan Diabetes Knowledge
    Test, but the deposited questionnaire is a 66-item battery in seven labelled blocks, of
    which these four are the 'Knowledge of exercise' block -- so the instrument is named as the
    study's own questionnaire rather than the published DKT-23. And although the paper says
    every question has one correct answer, neither the paper nor the codebook says which, so
    correct_response is left blank rather than asserted by IRW. The questionnaire was
    administered in English or Dagbani depending on the participant; the English version ships
    here and the Dagbani form is not published in the deposit.
- table: afaya_2020_footcare_knowledge
  issue: |-
    Item wording and the Yes / No / Don’t know anchors are transcribed verbatim from the study's
    own deposited codebook (S1 Data), and the item codes are that file's own data-sheet column
    headers, so the code-to-text mapping is tied at the source. Three caveats. The paper's
    Methods describes a 23-item Michigan Diabetes Knowledge Test, and the deposited English
    questionnaire (S1 File) does contain that multiple-choice test -- but it is not what this
    table holds: these 14 items are the 'Knowledge of Foot Care' block of a separate 66-item
    Yes/No/Don’t-know battery that appears only in the deposit's codebook and data sheet, so the
    instrument is named as the study's own questionnaire rather than as the DKT-23. Two source
    defects are shipped as recorded rather than corrected: kf11_advice's text ends mid-word
    ('when they have ulce') and kf10_drytoes carries a double space. And although every question
    is said to have one correct answer, neither the paper nor the codebook says which, so
    correct_response is left blank rather than asserted by IRW. The questionnaire was
    administered in English or Dagbani; the English version ships here, and the deposited
    Dagbani questionnaire does not include this block.
- table: afaya_2020_general_knowledge
  issue: |-
    Item wording and the Yes / No / Don’t know anchors are transcribed verbatim from the study's
    own deposited codebook (S1 Data), and the item codes are that file's own data-sheet column
    headers, so the code-to-text mapping is tied at the source; all 33 item-by-level cell counts
    computed from the raw spreadsheet match the live table exactly (n=330 per item). Three
    caveats. The paper's Methods describes a 23-item Michigan Diabetes Knowledge Test, and the
    deposited English questionnaire does contain that multiple-choice test -- but it is not what
    this table holds: these eleven items are the 'Basic general knowledge on diabetes' block of
    a separate 66-item Yes/No/Don’t-know battery that appears only in the deposit's codebook and
    data sheet, so the instrument is named as the study's own questionnaire rather than as the
    DKT-23. Although every question is said to have one correct answer, neither the paper nor
    the codebook says which, so correct_response is left blank rather than asserted by IRW. And
    the source's own typography is shipped unnormalised (inconsistent terminal full stops, mid-
    sentence capitals in 'Obesity' and 'Increases'). The questionnaire was administered in
    English or Dagbani depending on the participant; the English version ships here, and the
    deposited Dagbani questionnaire does not include this block.
- table: afaya_2020_medication_knowledge
  issue: |-
    Item wording and the Yes / No / Don’t know anchors are transcribed verbatim from the study's
    own deposited codebook (S1 Data), and the item codes are that file's own data-sheet column
    headers, so the code-to-text mapping is tied at the source; all 30 item-by-level cell counts
    in the raw spreadsheet match the live table exactly (n=330 per item). Three caveats. These
    ten items are the 'Knowledge of medication' block -- medication knowledge, not medication
    adherence: the same study's Morisky adherence scale is a separate instrument and is not part
    of this table. The paper's Methods describes a 23-item Michigan Diabetes Knowledge Test, and
    the deposited English questionnaire does contain that multiple-choice test, but it is not
    what this table holds; these items belong to a separate 66-item Yes/No/Don’t-know battery
    that appears only in the deposit's codebook and data sheet, so the instrument is named as
    the study's own questionnaire rather than as the DKT-23. And although the paper says every
    question has one correct answer, neither the paper nor the codebook says which -- and two
    items are self-report questions with no correct answer at all -- so correct_response is left
    blank rather than asserted by IRW. The questionnaire was administered in English or Dagbani;
    the English version ships here, and the deposited Dagbani questionnaire does not include
    this block.
- table: afaya_2020_monitoring_knowledge
  issue: |-
    The item wording for this table comes from the study's own deposited codebook (S1 Data). The
    paper's Methods describes the knowledge measure as the 23-item Michigan Diabetes Knowledge
    Test, but the deposit actually administers 66 knowledge items in seven blocks, of which this
    table is the seven-item self blood glucose monitoring block; the shipped instrument name
    reflects the deposit rather than the paper's description. The instrument was administered in
    English or Dagbani and the shipped wording is the English
- table: busch_2022_course_exacerbate
  issue: |-
    This battery is a select-all-that-apply checklist, so `resp` is a checkbox state rather than
    a chosen response option, and the `option_text` values 'Selected' and 'Not selected'
    describe that 0/1 coding rather than transcribing anything the survey printed -- the source
    publishes no response labels for it, only the stem 'Please select all aspects of ONLINE
    college science courses that might make your feelings of depression worse.' Item text and
    instructions are verbatim from the study's own S1 Appendix survey copy.
- table: covid_travel_mackenzie_2021
  issue: |-
    The resp values 0-5 carry two different scales in this table: 48 behaviour-frequency items
    run Never=0 to Everyday=5, while 26 attitude items run Strongly disagree=0 to Strongly
    agree=5, so resp should be read against each item's own option_text rather than pooled
    across items
- table: goldberg_2018_bri_bri
  issue: |-
    The response-option wording shipped here is the scale definition printed on page 1 of the
    questionnaire. The running header on the later pages abbreviates the top two anchors
    differently -- "THREE to 15 times in the past year" and "15 or MORE times in the past year"
    -- which places exactly 15 occurrences in category 5, whereas the page-1 wording places it
    in category 4. The SPSS value labels agree with the abbreviated header. The page-1
    definitional wording was shipped; the boundary case of exactly 15 times is ambiguous in the
    source form itself.
- table: goldberg_2018_bri_feel
  issue: |-
    The four positively worded items (feel5, feel10, feel14, feel17) are stored as administered
    and are NOT reverse-scored: their means are 3.95-4.32 while every other item averages
    1.09-2.46, so a depression total must reverse them first.
- table: goldberg_2018_bri_food
  issue: |-
    In this table resp=5 is 'Not Applicable' - the questionnaire's explicit escape for items
    that do not apply (e.g. 'take the skin off chicken' for a non-chicken-eater) - so the scale
    is ordinal only over 1-4 (Usually or Always to Rarely or Never) and 5 should be treated as a
    separate category rather than the low end. It is used at 0.1-11.1% per item.
- table: goldberg_2018_bri_ofood
  issue: |-
    This table pools two response scales under one resp column: items ofood1-ofood18 (page 14 of
    the form) are anchored 1 = 'Never or less than once a MONTH' to 5 = '5 times a WEEK or
    more', while ofood19-ofood29 (page 15) are anchored 1 = 'Never or less than once a WEEK' to
    5 = 'About once a DAY or more'. The codes 1-5 are ordinal within each block but are not on a
    common frequency metric across the two, so resp values must not be compared or summed across
    the ofood1-18 and ofood19-29 blocks without rescaling. The shipped option_text gives the
    correct anchor per item.
- table: goldberg_2018_sbo
  issue: |-
    resp=3 on this table is the form's middle box, which is printed as '?' rather than a number
    and is labelled 'Neither agree nor disagree: neutral, uncertain, or don't understand the
    statement' -- so a 3 combines genuine neutrality with uncertainty and non-comprehension, and
    is not purely a scale midpoint
- table: iwasa_2016_padua_inventory
  issue: |-
    This study administered a Japanese translation of the Padua Inventory. The item and option
    wording shown here is the English original, not the Japanese text respondents actually saw:
    the source paper and its supplements do not reproduce the administered Japanese wording.
- table: mede_2025_goals_priority

  issue: |-
    Item text is the TISP English core questionnaire; most respondents (68 countries, 37

  issue: |-

- table: mede_2025_trust_scientists
  issue: |-
    Item text is the TISP English core questionnaire; most respondents (68 countries, 37
    languages) answered a local translation, which is published per sample in the OSF deposit
    (05_survey-materials/questionnaire/countries/) but is not reproduced here
- table: mede_2025_willvul
  issue: |-
    Item text is the English core questionnaire; the TISP survey was administered in 37
    languages across 68 countries, so most respondents read a translation published per sample
    in the OSF deposit rather than the wording shown here.
- table: mekheimer_2026_flp
  issue: |-
    The instrument offers five anchors (Beginner through Expert), but no respondent selected
    Beginner, so the live response set runs 2-5 and only four option rows ship for each item.
    The Beginner anchor is absent from this item table by design rather than by omission.
- table: offlinefriend_ofaq
  issue: |-
    Item text is transcribed verbatim from the questionnaire as administered (the study's own
    OSF file), not from the companion scale document, because the administered form is what
    respondents read. The two disagree on three items, and the administered wording ships
    unchanged in each case including its typographical errors: item 18 reads "Arguments with
    arisen with others..." where the scale document and the paper print "have arisen"; item 33
    lacks the scale document's repeated "regularly"; item 35 reads "I had a strong craving"
    where the others print "I have". Separately, the postprint's Table 1 appears to misprint
    item 37's mean as 2.82, a repeat of item 35's printed value; the observed mean is 2.276,
    while its printed SD of 1.12 does reproduce (1.123).
- table: opladen2025_fkg
  issue: |-
    The English in this table's item_text_translated column is the OSF deposit's own short
    content gloss for each item (e.g. 'joint pain as a sign of paralysis'), not a sentence-level
    translation; the German item_text is the wording respondents actually read. The deposit
    publishes only the abbreviation FKG, so the instrument name shipped here (Fragebogen zu
    Koerper und Gesundheit, Hiller et al. 1997) is an attribution from item content rather than
    a statement by the study, and the 20 items are a selection from that 53-item questionnaire
- table: opladen2025_fks
  issue: |-
    The English in item_text_translated is the deposit's own short content gloss per item (e.g.
    'body-related comparison'), not a sentence-level translation of the administered German,
    which is what item_text holds
- table: preschool_sel_emt
  issue: |-
    For the twelve Part 1 items and emta3_1s_t1 the item text is the study's SPSS variable
    label, which SPSS truncated at 255 characters, so those prompts end mid-sentence; the child-
    facing question in Part 1 is 'Show me which one of these feels the same as this one'. Item
    text is the interviewer's administration script, including instructions to point at the
    stimulus, rather than a cleaned item stem.
- table: ramadan_2026_ai_awareness
  issue: |-
    Item wording for this table is the administered Arabic with the depositor's own English
    alongside it, but the 1-5 response anchors are shipped in English only (strongly disagree
    ... strongly agree): the Mendeley deposit publishes the scale labels solely as an English
    coding string and never gives the Arabic anchors respondents actually read
- table: ramadan_2026_applied_practice
  issue: |-
    The Arabic wording of the five response anchors is not published in the deposit, so
    option_text carries the codebook's English anchors (5 = strongly agree to 1 = strongly
    disagree) while the item wording is the administered Arabic.
- table: ramadan_2026_attitudes
  issue: |-
    The item wording ships in the administered Arabic with the authors' own English alongside,
    but the five response anchors ship only in English: the deposit states the 1-5 coding in
    English in its codebook and never prints the Arabic anchors respondents read.
- table: ramadan_2026_perceived_competence
  issue: |-
    Item wording for this table is the administered Arabic with the depositor's own English
    alongside it, but the 1-5 response anchors are shipped in English only (strongly disagree
    ... strongly agree): the Mendeley deposit publishes the scale labels solely as an English
    coding string in its codebook and never gives the Arabic anchors respondents actually read
- table: skalka2025_ai_literacy
  issue: |-
    resp 0 in this table is a no-answer code rather than a scale point -- the deposit documents
    only a 5-point 1-5 agreement scale, 0 occurs in just the 19 IM/S/C/BI items and is
    concentrated in students reporting no AI coursework, so it ships with blank option_text and
    should be treated as missing, not as a value below 'strongly disagree'
- table: wesselmann_2018_social_support
  issue: |-
    The response anchor for 1 is shipped as 'Strongly Disagree' although the authors' own
    codebook prints it as 'Strongly Agree' -- a misprint that duplicates the anchor for 5,
    corrected against the paper's '1-Strongly Disagree, 5-Strongly Agree' and the published DRRI
    scale page; item wording is the deposited SPSS file's own variable labels, shipped as
    administered
- table: wolf_2017_study2_video_liking
  issue: |-
    Despite the table name, this 6-item scale is not described, named or reported anywhere in
    the published paper -- it exists only in the study's Study 2 data deposit, whose SPSS
    variable labels are the sole source of the wording, and it mixes liking ('I liked the
    video') with calm, happiness and satisfaction; three items (like2, like4, like6) are
    negatively worded and are stored RAW, so they must be reverse-scored before a liking score
    is computed (doing so reproduces the deposit's own video_like composite exactly).
- table: wooly_hartman2022
  issue: |-
    The responses here are right/wrong scores rather than the alternative each person chose. On
    the four TV-show items (Q4, Q6, Q8, Q75) the source gives 'I Don't Know' no code, so those
    responses are absent rather than scored 0 -- only 1023-1286 of the 1561 respondents carry a
    score on those items -- whereas on the 15 song items 'I Don't Know' is scored incorrect
- table: yang_2025_intercultural_contact
  issue: |-
    The item wording, instructions and response anchors are transcribed verbatim from the
    study's own questionnaire (S1 File of the CC BY article), including its typos -- item FICA5
    reads 'lving in a homestay familiy abroad' as printed. Two things are worth knowing. First,
    the anchors shipped here are Never / Rarely / Sometimes / Often / Always, which is what the
    questionnaire prints above every item of this scale and what its instruction to answer
    'based on the frequencies of your engaging in' implies; the paper's Methods section instead
    describes Sections II and III as running '1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree)',
    which matches neither section's printed anchors, so a reader comparing the two will find a
    discrepancy the questionnaire settles. Second, the workbook's column headers are bare codes
    (FSM1, FICA1, ...) and the questionnaire numbers its lines under the block headings 'Foreign
    Social Media (FSM)' and 'Foreign Intercultural Communication Activity (FICA)', so the block
    each item belongs to is certain but the order of the three FSM texts among themselves, and
    of the six FICA texts among themselves, follows that printed numbering and could not be
    checked against the data: the paper reports no per-item statistics and the nine item means
    span only 2.88 to 3.22. What was checked: all 45 item-by-response-level counts in the
    deposited workbook match the live table exactly, so no code was permuted in processing and
    the 1-5 integers are the source's own.
- table: chile_2023_children-adolescents-survey_aa
  issue: |-
    The English in the _translated columns of this table was produced by IRW, not by the study: EANNA 2023 published its questionnaire only in Spanish, and the Spanish in the base fields is what respondents actually heard. Note also that ten of the 38 items (a8_78, a8_87, a8_88, a8_99, a9_78, a9_87, a9_88, a9_99, a11_88, a11_99) are the 'nobody', 'not applicable', 'don't know' and 'no answer' checkboxes of three multiple-select questions rather than substantive items
- table: christensen_2018_wsssf_2171
  issue: |-
    resp is the SCORED value, not the literal answer: 1 always means the schizotypy-keyed response, and option_text records which literal True/False answer that was for each item, because the keying direction differs item by item (e.g. resp=1 is 'True' for pb01 but 'False' for py01). Item codes mi/pb/py/sa do not encode item content.
- table: dwyer_2019_clinton_activist
  issue: |-
    Respondents answered the Activist Identity and Commitment Scale on a 0-to-5 scale, but IRW stores the SPSS codes 1-6, so each resp value is one higher than the number on the scale the respondent saw; option_text gives the anchor wording for the corresponding point.
- table: kermen_2022_self_efficacy
  issue: |-
    The 11 reverse-scored items of this scale are stored already reversed, so the response anchors shipped for them run in the opposite direction to the other six: for b2, b4, b5, b6, b7, b10, b11, b12, b14, b16 and b17 a stored resp of 1 is the administered answer 'cok iyi' (very well) and 5 is 'hic' (not at all). The English item text was translated by IRW from the published Turkish form; only the two scale endpoints were labelled in the source, so resp 2-4 carry no option text
- table: kumlander_2018_scs
  issue: |-
    English for the three middle response anchors (resp 2, 3 and 4) was rendered by IRW from the Finnish; the study published English only for the two endpoints, and the Finnish in option_text is what respondents actually read.
- table: milavic_2019_psisysf
  issue: |-
    Item wording for this table is English while the instrument was administered in Croatian: the study's data deposit and its single supplementary file carry no Croatian text, so the English printed in the paper's Table 1 is shipped in its place, and the anchors in option_text (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree) are taken from that table's footnote even though the same paper's Methods section instead describes the scale as running from 1 = almost never to 5 = almost always
- table: rdatasets_gssabortion
  issue: |-
    Item text comes from the published original instrument rather than this study's own materials
- table: risticdedic_2025_dhq_currentstate
  issue: |-
    The DHQ was administered in ten languages across nine EU countries (Croatian, Dutch, Finnish, German, English, Catalan, Slovenian, French, Greek and Spanish); the item text shipped here is the English master version, which 87 of the 834 schools answered directly and from which the other nine versions were translated. All ten language versions are published by the authors at doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.13767190. The 0-100 slider is labelled only at its endpoints, so option_text is populated for resp=0 and resp=100 only.
- table: risticdedic_2025_dhq_expectation
  issue: |-
    The DHQ was administered in ten languages across nine EU countries (Croatian, Dutch, Finnish, German, English, Catalan, Slovenian, French, Greek and Spanish); the item text shipped here is the English master version, which 87 of the 834 schools answered directly and from which the other nine versions were translated. All ten language versions are published by the authors at doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.13767190. The 0-100 slider is labelled only at its endpoints, so option_text is populated for resp=0 and resp=100 only.
- table: risticdedic_2025_dhq_importance
  issue: |-
    The DHQ was administered in ten languages across nine EU countries (Croatian, Dutch, Finnish, German, English, Catalan, Slovenian, French, Greek and Spanish); the item text shipped here is the English master version, which 87 of the 834 schools answered directly and from which the other nine versions were translated. All ten language versions are published by the authors at doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.13767190. The 0-100 slider is labelled only at its endpoints, so option_text is populated for resp=0 and resp=100 only
- table: spain_2025_ageism_agreement
  issue: |-
    The English item, instruction and response-option wording for this table was produced by IRW, not by CIS, which publishes Estudio 3493 in Spanish only; the administered Spanish is in the base fields. Note also that the response values run 1, 2, 4, 5 with no option row for 3: respondents could volunteer a middle 'Regular (ni de acuerdo ni en desacuerdo)' answer (CIS code 3, not read aloud) which the IRW processing script drops to missing along with 8 'N.S.' and 9 'N.C.'.
- table: spain_2025_ageism_bureaucracy
  issue: |-
    The English item, instruction and response-option wording for this table was produced by IRW, not by CIS, which publishes Estudio 3493 in Spanish only; the administered Spanish is in the base fields. Two things to know about the responses: the P.11 block was asked only of respondents aged 65 and over (1,030 of the study's 5,006 interviews), and the scale runs from 1 'En muchas ocasiones' (most frequent) to 4 'Nunca', with the not-read-aloud category 6 'No he realizado nunca esta gestion' plus 'N.S.'/'N.C.' dropped to missing by the IRW processing script, so those have no option row.
- table: spain_2025_ageism_comparison
  issue: |-
    The English item and response-option wording for this table was produced by IRW, not by CIS, which publishes Estudio 3493 in Spanish only; the administered Spanish is in the base columns. Note also that each of the three questions allowed a volunteered, not-read-aloud 'both equally' answer (CIS code 3, worded differently in each question) which the IRW processing script drops to missing along with 8 'N.S.' and 9 'N.C.', so the live scale is the two read-aloud categories only and no option row exists for those codes.
- table: spain_2025_ageism_difficulty
  issue: |-
    The English item, instruction and response-option wording for this table was produced by IRW, not by CIS, which publishes Estudio 3493 in Spanish only; the administered Spanish is in the base fields. Note also that P.12 was asked only of respondents aged 65 and over (the questionnaire routes anyone under 65 past the block), and that the response values run 1, 2, 4, 5 with no option row for 3 or 6: respondents could volunteer a middle 'Regular (ni facil ni dificil)' answer (CIS code 3) or 'nunca ha necesitado realizar esta gestion' (code 6), neither of which the interviewer read aloud, and the IRW processing script drops both to missing along with 8 'N.S.' and 9 'N.C.'.
- table: spain_2025_ageism_elderpriority
  issue: |-
    The English item, instruction and response-option wording for this table was produced by IRW, not by CIS, which publishes Estudio 3493 in Spanish only; the administered Spanish is in the base fields. Note also that the 0-10 priority scale was labelled at its two ends only -- 0 'Ninguna prioridad' and 10 'Maxima prioridad' -- so values 1 to 9 carry no option text because the study printed none, and 'N.S.'/'N.C.' (CIS codes 98 and 99) are dropped to missing by the IRW processing script.
- table: spain_2025_ageism_elderslights
  issue: |-
    The English item, instruction and response-option wording for this table was produced by IRW, not by CIS, which publishes Estudio 3493 in Spanish only; the administered Spanish is in the base fields. Two things to know about the responses: the P.13 block was asked only of respondents aged 65 and over (1,030 of the study's 5,006 interviews), and the fourth response category was coded 7 'Ninguna vez' by CIS and recoded to 4 by the IRW processing script to give a contiguous 1-4 scale, so resp runs from 1 'Muchas veces' (most frequent) to 4 'Ninguna vez' (never).
- table: spain_2025_ageism_problems
  issue: |-
    The English item and response-option wording for this table was produced by IRW, not by CIS, which publishes Estudio 3493 in Spanish only; the administered Spanish is in the base columns. Two things to know about the responses: the scale runs from 1 'Muchos problemas' (most problems) to 5 'Ningun problema' (none), so a higher value means fewer perceived problems; and the values 1, 2, 4, 5 are non-contiguous because respondents could volunteer a middle 'Ni muchos ni pocos' answer (CIS code 3) that the interviewer did not read aloud, which the IRW processing script drops to missing along with 'N.S.' and 'N.C.', so no option row exists for it. Note also that p2's administered wording is elliptical -- the interviewer asked only 'And young people under 35?' immediately after p1, so p2's response frame is the one stated in p1's question.
- table: spain_2025_ageism_youthpriority
  issue: |-
    The English item, instruction and response-option wording for this table was produced by IRW, not by CIS, which publishes Estudio 3493 in Spanish only; the administered Spanish is in the base fields. Note also that the 0-10 priority scale was labelled at its two ends only -- 0 'Ninguna prioridad' and 10 'Maxima prioridad' -- so values 1 to 9 carry no option text because the study printed none, and 'N.S.'/'N.C.' (CIS codes 98 and 99) are dropped to missing by the IRW processing script.
- table: spain_2025_ageism_youthslights
  issue: |-
    The English item, instruction and response-option wording for this table was produced by IRW, not by CIS, which publishes Estudio 3493 in Spanish only; the administered Spanish is in the base fields, and item 1's diminutives 'nino/a' and 'nene/a' have no exact English equivalent. Two things to know about the responses: the P.16 block was asked only of respondents aged 18 to 34 (975 of the study's 5,006 interviews), and the resp scale is deliberately non-contiguous -- CIS coded the volunteered '(NO LEER) Regular' category 3 and the IRW processing script drops it, while recoding CIS's 'Ninguna vez' from 7 to 5, so resp runs 1 'Muchas veces' (most frequent), 2 'Bastantes veces', 4 'Pocas veces', 5 'Ninguna vez' (never) with no value 3.
- table: spain_2025_democracy_efficacy
  issue: |-
    The English item, instruction and response-option wording for this table was produced by IRW, not by CIS, which publishes this questionnaire only in Spanish; the administered Spanish is in the base fields. Note also that respondents could volunteer a middle 'Ni de acuerdo ni en desacuerdo' answer (CIS code 3, not read aloud, chosen by 0.1-0.7% of the sample) which the IRW processing script treats as missing, so the response values run 1, 2, 4, 5 with no option row for 3.
- table: spain_2025_democracy_internal
  issue: |-
    The item and response wording for this CIS survey question is in Spanish, as administered; the English in the _translated columns was produced by IRW, not by CIS.
- table: spain_2025_democracy_judiciary
  issue: |-
    The response scale respondents heard was 1 Muy de acuerdo / 2 De acuerdo / 4 En desacuerdo / 5 Muy en desacuerdo, with a fifth, not-read-aloud category 3 'Ni de acuerdo ni en desacuerdo' plus 8 'N.S.' and 9 'N.C.' that the IRW processing script drops to missing, which is why resp jumps from 2 to 4 and no option row exists for 3; the English in the _translated columns was produced by IRW, not by CIS.
- table: spain_2025_democracy_media
  issue: |-
    The response scale respondents heard was 1 Muy de acuerdo / 2 De acuerdo / 4 En desacuerdo / 5 Muy en desacuerdo, with a fifth, not-read-aloud category 3 'Ni de acuerdo ni en desacuerdo' plus 8 'N.S.' and 9 'N.C.' that the IRW processing script drops to missing, which is why resp jumps from 2 to 4 and no option row exists for 3; the English in the _translated columns was produced by IRW, not by CIS, which publishes this questionnaire in Spanish only.
- table: spain_2025_democracy_parties
  issue: |-
    The English item, instruction and response-option wording for this table was produced by IRW, not by CIS, which publishes Estudio 3497 in Spanish only; the administered Spanish is in the base fields. Note also that the response values run 1, 2, 4, 5 with no option row for 3: respondents could volunteer a middle 'Ni de acuerdo ni en desacuerdo' answer (CIS code 3, not read aloud) which the IRW processing script drops to missing along with 8 'N.S.' and 9 'N.C.'.
- table: spain_2025_democracy_priorities
  issue: |-
    The item, instruction and response-option wording in the _translated columns is IRW's own English; CIS publishes this questionnaire only in Spanish, and the administered Spanish is in the base fields.
- table: spain_2025_democracy_system
  issue: |-
    The English item, option and question text for this table was machine-translated by IRW from the Spanish that CIS actually administered in Estudio 3497; the administered Spanish is the authoritative text and sits in the base columns.
- table: spain_2025_democracy_trust
  issue: |-
    Respondents answered on an 0-10 trust scale on which only the endpoints were labelled ('Ninguna confianza' at 0, 'Total confianza' at 10), so option_text is deliberately blank for resp 1-9 rather than repeating the numeral; the codes 98 'N.S.' and 99 'N.C.' are dropped to missing by the IRW processing script and have no option row; and the English in the _translated columns was produced by IRW, not by CIS, which publishes this questionnaire in Spanish only.
- table: trivia_fastrich_2017
  issue: |-
    Five of the 244 trivia questions were reworded part way through data collection, so the item text IRW ships is the later of two administered wordings: item 135 and 234 read 'poisonous' rather than 'venomous' for the first 387 and 266 responses, item 167 read 'what county' for its first 370, item 224 read 'gas marks' for its first 330, and item 267's 'Hippolyte Mege-Mouries' appeared for 322 responses with its accented characters corrupted; both wordings of each are visible in the response table's own cov_question column.
- table: christensen_2018_wsssf_5831
  issue: |-
    option_text is item-dependent for this table, because it stores keyed scores rather than raw answers: resp=1 reads 'True' on the 42 items the study does not mark reversed and 'False' on the 18 it does, all items having been scored so that a higher score means more schizotypy. The endorsement rates confirm it (the reverse-keyed items are ordinary pleasant experiences and run 0.036-0.276, not the ~0.9 a raw true/false coding would give). The authors' ' (reversed)' annotation was stripped from item_text as scoring notation rather than administered wording, and no instruction text is published anywhere in the deposit or article, so instructions is empty.
- table: schmidt_2017_fas
  issue: |-
    The item and response text is the German the study administered, taken from the
    deposited SPSS file's own variable and value labels (including a lowercase first letter
    on the bedroom item and a missing question mark on the holidays item); no printed
    questionnaire is published, so these labels are the only record of the wording. It is
    the study's own German rendering of the HBSC Family Affluence Scale II, not text from
    the HBSC protocol. The English in the `_translated` columns was produced by IRW, not by
    the study's authors.
- table: shin2024_creactability_adaptability
  issue: |-
    The scale was administered in Korean (coaches rating their players), but no Korean
    wording is published, so the item and response text is the English rendering printed in
    the authors' article rather than what raters read. The article lists the three
    adaptability items without numbers, so which wording belongs to Adaptability1-3 follows
    the order listed; the data confirm that order matches the paper's item numbering but
    cannot confirm it for the wording itself.
- table: shin2024_creactability_creativity
  issue: |-
    The scale was administered in Korean (coaches rating their players), but no Korean
    wording is published, so the item and response text is the English rendering printed in
    the authors' article rather than what raters read. The article lists the three
    creativity items without numbers, so which wording belongs to Creativity1-3 follows the
    order listed; the data confirm that order matches the paper's item numbering but cannot
    confirm it for the wording itself. The 'not at all' label for response 1 is absent
    because no rating used it.
- table: shin2024_creactability_quickness
  issue: |-
    The scale was administered in Korean (coaches rating their players), but no Korean
    wording is published, so the item and response text is the English rendering printed in
    the authors' article rather than what raters read. The article lists the three
    quickness items without numbers, so which wording belongs to Quickness1-3 follows the
    order listed; the data confirm that order matches the paper's item numbering but cannot
    confirm it for the wording itself.
- table: wesselmann_2018_drri
  issue: |-
    The five response labels come from the published DRRI-2 form rather than from the
    study, because the deposited SPSS file carries no value labels and the authors' own
    codebook misprints the anchor for 1 as 'Strongly Agree' (it is 'Strongly disagree', as
    the paper states). Item wording is the deposited file's own variable labels, shipped as
    administered; it differs from the DRRI-2 form only in omitting the form's shared
    'During deployment...' stem and the final period on drri2.
- table: chile_2023_children-adolescents-survey_cp_a
  issue: |-
    The English in the _translated columns of this table was produced by IRW, not by the study: EANNA 2023 published its questionnaire only in Spanish, and the Spanish in the base fields is what respondents heard. Note also that these are household-level questions but the table has one row per selected child's caregiver, so the 17,659 ids come from 13,867 households and the answers of 3,792 ids repeat another id's household exactly
- table: chile_2023_children-adolescents-survey_cp_c
  issue: |-
    The English in the _translated columns was produced by IRW, not by the study: EANNA 2023 published this questionnaire only in Spanish. Two defects in the response data itself: in cp9_1-cp9_4 the value 89.5 is the survey's 'don't know' code (entered as 88:88, converted to hours), not a number of hours, and should be treated as missing; and in cp2_1-cp2_9 (reasons for starting work) 3,493 of 8,793 caregivers have all nine reasons marked, a pattern already present in the source deposit that looks like a coding fault, so those nine items should not be analysed as recorded
- table: chile_2023_children-adolescents-survey_g
  issue: |-
    The English in the _translated columns of this table was produced by IRW, not by the study: EANNA 2023 published its questionnaire only in Spanish, and the Spanish in the base fields is what respondents read. The eight items are the bullying sub-scale of the Escala de Clima Social Escolar (ECLIS; Aron, Milicic & Armijo, 2012), stored raw as 1=Nunca to 4=Siempre with no reverse-scoring applied (g1_3 is positively worded)
- table: chile_2023_children-adolescents-survey_n
  issue: |-
    The English in the _translated columns of this table was produced by IRW, not by the study: EANNA 2023 published its questionnaire only in Spanish, and the Spanish in the base fields is what the children (aged 5-8) heard from the interviewer. Response codes run in different directions across items (n5 1=Mal to 3=Bien, but n6 1=Mucho to 3=Nada and n9 1=Muy contento to 3=Nada contento), n10 is a nominal who-does-the-housework item, and n7_*/n8_* are 0/1 dummies of a multiple-select question that include non-substantive alternatives (A nadie, No aplica, No sabe, No responde)
- table: imos_1984
  issue: |-
    The six problems of the 1984 International Mathematical Olympiad, each marked 0-7. The mathematical notation is rendered in plain text (superscripts as ^, the fraction and floor brackets of problem 5 written inline), so use the official paper if you need the exact typeset statement.
- table: mboya_2020_gds15
  issue: |-
    Responses are stored pre-scored (1 = the depressive answer), so for the five positively worded items (satisfy0, spirt0, hapy0, alive0, energy0) resp 1 means the respondent answered 'no'; the source data file does not label those five items' values, and this direction was established from the data. The item wording is the English of the study's data file; the language the interviews were conducted in is not stated in any accessible source.
- table: hyatt_2023_aggression_aeq
  issue: |-
    This table pools the whole development of the Aggression Expectancy Questionnaire: prelim1_*, prelim2_* and s1_* are the 84-, 40- and 31-item development pools under each study's own item numbering (only 66 and 27 of the first two pools are in the deposited data), and aeq01-aeq16 are the final form answered in Studies 2 and 3; the five prelim1 items ending _r are stored reverse-scored, so their option_text runs from 'Very likely' at 1 to 'Very unlikely' at 5; and the paper's Tables 2-3 list aeq09-aeq16 in a different order (and with 'The other person will really suffer' for aeq13) than the final instrument and the Study 3 data file, which this table follows
- table: hyatt_2023_aggression_s3_acme
  issue: |-
    The 22 items whose codes end in 'r' (e.g. acme_2dr, acme_12rr, acme_31cr) are stored already reverse-scored, so for them resp 1 = Strongly agree and 5 = Strongly disagree, the opposite of the source file's value labels; the option_text shipped here follows the stored direction, and higher resp means more empathy on every item
- table: moon_2023_korean_proficiency
  issue: |-
    Item text is the study's English questionnaire; most respondents (e.g. 159 of 206 Vietnamese nationals) answered Korean, Vietnamese, Chinese or Filipino versions that were not published, and the paper's text describes the scale as '1 = not at all to 4 = very good' whereas the questionnaire and data file use five points from 1 = Never to 5 = Very good.
- table: milson_2026_self_esteem
  issue: |-
    Item text is the canonical English Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale; the study's deposit carries no item wording or labels, so the assignment of Rosenburg_esteem_1..10 to items follows the commonly circulated RSES numbering (not the different order printed on the University of Maryland sheet), which the data support by keying structure and marker items but do not pin item-by-item. Responses are stored already reverse-scored (higher = higher self-esteem), so the anchors shown for items 2, 5, 6, 8 and 9 run from Strongly Agree (1) to Strongly Disagree (4).
- table: temesgen_2025_elephant_conserv_attitude
  issue: |-
    Respondents were interviewed in Tigrinya from a questionnaire the authors wrote in English, and no Tigrinya wording was published, so the item text is the authors' English
)---")

issues <- issues[order(vapply(issues, \(x) x$table, character(1)))]
```

## Known issues

The below are known issues affecting the match between item text and the IRW
tables. `r length(issues)` tables are listed. Start typing to search across
table names and issue descriptions.

```{=html}
<input type="text" id="issueSearch" placeholder="Search known issues..." oninput="filterIssues()" style="width: 100%; padding: 10px; margin-bottom: 10px; font-size: 16px;">
<p id="issue-count" style="color: #888; margin-bottom: 20px;"></p>

<style>
#issues-table table { width: 100%; table-layout: fixed; }
#issues-table th, #issues-table td { vertical-align: top; padding: 8px; }
#issues-table th:nth-child(1), #issues-table td:nth-child(1) { width: 28%; word-break: break-word; }
#issues-table th:nth-child(2), #issues-table td:nth-child(2) { width: 72%; }
</style>

<script>
function filterIssues() {
  const filter = document.getElementById('issueSearch').value.toLowerCase().trim();
  const rows = document.querySelectorAll('#issues-table tbody tr');
  let shown = 0;
  rows.forEach(r => {
    const hit = filter === '' || (r.textContent || '').toLowerCase().includes(filter);
    r.style.display = hit ? '' : 'none';
    if (hit) shown++;
  });
  const count = document.getElementById('issue-count');
  count.textContent = filter === '' ? '' :
    shown + (shown === 1 ? ' table matches "' : ' tables match "') + filter + '"';
}
</script>
```

::: {#issues-table}

```{r}
#| label: issues-table
#| results: asis

cat("| Dataset | Issue |\n", "|---|---|\n", sep = "")
cat(sprintf("| `%s` | %s |", vapply(issues, \(x) x$table, character(1)),
            vapply(issues, \(x) gsub("\n", " ", x$issue), character(1))),
    sep = "\n")
cat("\n")
```
